items.title: Balancing Speech, Language and Hearing Science with Machine Learning Modeling in the Age of AI: “Know your Problem, Data, and Solution”
items.authors: John H. L. Hansen
items.abstract: The talk connects speech, language and hearing science with machine-learning modeling in the age of AI. It reviews how problem formulation, data, and solution design must stay coupled, contrasts earlier speech modeling with more recent innovations used in today's systems, and offers guidance for researchers entering the field. The take-home theme is: know your problem, know your data, and know your solution. Hansen's research has shaped speech recognition, speaker recognition and robust speech processing in noisy, stressed or emotional conditions, spanning speech production, speaker models, telecommunications, security/privacy, and assistive speech and hearing technologies.

items.title: English Vowel Perceptual Training under Multitalker Babble: A Comparison of Humans and Large Language Models
items.authors: Wenwei Dong(Radboud University); Alif Silpachai(Radboud University); Catia Cucchiarini(Radboud University); Helmer Strik(Radboud University)
items.abstract: Perceptual training with multitalker babble might benefit second language (L2) listeners. However, conducting perception experiments with L2 listeners to determine the optimal number of talkers is complex and time-consuming. Neural models are inspired by the function of the human brain and could potentially serve as an alternative. A previous study examined how babble produced by 2 and 6 talkers affected the perceptual learning of L2 listeners and compared human results with Wav2Vec2.0. In this study, we extend this work by exploring multilingual models (the Whisper model and a speech large language model [LLM]: Qwen2.5-Omni-7B) and by evaluating how closely their performance aligns with that of L2 listeners. Our results show that the speech LLM not only improves accuracy through babble training, but also exhibits trends more similar to those of L2 listeners, and it achieves closer accuracy to L2 listeners under speech-shaped noise conditions than the Whisper and Wav2Vec2.0 models.

items.title: How Speaker Normalization Procedures Influence the Computational Modelling of Non-native Vowel Perception: Implications for the L2LP model
items.authors: Jooyoung Lee(Western Sydney University); Kakeru Yazawa(University of Tsukuba); James Whang(Seoul National University); Paola Escudero(Western Sydney University)
items.abstract: This study investigates how normalization methods shape L2 vowel perception modelling. We trained multi-layer perceptrons to classify L1 Spanish vowels using F1-F2 data from DIMEx100, varying only the normalization (raw, gender-wise Z, Lobanov, Nearey 1/2, Gerstman). English vowel data from TIMIT were then fed to compare each model's predicted categorization of L2 English vowels into L1 Spanish ones with human data. Lobanov yielded the strongest fit (lowest MAE/RMSE, highest correlation and category match), despite expectations it would overnormalize cross-linguistic differences. Using the L2LP framework, we argue that Lobanov's collapsing of between-language variation simulates L2LP's full copying of L1 categories and normalization patterns for Spanish listeners with no English knowledge. These results suggest that optimal normalization depends on the target listener profile, with Lobanov capturing the initial state and Nearey potentially better modelling further L2 development.

items.title: Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
items.authors: Shubham Gupta(Mila – Québec AI Institute; ServiceNow Research; Université Laval); Siva Reddy(Mila – Québec AI Institute; ServiceNow Research; McGill University); Perouz Taslakian(Mila – Québec AI Institute; ServiceNow Research; McGill University); Valentina Zantedeschi(ServiceNow Research; Université Laval); Cem Subakan(Mila – Québec AI Institute; Université Laval)
items.abstract: While multimodal contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP successfully learn shared representations, their embeddings typically exhibit a persistent modality gap. We propose addressing this separation through a purely geometric approach: changing the embedding domain from the unit sphere, Sᵈ⁻¹, to the probability simplex, Δᵈ⁻¹. Although both manifolds share the same intrinsic dimension, the simplex acts as a structural prior; its nonnegative, unit-mass constraints serve as a cross-modal calibration that forces both modalities to ground themselves in the same coordinate system. By attaching lightweight softmax adapters and using Total Variation similarity, we reduce the centroid ℓ₂ gap by 97–99% across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks. This confirms that simplicial geometry induces genuine semantic alignment, matching or exceeding the retrieval performance of standard unconstrained models.

items.title: Effects of distributional bias in vowels and consonants on the Speech-to-Song Illusion
items.authors: Haruki Kagotani(University of Tsukuba); Hiroko Terasawa(University of Tsukuba); Makiko Sadakata(University of Amsterdam)
items.abstract: This study investigates how the distribution of phonemes in speech samples (proportions and types of vowels and consonants) as well as the instruction method (either speech-song or speech-rap scale) affect the perceived strength of the Speech-to-Song (STS) illusion. We conducted a listening experiment with 120 native Japanese-speakers using Japanese short phrases in which the distribution of phonemes was systematically manipulated. Participants rated song-likeness or rap-likeness of stimuli before and after repeated presentation of the phrases. Results revealed that stimuli with biased vowel/consonant distribution elicited significantly stronger illusions than non-biased counterparts. Moreover, the Rap instruction (the instruction to judge rap-likeness rather than song-likeness) yielded consistently higher ratings than the Song instruction. These results demonstrate both phonological structure of stimuli and listening modes play important roles in perception of the STS illusion.

items.title: Deep learning-based predictions of perceived listening effort and intelligibility across enhanced, synthetic, natural, and binaural speech
items.authors: Dirk Eike Hoffner(Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg); Hartmut Schoon(Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg ); Rainer Huber(Communications Acoustics, Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg; Fraunhofer Institute for Digital Media Technology IDMT, Branch Hearing, Speech and Audio Technology HSA); Jan Rennies(Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg; Fraunhofer Institute for Digital Media Technology); Bernd T. Meyer(Communications Acoustics, Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg; Cluster of Excellence Hearing4all, Carl von Ossietzky Universit¨at Oldenburg)
items.abstract: Models of auditory perception that accurately predict subjective listening effort (LE) and speech intelligibility (SI) are important tools in hearing research. In this paper, we analyze the predictive power of two deep-learning models for a wide range of tasks, which cover speech enhancement in hearing aids, perception in binaural scenes, as well as synthetic speech. The PHOne-based Binaural Intelligibility model (PHOBI) is based on phone posteriors obtained from a deep neural net trained as part of speech recognizer, while HASANet+ is a teacher-student model trained to mimic intrusive measures of SI. We analyze over 10,500 LE and SI ratings collected from 39 listeners and find that both models produce high correlations between measurement and prediction over 0.88, which included LE metrics for which the models were not explicitly designed. While PHOBI produces slightly better results on average, both models seem to be applicable to conditions that are not covered in training.

items.title: Mutual Cancellation between Masking Effects Benefits Speech Intelligibility
items.authors: Yixin Gu(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Yan Tang(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology)
items.abstract: Informational masking (IM) induced by competing speech impairs listeners' ability to understand target speech. This interference is strongest when the target and masker share similar acoustic and linguistic features. Intelligibility also suffers from modulation masking (MM), where the masker's modulation disrupts that of the target in multiple domains during auditory processing. In this study, energetic masking (EM) was constrained using an intelligibility model by equalizing high-energy glimpses. English sentences were masked by competing speech in English, Mandarin, or modulation-controlled noise. Word recognition results showed that listener performance was a consequence of IM release benefited from language dissimilarity that was counterbalanced by IM due to the reduced level cue between the target and masker. Reducing masker modulation in spectro-temporal and temporal domains improved listening performance. The release from MM could even cancel EM for improved intelligibility.

title: Speaker Verification: Advances in Speaker Embeddings

items.title: Beyond Short Segments : Expanding Speaker Embeddings with Vector Archives
items.authors: Hyunku Kang(Korea University); Minkyu Cho(Korea University); Chanwoo Kim(Korea University)
items.abstract: The performance of state-of-the-art speaker verification (SV) systems severely degrades on short utterances due to insufficient speaker-specific information. To address this critical challenge, we propose the Vector Archive Mapping ECAPA (VAM-ECAPA), a novel system designed to enhance feature extraction from short-duration speech. The core of our system is the Transformer-based Vector Archive Mapping with Statistical Pooling (TVAMSP) module, which enriches information-scarce features by mapping them against a learnable Vector Archive of canonical speaker traits. By integrating the TVAMSP module into a strong WavLM+ECAPA-TDNN baseline, our system learns to map sparse features from short segments into robust, discriminative speaker representations. Experiments on the VoxCeleb1 benchmark show that our proposed VAM-ECAPA achieves a highly competitive EER of 8.334% on 1-second test segments, a 54.8% relative error reduction compared to a conventionally-trained baseline.

items.title: Revisiting Label-Free Speaker Embedding Enhancement with vMF Profile Likelihood
items.authors: Seunghwan Kim(Seoul National University); Jinyong Kim(Seoul National University); Sooyoung Yang(Seoul National University); Youngjin Ko(Seoul National University); Myungjoo Kang(Seoul National University; Research Institute of Mathematics)
items.abstract: Embedding enhancement improves speaker verification under acoustic mismatch without modifying a frozen backbone. Recent work has established a practical label-free setting for this task, but often adopts increasingly structured formulations. Here, the clean target is directly observed during training, making enhancement a matching problem on the unit hypersphere. We model the clean target with a von Mises-Fisher (vMF) likelihood and profile out a sample-wise concentration parameter, yielding a simple closed-form objective with adaptive weighting. Across VoxCeleb1, VoxSRC23, CN-Celeb, VOiCES, and VC-Mix, the proposed method largely preserves the baseline and gives clearer gains on challenging mismatch sets. It also remains stable under a broad single-view recipe, where a recent diffusion baseline becomes less reliable in controlled comparisons. These results suggest that effective label-free embedding enhancement in this setting does not require a highly structured formulation.

items.title: On the Robustness of Speaker Embeddings for Cross-Domain Speaker Retrieval
items.authors: Chuanqi Huang(Guangxi University); Wei Xie(Guangxi University; Guangxi Key Laboratory of Multimedia Communications and Network Technology); Xilu Wang(University of Surrey)
items.abstract: Deploying speaker retrieval systems requires robust cross-domain embedding generalization. However, existing benchmarks focus on verification metrics, leaving ranking stability under retrieval constraints under-explored. This paper evaluates six pre-trained embedding models across multiple cross-domain scenarios. First, while supervised multi-scale models resist channel filtering and aging drift, most architectures overfit to language-specific phonetic variations under cross-lingual mismatch. Second, we leverage adaptive symmetric normalization as a training-free backend strategy to improve retrieval performance. By selecting high-scoring background cohorts to estimate localized score statistics, this strategy normalizes global shifts caused by channel distortions and restores ranking consistency across all models. These insights demonstrate that combining multi-scale local features with adaptive backend calibration is effective for cross-domain speaker retrieval.

items.title: Toward Open-Set Speaker Attribute Prediction with Keyword-Appended LLM Embeddings
items.authors: Byoungjun So(Seoul National University); Jaejun Lee(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Understanding speaker attributes is crucial for voice-related applications, yet conventional approaches rely on fixed categorical labels, lacking semantic richness and zero-shot generalizability. We propose a novel framework for open-set speaker attribute prediction leveraging Large Language Model (LLM) embed-dings to represent attributes in a continuous semantic space. To bridge the cross-modal gap, we introduce a keyword-appending strategy that structures broad semantic representations into a compact, discriminative manifold. Furthermore, we employ a top-k negative loss to establish robust decision boundaries in crowded semantic regions. Experimental results on LibriTTS-P demonstrate that our method outperforms closed-set benchmarks and generalizes effectively to unseen synonyms. Geometric analysis suggests that our strategies regularize the embedding manifold, balancing semantic cohesion with predictive clarity.

items.title: Rethinking Speaker Embeddings for Speech Generation: Sub-Center Modeling for Capturing Intra-Speaker Diversity
items.authors: Ismail Rasim Ulgen(Johns Hopkins University); John L. Hansen(The University of Texas at Dallas); Carlos Busso(Carnegie Mellon University); Berrak Sisman(Johns Hopkins University)
items.abstract: Modeling speech variation is key to natural, expressive generation. Speaker embeddings are commonly used to condition personalized speech systems, but they are typically trained for speaker recognition, where intra-speaker variability is suppressed and inter-speaker separation is maximized. This objective leads to overly compact representations that may discard variations crucial for generation. We revisit this design choice and propose a sub-center modeling framework for speaker embeddings. Instead of a single prototype per speaker, we learn multiple sub-centers during discriminative training, allowing utterances to align with different prototypes. This strategy preserves structured intra-speaker variability while maintaining discriminability. In zero-shot voice conversion, our method improves intelligibility, increases pitch variability, achieves higher naturalness ratings, and retains strong speaker verification performance.

items.title: NoiseLoRA-SV: Hierarchical Noise-Conditioned Adaptation with Embedding Distillation for Robust Speaker Verification
items.authors: Dai Gao(Soochow University); Chen Jiang(Beijing Jiaotong University); Sizhe Liu(Renmin University of China); Peng Zhang(Qilu University of Technology)
items.abstract: Current speaker verification (SV) models, including Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) variants, rely on static inference-time parameters and show limited robustness to non-stationary noise. We propose NoiseLoRA-SV, a dynamic framework that generates instance-adaptive weights on-the-fly during inference. Instead of full end-to-end fine-tuning, it injects noise-conditioned LoRA modules into a lightly fine-tuned backbone with moderate additional parameter overhead. A Convolutional Recurrent Network (CRN) extracts hierarchical noise representations: global embeddings drive a hypernetwork to generate LoRA matrices, while local embeddings control a frame-level time-varying gate. Optimized via InfoNCE-based contrastive distillation, NoiseLoRA-SV aligns noisy embeddings with clean speaker representations. Evaluated on the VoxCeleb1 corpus with MUSAN and unseen NonSpeech100 noises, NoiseLoRA-SV consistently yields lower equal error rates (EERs) than static baselines.
