items.title: Positional Encoding in the Context of Memristor-Based Analog Computation for Automatic Speech Recognition
items.authors: Benedikt Hilmes(RWTH Aachen University; AppTek.ai); Nick Rossenbach(RWTH Aachen University; AppTek.ai); Ralf Schlüter(RWTH Aachen University; AppTek.ai)
items.abstract: Memristors provide a new chance for resource-efficient computation of neural models for natural language processing by enabling analog execution of vector-matrix-multiplication. Yet, computations on these devices are currently subject to larger distortion, both in weight programming and execution. In this work, we identify large output values of transformed positional encodings to cause major degradation within analog-to-digital conversion (ADC) as part of memristor-based computation. By adjusting the proportion of weight and precision bits of the ADC of specific memristor layers, we reduce the degradation of the execution by ~50% relative, while keeping the estimated energy consumption stable. Additionally, we investigate scenarios where the ADC cannot be modified. In that case the degradation can be reduced by ~30% relative after removing encoding-related linear transformations.

items.title: Systematic PTQ Study of Integer and Floating-Point Formats for On-Device Whisper ASR
items.authors: Woosuk Choi(LG Electronics; Sogang University); Dohyeon Lee(Sogang University); Taehyung Kim(Sogang University); Hyukjun Lee(Sogang University)
items.abstract: Whisper and similar encoder-decoder ASR models are increasingly deployed on mobile and edge devices, yet it remains unclear how quantization format choices affect their accuracy in practice. We systematically evaluate post-training quantization (PTQ) for Whisper (tiny.en,base.en) across 80+ configurations covering INT8/4/3 and FP8/FP4/NVFP4/MXFP4. Our main finding is that activation bit-width matters far more than weight format: dropping activations from 16-bit to 8-bit costs 1-3% absolute WER, while INT16 and FP16 activations are indistinguishable in accuracy. Among 4-bit formats, NVFP4 W4A16 comes within 0.07% of full-precision at 6.4× compression, whereas MXFP4 fails under standard PTQ and needs additional fixes. FP activation paths are also the better hardware choice, since FP multipliers are more area-efficient than INT at the same bit-width. We close with a Pareto analysis and six practical guidelines for format selection across memory budgets from 20 to 80 MB.

items.title: Pushing the Limits of Compression: Sub-1-Bit Conformer via Variable-Rank Binary Decomposition
items.authors: Jinsu Yeo(Samsung Electronics); Banseok Lee(Samsung Electronics); Youngmin Kim(Samsung Electronics)
items.abstract: While Conformer-Transducers offer state-of-the-art ASR performance, their excessive memory footprints create a bottleneck for on-device deployment. Conventional integer quantization is fundamentally constrained by a discrete grid, imposing a structural lower bound of 1 bit per parameter. To address this challenge, we propose LittleASR, a mixed-precision framework based on variable-rank binary decomposition. Guided by a gradient-aware sensitivity metric, LittleASR identifies and compresses non-critical layers to the sub-1-bit regime, pushing the limits of compression beyond the boundaries of standard quantization while maintaining a favorable trade-off between extreme memory reduction and recognition accuracy.

items.title: Pruning as Regularization: Sensitivity-Aware One-Shot Pruning in ASR
items.authors: Julian Irigoyen(Danske Bank); Arthur Söhler(Copenhagen Business School); Andreas Søeborg Kirkedal(Jabra (GN Group))
items.abstract: Neural network pruning is typically framed as a post-training compression technique. We show that for encoder-decoder ASR Transformers, one-shot magnitude pruning can act as a strong implicit regularizer: removing redundant parameters improves generalization without fine-tuning. Using Whisper-small, we introduce a sensitivity diagnostic combining gradient and Fisher criteria to identify pruning-fragile vs. pruning-resilient components. This reveals an encoder-decoder asymmetry: decoder FFNs are pruning-fragile, whereas decoder self-attention and late encoder layers contain removable redundancy. Without fine-tuning, pruning 50% of decoder self-attention improves WER by 2.38% absolute on LibriSpeech test-other; pruning the last four encoder layers at 50% yields 1.72% improvement. Gains persist on Common Voice and TED-LIUM, demonstrating cross-corpus generalization. At 40.8% sparsity, sensitivity-aware compression preserves near-baseline accuracy where global magnitude pruning collapses.

items.title: Leveraging Temporal Redundancy via Layer-wise Key-Value Pooling Attention for Efficient ASR
items.authors: Yi Wu(Harbin Institute of Technology); Guibin Zheng(Harbin Institute of Technology); Chenhao Jing(Harbin Institute of Technology); Jiqing Han(Harbin Institute of Technology); Jiarui Zhang(Harbin Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Transformer-based models have revolutionized Automatic Speech Recognition. However, the quadratic complexity of self-attention and feature redundancy necessitate deep stacking, limiting long-sequence efficiency. To address this, we propose Key-Value Pooling Attention (KV-Pooling), which leverages high temporal redundancy in speech by average pooling to compress Key/Value tensors, smoothing feature distribution spikes while retaining Query resolution to maintain modeling precision. This reduces reliance on network depth. Building on this, we introduce KV-Pooling-Zipformer, integrating this mechanism into Zipformer by pre-setting differential pooling strides based on layer-wise feature abstraction. Compared to the native Zipformer, RNN-T experiments show absolute reductions of 0.2% CER on AISHELL-1 and 0.3% WER on LibriSpeech. Notably, it improves inference RTF by 10% on an AMD EPYC 7763, achieving synergistic gains in accuracy and efficiency.

title: Datasets
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 12 - Oral 5 - Datasets

items.title: GLAD-CSpeech: A Dialectologically Comprehensive Benchmark for Genuine Chinese Dialect Speech
items.authors: Ke Xu(Alibaba Group; Nankai University); Lihan Xu(Alibaba Group; Fudan University); Jiayi Lin(Nankai University); Bin Zhang(Alibaba Group); Yunfei Chu(Alibaba Group); Shuting Yuan(Alibaba Group; Nankai University); Ruiye Lv(Nankai University); Guangxuan Zheng(Nankai University); Qi Han(Alibaba Group); Jin Xu(Alibaba Group); Bing Zhao(Alibaba Group); Hu Wei(Alibaba Group); Yang Bai(Alibaba Group); Ziyi Cheng(Alibaba Group); Qibin Ran(Nankai University)
items.abstract: We introduce GLAD-CSpeech, a linguistically-grounded benchmark for genuine Chinese dialect speech supporting automatic speech recognition (ASR), text-to-speech (TTS), and dialect identification (DID). The dataset spans 16 dialect divisions—8 Mandarin subgroups and 8 major non-Mandarin groups—covering all dialect regions recognized in Chinese dialectology. It includes speech from 23 representative locations and distinguishes Genuine Dialect from Accented Mandarin to enable controlled study of the Mandarin-Dialect continuum. The corpus contains over 163 hours of speech, with studio recordings for TTS and diverse real-world recordings for ASR, covering daily and application-oriented scenarios. We provide dialect-aware transcriptions and Mandarin-dialect parallel texts for all utterances. Baseline systems for ASR, TTS, and DID are reported. GLAD-CSpeech is released free for non-commercial research use.

items.title: Dialogs: a studio-quality expressive conversational Russian speech corpus for dialog assistants
items.authors: Ilya Shigabeev(Langswap); Ilia Latyshev(Langswap)
items.abstract: We introduce Dialogs, a studio-quality Russian conversational speech corpus for dialog assistants. The dataset contains 20.6 hours of face-to-face acted dialogs recorded in a professional studio (44.1 kHz stereo) and segmented into 11,796 utterances across 3 speakers. Unlike read-speech resources, Dialogs captures turn-taking rhythm and expressive prosody, and provides per-utterance style/emotion labels spanning 12 categories. We validate corpus quality with crowd MOS tests, showing comparable audio quality and intelligibility to strong Russian studio baselines while achieving higher ratings for expressiveness and conversational naturalness. Finally, we train a VITS2 model as a proof of concept, demonstrating that Dialogs supports training expressive, dialog-like TTS despite limited per-speaker data.

items.title: HaessigDB: A Database of Irritable Speech with Intensity Grading
items.authors: Niklas Weller(University of St.Gallen); Marc Grau(University of St.Gallen); Ivo Blohm(University of St.Gallen)
items.abstract: We introduce HaessigDB, a curated collection of human-annotated emotional speech snippets with intensity grading. The database contains acted call-center style speech snippets with human ratings on three irritability dimensions, namely annoyance, frustration, and aggression. Each snippet is rated on an ordinal intensity scale, which supports fine-grained analysis beyond binary emotion detection. To improve annotation quality, we construct high-agreement subsets per dimension through iterative processing steps. The resulting corpus preserves temporal ordering, enabling research on irritability development in conversations and early escalation signals. HaessigDB addresses a data gap in speech-based emotion research for service settings, where intervention decisions depend on both intensity and temporal development. The database can support supervised learning, trajectory modeling, and design of escalation-aware conversational systems.

items.title: Contextual Earnings-22: A Speech Recognition Benchmark with Custom Vocabulary in the Wild
items.authors: Berkin Durmus(Argmax, Inc.; University of California); Chen Cen(Argmax, Inc.); Eduardo Pacheco(Argmax, Inc.); Arda Okan(Argmax, Inc.); Atila Orhon(Atila Orhon: Argmax, Inc.)
items.abstract: The accuracy frontier of speech-to-text systems has plateaued on academic benchmarks.¹ In contrast, industrial benchmarks and adoption in high-stakes domains suggest otherwise. We hypothesize that the primary difference between the two is contextual conditioning: Academic benchmarks are dominated by frequently encountered general vocabulary that is relatively easy to recognize compared with rare and context-defined custom vocabulary that has disproportionate impact on the usability of speech transcripts. Despite progress on contextual speech-to-text, there is no standardized benchmark. We introduce Contextual Earnings-22, an open dataset built upon Earnings-22, with realistic custom vocabulary contexts to foster research and reveal latent progress. We set six strong baselines for two dominant approaches: keyword prompting and keyword boosting. Experiments show comparable and significantly improved accuracy when scaled from proof-of-concept to commercial-scale systems.

items.title: VIP-MINGLE: A Corpus for Videoconference and In-Person Multimodal Interaction in Group Language Engagement
items.authors: Andrew Chang(New York University); Abhinay K Bodi(New York University); Wenxin Deng(New York University); Junrui Huang(New York University); Venu G Kadamba(New York University); Sumanth B H Karanam(New York University); Dhiwahar A Kennady(New York University); David Poeppel(New York University); Dustin Freeman(New York University)
items.abstract: Group conversations are a fundamental yet complex form of social interaction central to human cognition and telecommunication technology. While understanding and facilitating these interactions has been a long-standing goal, findings are often isolated within specific in-person or videoconferencing settings due to a scarcity of datasets that bridge the two. We introduce VIP-MINGLE, a multimodal dataset comprising 59 hours of recordings (32 groups, 105 participants), featuring paired within-subject sessions in both settings. The dataset includes raw audio/video, psychometric data, processed multimodal features (e.g., diarized speech, facial expressions, transcriptions), and time-resolved human annotations. Our analysis reveals significant behavioral distribution shifts across multiple modalities between settings, reinforcing the need for a cross-setting corpus. VIP-MINGLE serves as a critical resource for developing robust models of group conversations across settings.

items.title: Earnings25: A Comprehensive 500-Hour Speech Benchmark for Finance
items.authors: Denglin Jiang(Bloomberg); Haoran Zhou(Bloomberg); Anshul Wadhawan(Bloomberg); Brendan Fahy(Bloomberg); Vinay Ramesh(Bloomberg); David Weisberg(Bloomberg); Dmitriy Derkachevskiy(Bloomberg); Helen Sheehan(Bloomberg); Srivas Prasad(Bloomberg); Michele Franceschini(Bloomberg)
items.abstract: We introduce Earnings25, a finance-domain benchmark for evaluating automatic speech recognition (ASR) on English-language earnings calls under realistic conditions. Earnings25 comprises two complementary test sets: (i) testset-full, 498 hours of full English-language S&P 500 earnings calls from Q4 2025, and (ii) testset-segmented, a 46-hour industry-balanced set of 290 segments sampled from English-language U.S. earnings calls in 2025. The benchmark provides aligned transcripts and structured metadata, including speaker roles, industry labels, and call structure, enabling speaker- and industry-aware evaluation beyond aggregate word error rate (WER). We report reproducible baselines for Whisper and Parakeet-TDT using standardized scoring.

title: Multimodal and Non-Speech Healthcare Applications
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 13 - Oral 9 - Multimodal and Non-Speech Healthcare Applications

items.title: Zero-Shot Respiratory Sound Classification through LLM-Augmented Audio-Text Alignment
items.authors: Mustafa Talha İlerisoy(Eindhoven University of Technology); Hung Manh Pham(Singapore Management University); Mathias Funk(Eindhoven University of Technology); Mykola Pechenizkiy(Eindhoven University of Technology); Aaqib Saeed(Eindhoven University of Technology)
items.abstract: Self-supervised respiratory encoders lack semantic grounding in clinical domain needed for zero-shot inference, limiting their utility without task-specific labeled data. We propose a framework that aligns these encoders with medical terminology in a shared latent space turning them into a zero-shot-capable foundation model. To address paired data scarcity, we use a medical LLM to synthesize structured reports from metadata, creating dense semantic anchors for contrastive learning. Our training combines a sigmoid-based contrastive loss with encoder's native SSL objective and similarity-aware negative sampling to sharpen pathological boundaries. Across 9 tasks on 6 datasets, our method achieves a 61.3% mean zero-shot AUC, surpassing CLAP (51.4%) and Qwen2-Audio (54.9%) while reaching the highest linear probing AUC (71.6%) with only 43% of data used by full-scale baselines, showing that structured semantic alignment outperforms large-scale, general-purpose models in clinical diagnostics.

items.title: From Lab to Laptop: Validating 3D Speech Kinematics with MediaPipe Face Mesh
items.authors: Victoria Sanchez(Harvard University; Massachesetts General Hospital Institute of Health Professions); Oliver Roesler(Modality.AI); Michael Neumann(Modality.AI); David Pautler(Modality.AI); Brian Richburg(Massachesetts General Hospital Institute of Health Professions); Karen Chenausky(Massachesetts General Hospital Institute of Health Professions); Yana Yunusova(Sunnybrook Research Institute; University of Toronto); Vikram Ramanarayanan(Modality.AI; University of California San Francisco); Jordan Green(Massachesetts General Hospital Institute of Health Professions; Harvard University)
items.abstract: Measuring articulatory movement traditionally requires expensive laboratory equipment, constraining scale and clinical translation. We analytically validated a markerless pipeline using MediaPipe's Face Mesh model to capture 3D articulator movement trajectories from a single standard RGB camera. Per-participant calibration transformed model outputs into millimeters, enabling direct benchmarking against optical motion capture. Accuracy was quantified with 3D positional error, and movement fidelity was evaluated relative to each landmark's excursion and speed at 30 and 15 fps under matched filtering. The system achieved millimeter-scale tracking accuracy (mean 3D uRMSE 2.03 ± 0.59 mm), low normalized displacement error (6.63 ± 1.28%), robust depth recovery, and no loss of utility at 15 fps—establishing single-camera 3D tracking as a scalable, analytically viable technology.

items.title: Toward an Articulatory Weakness Index for Speech Kinematics in Parkinson’s Disease
items.authors: Shrishail Baligar(Massachusetts General Hospital); Ahmed Yousef(Massachusetts General Hospital); Daryush Mehta(Massachusetts General Hospital)
items.abstract: Many acoustic speech metrics often reflect a combination of respiratory, laryngeal, and articulatory contributions, thereby preventing direct measurement of articulatory dynamics. We have developed an articulatory weakness index (AWI) derived from electromagnetic articulography (EMA) or acoustic data. We learn an articulatory-state coordinate Za from healthy EMA data, where higher values indicate restricted articulator motion. In cohorts of individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD) and controls, AWI is elevated in PD and correlates with motor severity, while remaining stable across in healthy controls and speakers with vocal hyperfunction. AWI provides an interpretable, disentangled articulatory weakness index from acoustic speech recordings, complementing respiratory and laryngeal measures.

items.title: Speech and Video Biomarkers Exhibit Reduced Within-Subject Variability in Early Parkinson’s Disease and Resistance to Placebo and Hawthorne Effects
items.authors: Hardik Kothare(Modality.AI, Inc.); Oliver Roesler(Modality.AI, Inc.); Lakshmi Arbatti(Modality.AI, Inc.); Michael Neumann(Modality.AI, Inc.); Karl Kieburtz(CLINTREX); Andrew McGarry(CLINTREX); Craig Thompson(Cerevance); Vikram Ramanarayanan(Modality.AI, Inc.; University of California)
items.abstract: Placebo and Hawthorne effects are well-known confounders in clinical trials, particularly in Parkinson's disease, contributing to variability in standard clinical scales like the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS). Using data collected as part of a Phase 2 clinical trial, we evaluated speech, facial and finger-tapping digital biomarkers for within-subject stability and resistance to these contextual influences. These objective measures exhibited correlation at baseline with, but lower variability and lower susceptibility to placebo or observation effects than the MDS-UPDRS, demonstrating robustness. These findings highlight the potential of audiovisual and motor digital biomarkers as reliable, reproducible endpoints in PD trials, enabling more sensitive detection of disease progression and treatment effects.

items.title: BACH: Benchmarking Audio Codecs for Bio-Acoustic Health
items.authors: Zixing Zhang(Hunan University); Xiaojun Mo(Hunan University); Zhongren Dong(Hunan University); Bin Wang(Beijing Xiaomi Mobile Software Co., Ltd.); Jing Han(Hunan University; Yuelushan Center for Industrial Innovation)
items.abstract: Bio-acoustic health signals are increasingly vital for remote diagnostics, yet efficient transmission remains a bottleneck for clinical adoption. While audio codecs offer strong compression for general audio, they preserve diagnostically critical information in bio-acoustic signals is unclear. To address this gap, we introduce BACH, the first systematic Benchmark for evaluating Audio Codecs on bio-acoustic Health tasks. BACH assesses eight codecs across five bio-acoustic health tasks, utilizing a unified framework covering original audio, compressed representations, and reconstructed audio. Our central finding reveals a critical misalignment between reconstruction fidelity and downstream task performance: codecs excelling at signal reconstruction do not always retain task-relevant semantic cues. This highlights a fundamental challenge for future research: codecs for medical applications must be co-designed to optimize for both perceptual quality and diagnostic information preservation.

items.title: Uncovering Latent Depression Severity for Binary Depression Detection via Advantage-weighting Ranking
items.authors: Manning Gao(South China Normal University); Tingyi Liu(South China Normal University); Leheng Zhang(South China Normal University); Haifeng Hu(Sun Yat-sen University); Yuncheng Jiang(South China Normal University); Sijie Mai(South China Normal University)
items.abstract: Automatic depression detection using audio-visual data faces significant challenges, particularly in disentangling overlapping feature distributions and establishing robust decision boundaries. To address this, we propose a fine-grained multimodal framework featuring a temporal encoder and a mutual transformer to facilitate deep cross-modal fusion. Our core contribution is the Binary Advantage-weighting Ranking Loss, which optimizes the latent space distribution through two complementary mechanisms: Advantage-weighted Separation, which mines hard pairs by computing a pairwise prediction difference matrix and dynamically weighting them based on their difficulty; and Advantage-weighted Compactness, which minimizes intra-class variance to force features to cluster around their respective class centers. Extensive experiments on D-vlog and LMVD demonstrate that our model reconstructs the latent ordinal structure by prioritizing hard pairs, thereby achieving state-of-the-art performance.

items.title: Decolonizing Linguistic Policies in Automatic Speech Recognition: A Framework for Cross-Culturally Competent Speech AI
items.authors: Jay L. Cunningham(DePaul University); Mark Atta Mensah(York University); Richard Martinez(Independent Researcher); João Vieira da Silva Neto(DePaul University); Efi Dawodu(DePaul University)
items.abstract: This paper focuses on automatic speech recognition (ASR) and ASR-mediated voice interfaces that shape access to public services, healthcare, and education. We argue that persistent failures for low-resource, Indigenous, and non-standard language varieties are not only technical errors, but also implicit linguistic policies that reproduce colonial language hierarchies. Drawing on linguistic capital, raciolinguistic ideology, language policy research, and decolonial computing, we show how data, metrics, and model priors determine whose voices become machine-legible. We introduce the Three Harms (3M) taxonomy--Misrecognition, Misalignment, and Mistrust--and a seven-layer situatedness model for linguistic diversity in ASR and ASR-mediated voice interfaces. We then propose a participatory framework and minimum audit protocol for culturally competent ASR, positioning affected communities as co-designers, evaluators, and governance partners.

items.title: Turning Speech Language Models into Multilingual Listeners
items.authors: Tolúlọpẹ́ Ògúnrẹ̀mí(Stanford University); Dan Jurafsky(Stanford University); Christopher D. Manning(Stanford University); Ahnmet Üstün(Cohere Labs; Cohere); Martijn Bartelds(Stanford University)
items.abstract: Speech Language Models (SLMs) that understand spoken language questions support only a few high-resource languages, limiting access to millions of people worldwide. This gap stems from the scarcity of multilingual speech instruction-tuning datasets. We present MULTISPEECHQA, a large-scale, synthetically generated and human-verified dataset comprising 9200 hours of 10.8 million spoken question-answer pairs in 23 typologically diverse languages. Using MULTISPEECHQA, we also introduce MULTISPEECH-BENCH, a multi-task benchmark for evaluating SLM performance on 23 languages. We compare the performance of a cascading system to open-weight and closed SLMs on MULTISPEECH-BENCH and find that the cascading system outperforms open-weight SLMs but not all closed SLMs. We use MULTISPEECHQA to finetune Qwen 2.5-Omni, which improves its performance on our benchmark. Our findings show that high-quality synthetic datasets offer a cheap solution to improving the multilingual capabilities of SLMs.

items.title: Preserving the Iranian Turkic Language: Community-Driven ASR Datasets and Benchmarking for South Azerbaijani
items.authors: Farhan Farsi(Amirkabir University of Technology); Shayan Bali(King's College London); Jalil Nourmohammadi Khiarak(Kartal Ol Foundation); Mohammad Hossein Aref(Amirkabir University of Technology); Taher Akbari Saeed(Kartal Ol Foundation)
items.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) is widely used, but its progress in low-resource languages like South Azerbaijani, a Turkic language with Arabic script, remains limited due to scarce data. To address this gap, we introduce the first community-driven ASR datasets for South Azerbaijani. These include: a dataset comprising +255,743 transcribed utterances from multiple sources; a dataset collected by the authors from the South Azerbaijani-speaking community; and the AZB ASR GoldSet, a challenging benchmark dataset for future evaluation. To establish strong baselines, we benchmark eight models, including MMS-1b-all and seven Whisper-family models fine-tuned on our datasets. Our results demonstrate that using the full dataset improves performance, and language-specific fine-tuning is crucial for low-resource settings. Error analysis further reveals that Arabic script ambiguity and deletion-heavy decoding are the primary error sources. The code and datasets are also publicly available.

items.title: WazobiaSpeech: A Large-Scale Multilingual Speech Corpus for Robust and Fair ASR in Four Nigerian Languages
items.authors: Ife Adebara(University of Alberta, EqualyzAI, Data Science Nigeria; Amii; CIFAR AI Chair); Oluwaseun Nifemi(Data Science Nigeria; EqualyzAI); Olubayo Adekanmbi(Data Science Nigeria; EqualyzAI); Rashidat Sikiru(EqualyzAI); Ololade Anjuwon(EqualyzAI); Ronke Akinmosin(EqualyzAI); Faiza Sani(EqualyzAI)
items.abstract: African languages remain severely underrepresented in large-scale speech resources, particularly for spontaneous speech reflecting real-world use. We present WazobiaSpeech, an ethically governed corpus spanning four Nigerian languages, 2,540.8 hours of audio, and 2,865 speakers, with emphasis on naturally occurring speech across diverse sociolinguistic contexts. Although a small portion - 4% of the entire data includes scripted recordings to ensure lexical and domain coverage, the dataset is predominantly spontaneous. Unlike prior corpora built mainly on scripted speech, WazobiaSpeech captures authentic variation in accent, dialect, register, and code-switching, enriched with demographic and contextual metadata. We detail data collection and transcription workflows, and report baseline ASR results with cross-lingual error analyses, including fine-grained evaluation of tone sensitivity in speech recognition.

items.title: NaturalFlow: Reducing Disruptive Pauses for Natural Speech Flow in Simultaneous Speech-to-Speech Translation
items.authors: Dongwook Lee(Seoul National University); Youngho Cho(Seoul National University); Sangkwon Park(Seoul National University); Heeseung Kim(University of Seoul); Sungroh Yoon(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Simultaneous speech-to-speech translation aims to enable near-real-time communication by minimizing latency, offering a compelling, real-time alternative to the high latency of consecutive translation. However, the excessive pursuit of low latency often results in fragmented chunk-wise speech. Consequently, listeners are subjected to an unnatural acoustic flow punctuated by frequent pauses, which could increase their cognitive load. To bridge this gap, we introduce a fluency-aware optimization framework designed to discover the sweet spot between the low-latency benefits of simultaneous translation and the natural flow of consecutive translation. Our framework minimizes inter-chunk silences by leveraging model-internal signals, including linguistic diversity and induced temporal variability in speech durations. Experiments on short- and long-form benchmarks show that our framework produces natural speech flow while maintaining competitive latency and translation quality.

items.title: Better Late Than Never: Meta-Evaluation of Latency Metrics for Simultaneous Speech-to-Text Translation
items.authors: Peter Polák(Charles University; AppTek); Sara Papi(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Luisa Bentivogli(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Ondřej Bojar(Charles University)
items.abstract: Simultaneous speech-to-text translation systems must balance translation quality with latency. Although quality evaluation is well established, latency measurement remains a challenge. Existing metrics produce inconsistent results, especially in short-form settings with artificial presegmentation. We present the first comprehensive meta-evaluation of latency metrics across language pairs and systems. We uncover a structural bias in current metrics related to segmentation. We introduce YAAL (Yet Another Average Lagging) for a more accurate short-form evaluation and LongYAAL for unsegmented audio. We propose SOFTSEGMENTER, a resegmentation tool based on soft word-level alignment. We show that YAAL and LongYAAL, together with SOFTSEGMENTER, outperform popular latency metrics, enabling more reliable assessments of short- and long-form simultaneous speech translation systems. We implement all artifacts within the OMNISTEVAL toolkit: https://github.com/pe-trik/OmniSTEval.

title: Pronunciation Diversity
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Long Oral 11 - Pronunciation Diversity [Cross-area long papers Oral session]

items.title: Pronunciation Diversity
items.abstract: Variability in natural speech is largely shaped by syntactic and pragmatic structure. Non-deterministic Generative Speech Models (GSMs), however, may produce intonation that diverges from these patterns. In the first part of this talk, I will review existing studies evaluating GSMs’ ability to simulate probabilistic intonational variation. The second part will focus on the Hindi discourse particle ‘-hii’, examining its pragmatic associations and intonational realizations in both human- and GSM-generated speech. I employ Functional Principal Component Analysis and Bayesian regression to characterize and compare intonational variability across the two sources. Using objective acoustic measures, I asses the extent to which contemporary GSMs capture naturally occurring intonational variability and its pragmatic conditioning. Overall, this talk aims to highlight both the potential and the limitations of GSMs for generating pragmatically appropriate spoken language.

items.title: Layer-wise Probing of wav2vec 2.0 and Whisper for Consonant Cluster Reduction in African American English
items.authors: Hamid Mojarad(Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf); Kevin Tang(Department of English Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, Germany; University of Florida)
items.abstract: Self-supervised and supervised speech models are increasingly used to investigate which linguistic information their internal representations encode, and at what level of abstraction they encode it. One underexplored phenomenon is consonant cluster reduction (CCR) in African American English (AAE), a widespread phonological process and a source of automatic speech recognition (ASR) disparity. To examine how CCR is represented, we conduct speaker-independent layer-wise probing of wav2vec2-base and Whisper-small using two tasks: segmental reduction detection and segmental restoration of underlying cluster identity. Both models distinguish reduced and canonical forms with high accuracy. Crucially, reduced segments retain cues to their underlying stops, indicating that CCR is encoded as structured gradient phonological variation rather than simple segmental deletion. These results demonstrate structured phonological encoding of AAE CCR patterns in modern speech models.

items.title: Bilingual Speaker Phonetic Alignment to Voice Assistants
items.authors: Alyssa Allen(The Ohio State University); Kathryn Campbell-Kibler(The Ohio State University)
items.abstract: Users engage in conversation with ASR-powered voice assistants, but these models favor Standard American English (SAE) speech. Model bias impacts how non-SAE users engage with human versus system voices. Linguistic accommodation measures how interlocutors engage with each other and can be used to examine individuals' relative acceptance of voice assistants as social agents. This study asks how Spanish dominant Spanish-English bilingual speakers phonetically align on voice onset time (VOT) and vowel duration to human versus machine voices in each language. Participants (N=50) in an online lexical shadowing experiment read a list of words, then shadowed a human or voice assistant saying each word. Convergence was found in terms of vowel duration and VOT across languages and conditions, signaling bilingual speakers respond to machine voices in human-like ways across languages. Condition and language effects were mitigated by social information like dialectal region and gender.

items.title: Controllable Accent Normalization via Discrete Diffusion
items.authors: Qibing Bai(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Tencent); Yuhan Du(Nanjing University); Tom Ko(Shenzhen Loop Area Institute); Shuai Wang(Nanjing University; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute); Yannan Wang(Tencent); Haizhou Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute)
items.abstract: Existing accent normalization methods do not typically offer control over accent strength, yet many applications—such as language learning and dubbing—require tunable accent retention. We propose DLM-AN, a controllable accent normalization system built on masked discrete diffusion over self-supervised speech tokens. A Common Token Predictor identifies source tokens that likely encode native pronunciation; these tokens are selectively reused to initialize the reverse diffusion process. This provides a simple yet effective mechanism for controlling accent strength: reusing more tokens preserves more of the original accent. DLM-AN further incorporates a flow-matching Duration Ratio Predictor that automatically adjusts the total duration to better match the native rhythm. Experiments on multi-accent English data show that DLM-AN achieves the lowest word error rate among all compared systems while delivering competitive accent reduction and smooth, interpretable accent strength control.

items.title: Beyond Acoustic Sparsity and Linguistic Bias: A Prompt-Free Paradigm for Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis
items.authors: Haopeng Geng(The University of Tokyo); Longfei Yang(The University of Tokyo); Xi Chen(The University of Tokyo); Haitong Sun(The University of Tokyo); Daisuke Saito(The University of Tokyo); Nobuaki Minematsu(The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis (MDD) requires modeling fine-grained acoustic deviations. However, current ASR-derived MDD systems often face inherent limitations. In particular, CTC-based models favor sequence-level alignments that neglect transient mispronunciation cues, while explicit canonical priors bias predictions toward intended targets. To address these bottlenecks, we propose a prompt-free framework decoupling acoustic fidelity from canonical guidance. First, we introduce CROTTC, an acoustic model enforcing monotonic, frame-level alignment to accurately capture pronunciation deviations. Second, we implicitly inject mispronunciation information via the IF strategy under the knowledge transfer principle. Experiments show CROTTC-IF achieves a 71.77% F1-score on L2-ARCTIC and 71.70% F1-score on the Iqra'Eval2 leaderboard. With empirical analysis, we demonstrate that decoupling acoustics from explicit priors provides highly robust MDD.

items.title: How Attention Shapes Emotion: A Comparative Study of Attention Mechanisms for Speech Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Marc Casals-Salvador(Barcelona Supercomputing Center; Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya); Federico Costa(Barcelona Supercomputing Center; Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya); Rodolfo Zevallos(Barcelona Supercomputing Center); Javier Hernando(Barcelona Supercomputing Center; Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya)
items.abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) plays a key role in advancing human-computer interaction. Attention mechanisms have become the dominant approach for modeling emotional speech due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies and emphasize salient information. However, standard self-attention suffers from quadratic computational and memory complexity, limiting its scalability. In this work, we present a systematic benchmark of optimized attention mechanisms for SER, including RetNet, LightNet, GSA, FoX, and KDA. Experiments on both MSP-Podcast benchmark versions show that while standard self-attention achieves the strongest recognition performance across test sets, efficient attention variants dramatically improve scalability, reducing inference latency and memory usage by up to an order of magnitude. These results highlight a critical trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, providing practical insights for designing scalable SER systems.

items.title: From Single to Multi-Label SER: Dataset and Mamba-Based Fusion Model
items.authors: Vu Long Tran(Hanoi University of Science and Technology); Long Duc Do(Hanoi University of Science and Technology); Vinh Quang Nguyen(Hanoi University of Science and Technology); Ngoc Minh Nguyen(Hanoi University of Science and Technology); Quang Minh Le Pham(Hanoi University of Science and Technology); Hieu Trung Nguyen(Hanoi University of Science and Technology); Trang Thu Thi Nguyen(Hanoi University of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: We present a reproducible multi-label benchmark for speech emotion recognition (SER) built from the MSP-Podcast V2.0 corpus. Our pipeline converts crowdsourced emotion votes into multi-hot labels with controlled ambiguity and sparsity via reliability filtering, deterministic vote-to-label construction, and lightweight time-shift augmentation. On this benchmark, we provide a compact Mamba-based fusion baseline over MFCC and log-mel features, following prior SER fusion practice, while using linear-time state-space backbones for efficient modeling of long audio. Using a validation-only global threshold sweep for checkpoint selection and a fixed test-time threshold for evaluation, our fusion model attains competitive micro-F1 on two MSP-Podcast test partitions (≈0.50 on both Test1 and Test2) while remaining substantially lighter than heavier baselines and recent methods. We release dataset splits, construction code, and training recipes to support future work on scalable multi-label SER.

items.title: Multi-Loss Learning for Speech Emotion Recognition with Energy-Adaptive Mixup and Frame-Level Attention
items.authors: Cong Wang(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Yizhong Geng(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Yuhua Wen(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Qifei Li(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Yingming Gao(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Ruimin Wang(Li Auto); Chunfeng Wang(Li Auto); Hao Li(Li Auto); Wei Chen(Li Auto); Ya Li(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
items.abstract: Speech emotion recognition (SER) is an important technology in human-computer interaction. However, achieving high performance is challenging due to emotional complexity and scarce annotated data. To tackle these challenges, we propose a multi-loss learning (MLL) framework integrating an energy-adaptive mixup (EAM) method and a frame-level attention module (FLAM). The EAM method leverages SNR-based augmentation to generate diverse speech samples capturing subtle emotional variations. FLAM enhances frame-level feature extraction for multi-frame emotional cues. Our MLL strategy combines Kullback-Leibler divergence, focal, center, and supervised contrastive loss to optimize learning, address class imbalance, and improve feature separability. We evaluate our method on four widely used SER datasets: IEMOCAP, MSP-IMPROV, RAVDESS, and SAVEE. The results demonstrate our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, suggesting its effectiveness and robustness.

items.title: Segment-wise Embedding based Graph Attention Network for Effective Speech Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Haoyu Song(Singapore Institute of Technology); Ian McLoughlin(Singapore Institute of Technology); Yan Song(University of Science and Technology of China); Lirong Dai(University of Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: With the advancement of pretrained speech models like Hubert-large, leveraging general representations for downstream tasks such as speech emotion recognition (SER) is of growing importance to both academia and industry. We propose a highly effective segment-wise embedding-domain graph-attention network (GAT) where a Swin-Transformer adapts a pretrained model to capture multi-scale information from utterances. Self-supervised adaptor post-training with both block masking prediction and utterance-level contrastive learning addresses distribution shift issues. During finetuning, a graph is constructed from multiple embedding crops per utterance, allowing GAT-based temporal aggregation to extract insightful information from variable-length utterances. In addition to cross entropy, supervised contrastive learning is used to improve robustness to ambiguous utterance labels. Extensive SER experiments on IEMOCAP and MER2023 demonstrate significant performance gains over SOTA solutions.

items.title: Dual-Stream DNN-KAN Networks with Bangla-Specific Features for Speech Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Kazi Reyazul Hasan(Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology); Muhammad Abdullah Adnan(Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology)
items.abstract: Speech emotion recognition (SER) is challenging due to the complex interplay of spectral and prosodic features. We propose a dual-stream DNN-KAN architecture for Bangla speech, processing MFCCs through efficient DNN blocks and statistically optimized prosodic features via lightweight Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) with learnable B-spline activations. With only 1.1M parameters, our model achieves 92.12% on SUBESCO and 82.79% on BanglaSER under speaker-independent (SI) evaluation. Most prior Bangla SER work omits SI evaluation, so published figures likely reflect speaker memorization rather than genuine generalization. Re-running our feature-selection pipeline on EmoDB yields 93.92%, showing that the selection methodology transfers across languages. At 1.1M parameters, the model surpasses emotion2vec (25M) by 2.70% and wav2vec2-xlsr (326M) by 1.07% on SUBESCO SI, showing that statistically grounded feature engineering can match large pre-trained models at a fraction of the cost.

items.title: EII-SCL: Harnessing Emotional Inertia for Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation
items.authors: Zilong Huang(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Chong-xin Gan(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Zezhong Jin(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Ruichen Zuo(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Man-Wai Mak(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
items.abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversation (MERC) achieves accurate predictions by integrating multimodal and contextual information in dialogues. While current MERC approaches focus on modeling complex contextual dependencies in conversation, they often overlook the impact of contextual emotional inertia in emotion shift, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel Emotional Inertia-Informed Supervised Contrastive Learning module (EII-SCL) that informs the contrastive objective by constructing inertia-affected samples within temporal windows, effectively leveraging emotional inertia as a prior while enabling seamless integration with existing MERC models without requiring additional data. Extensive experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD show that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

items.title: Leveraging Modality-Specific Label Distributions for Enhanced Multimodal Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Xiaohan Shi(Nagoya University); Xingfeng Li(City University of Macau); Tomoki Toda(Nagoya University)
items.abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition (MER) aims to recognize human emotions by jointly modeling multiple modalities. Existing approaches mainly focus on learning modality-specific representations through complex fusion strategies, often overlooking the potential value of modality-specific label distributions. To address this limitation, we propose MoLD, a Modality-specific Label Distribution-based framework that explicitly models modality-specific label distributions to enhance MER. Meanwhile, we introduce a modality similarity loss to enforce cross-modal consistency. In this study, we compare MoLD with representative baselines and conduct ablation studies to analyze the contribution of each component. Additionally, we evaluate the model under unimodal settings to assess its robustness. Experimental results demonstrate that MoLD consistently outperforms benchmark baselines, with each component contributing to overall performance and maintaining effectiveness under unimodal settings.

items.title: Learning from Annotation Uncertainty: Entropy-Aware Curriculum for Speech Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Zahra Omidi(University of Texas at Dallas); John Hansen(University of Texas at Dallas)
items.abstract: Speech emotion recognition (SER) often relies on hard consensus labels that collapse annotator disagreement. We study distribution-based supervision for 9-class SER on MSP-Podcast 2.0 using a WavLM-Base multitask model for categorical emotion and dimensional VAD. Hard-label training is compared with targets from primary and merged primary–secondary annotator vote distributions. Distributional objectives improve alignment with human vote distributions, reducing JSD/KLD relative to hard-label training. Analysis shows that hard supervision partly benefits from assigning ambiguous utterances to the residual Other class, whereas distributional supervision redistributes uncertainty across emotion categories. Entropy-stratified evaluation shows that high-ambiguity utterances remain challenging, but distribution-based supervision better captures perceptual uncertainty. These findings support moving beyond hard labels toward targets that reflect listener disagreement.

items.title: Revisiting Delay Compensation via Feature-Level Temporal Accumulation in Continuous Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Jian Xiang(The University of New South Wales); Jingyao Wu(Massachesetts Institute of Technology); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne); Vidhyasaharan Sethu(The University of New South Wales); Eliathamby Ambikairajah(The University of New South Wales)
items.abstract: Continuous emotion recognition (CER) relies on time-continuous annotations that reflect annotators' sustained emotion perception. In practice, ground-truth annotations are often observed to have a lag, which leads to temporal misalignment between model predictions and annotator labels. The most common solution is delay compensation based on a relative temporal shift between input and labels, assuming that annotations are delayed reports of judgements formed based on the signal at a given moment. While effective, this shift-based delay compensation (SDC) requires explicit temporal shifting and truncation at sequence boundaries, and its performance can be sensitive to the choice of delay parameter. In this paper, we revisit delay compensation and introduce accumulated delay compensation (ADC), implemented via feature-level temporal accumulation. Instead of explicitly shifting labels, ADC accumulates past input features, incorporating historical context while inducing an intrinsic delay without modifying the original input–label alignment. Experiments on the RECOLA corpus demonstrate ADC is substantially more robust to the choice of delay parameter when compared with SDC. Further analysis reveals dimension-specific temporal effects: arousal favours shorter integration windows, whereas valence benefits from a longer window. These findings suggest that ADC offers a superior approach for delay compensation compared to the standard approach for CER.

items.title: Two-Sided Fairness Transfer for Gender-Neutral Speech Emotion Recognition with Partially Observed Attributes
items.authors: Woan-Shiuan Chien(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Tomohiko Nakamura(AIST); Huan-Yu Chen(National Tsing Hua University); Satoru Fukayama(AIST); Hitoshi Suda(AIST); Jun Ogata(AIST); Chi-Chun Lee(National Tsing Hua University)
items.abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) powers applications by interpreting users' emotions from speech. Ensuring fairness in SER is inherently a two-sided challenge, as a truly fair system requires neutrality to both speaker-side and rater-side biases. However, existing debiasing methods rely on explicit attribute labels for both sides, which are often unavailable. In this work, we address the challenge of cross-dataset fairness transfer under partial attribute supervision, where only one side (speaker or rater) has gender labels in the target dataset. We present a two-stage framework that first fine-tunes a pre-trained CLAP model with an adversarial debiasing objective to build one-sided gender-neutral models. We then introduce the ATT2Fair task vector, derived from the difference between speaker- and rater-side fair models in a source dataset, and apply it to infer the absent-side fair model in the target dataset. Our results highlight the practicality of fairness transfer for building gender-neutral SER systems across diverse datasets.

items.title: Conflict-Aware Pseudo-Labeling via Acoustic Signals for Multi-Task Speech Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Haojie Zhou(Jiangnan University; Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Technology for Healthcare, Ministry of Education, Jiangnan University); Shunfei Liang(Jiangnan University); Chengze Li(Jiangnan University); Zhizhong Bai(Jiangnan University); Yicheng Feng(Jiangnan University); Ning Wang(Jiangnan University; Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Technology for Healthcare, Ministry of Education, Jiangnan University)
items.abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) typically relies on utterance-level annotations, obscuring temporal emotional dynamics. While recent multi-task approaches achieve fine-grained alignment via Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), they heavily depend on costly human transcripts. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel Conflict-Aware Pseudo-Labeling method that derives frame-level auxiliary supervision solely from acoustic signals. Using collaborative inference across diverse data partitions, it adaptively segments speech into consensus and conflict regions. We assign hard pseudo-labels to consensus frames to capture local discriminative cues, while introducing a global back-filling mechanism to rectify conflict regions using the utterance-level label as a global prior, mitigating pseudo-label noise. Experiments on three datasets, IEMOCAP, EmoDB, and MELD, show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance without auxiliary text or elaborate structural redesigns.

title: Audio signal analysis
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 5 - Poster 5 - Audio signal analysis

items.title: FCPE: A Fast Context-based Pitch Estimation Model
items.authors: Yuxin Luo(Fish Audio); Ruoyi Zhang(Fish Audio); Lu-Chuan Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Tianyu Li(Fish Audio); Hangyu Liu(Fish Audio)
items.abstract: Pitch estimation (PE) in monophonic audio is crucial for MIDI transcription and singing voice conversion (SVC), but current deep learning methods often struggle to balance robust noise tolerance with computational efficiency. In this paper, we propose FCPE, a fast context-based pitch estimation model that employs a modified convolutional architecture with depth-wise separable convolutions to effectively capture mel spectrogram features while maintaining low computational cost and robust noise tolerance. Experiments show that our method achieves 96.79% Raw Pitch Accuracy (RPA) on the MIR-1K dataset, on par with the state-of-the-art methods. The Real-Time Factor (RTF) is 0.0062 on a single RTX 4090 GPU, which significantly outperforms existing algorithms in efficiency.

items.title: Audio-Visual Feature Reconstruction Pretraining for Noise-Robust Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Ivan Halim Parmonangan(Queensland University of Technology (QUT)); Tharindu Fernando(Queensland University of Technology (QUT)); Simon Denman(Queensland University of Technology (QUT))
items.abstract: Audiovisual emotion recognition fuses speech and facial expressions, yet real-world corruption such as background noise, reverberation, and dropped/frozen frames, can make the fusion fragile. A degraded input may dominate attention and suppress the clean input. Prior audiovisual pretraining solutions primarily optimize cross-modal alignment which can lose input details and often rely on Transformers, where the quadratic cost hinders long sequences. We propose a Mamba2 state-space fusion network with a self-supervised denoising pretraining stage, where clean features are reconstructed from corrupted audio-visual inputs only during pretraining to learn noise-robust representations. When applied to a downstream emotion recognition task, the proposed multimodal feature-reconstruction pretrained model delivers improvements under noisy audio and consistent gains over unimodal feature-reconstruction pretraining across diverse noisy/clean video settings, demonstrating improved robustness with efficient sequence modeling.

items.title: Smooth Formant Tracking with Differentiable Linear Prediction
items.authors: Bryn Luisi(Aalto University); Lauri Juvela(Aalto University)
items.abstract: Linear prediction methods for formant estimation are fast and interpretable, but assume local stationarity and Gaussian residuals. Hybrid neural methods are robust and accurate but lack interpretability and differentiability. We present LP-DDSP, a differentiable all-pole model that estimates formants by directly optimizing log-area ratios via a novel loss function that combines L1, L2, and temporal regularization terms. This approach addresses the limitations of classic LP by allowing for non-Gaussian residuals and smooth parameter tracks across frames. We also introduce SMELP, an end-to-end neural formant tracker that incorporates our differentiable LP loss, enabling joint learning of interpretable intermediate representations and formant predictions. Both methods achieve competitive performance relative to baselines: KARMA and Praat. Our methods enable fully differentiable, interpretable, and smooth formant tracking and can be extended to other speech processing tasks.

items.title: Automatic identification of the onset of creaky voice according to F0 instability
items.authors: Rasmus Puggaard-Rode(University of Oxford); Joshua Penney(Macquarie University)
items.abstract: Creaky voice serves a number of linguistic and extra-linguistic functions and is a commonly studied feature in phonetics. While methods are available for automatically evaluating whether creak is present within a window of speech, researchers who wish to identify transitions between creaky and modal portions of speech, and their precise temporal patterning, usually rely on manual annotation. In this paper, we propose a method for automatically identifying the onset of creak based on F0 instability, building on the common observation that creak is often accompanied by octave shifts. We evaluate the method by comparing automatically estimated with human-annotated creak onset from a previous study on creak as a cue to the coda voicing contrast in Australian English. The automatic method performs similarly to human annotators, and we show that our proposed automatic method and manual annotation yield similar results for the questions posed in the previous study.

items.title: Less is More: Boosting Bimodal Music Emotion Recognition with Adaptive Audio Sequence Compression
items.authors: Dinghao Zou(Wuhan University of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: Fusing audio and symbolic MIDI modalities delivers comprehensive affective cues for music emotion classification, yet audio features suffer from severe temporal redundancy compared with compact MIDI representations, leading to prominent information density imbalance that may hinder effective bimodal fusion. To address this, we exploit music's inherent temporal dynamics-preserving salient features in high-variation regions and averaging low-variation regions-we propose PoolingVQ. It leverages Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) to quantize local audio features into index sequences indicating local variation intensity, which guides dynamic pooling (e.g., max pooling for high-variation segments) to filter redundancy while retaining emotional dynamics. Experiments on EMOPIA and VGMIDI show that audio sequence compression via PoolingVQ facilitates effective bimodal fusion, achieving state-of-the-art performance, thus offering a practical scheme for audio multimodal fusion.

items.title: Differentiable Pitch Matching with Auditory Models
items.authors: David Marttila(Queen Mary University of London); Joshua D. Reiss(Queen Mary University of London)
items.abstract: Differentiable Digital Signal Processing models for audio synthesis often rely on external fundamental frequency estimators, as common loss functions like Multi-Scale Spectral Loss (MSS) provide uninformative gradients for frequency-related parameters. While recent spectral-based losses offer improvements, they can fail on signals where perceived pitch does not correspond to a prominent spectral peak, like in the case of a missing fundamental. We propose a novel, perceptually-informed distance metric for pitch based on features from a differentiable computational auditory model. By processing auditory images to extract a timbre-normalized representation of periodicity, our metric is more robust to timbral variations. We evaluate our approach on a synthetic pitch-matching task and show that it can provide more informative gradients than Spectral Optimal Transport and MSS baselines. This work is a step towards allowing end-to-end training of DDSP models without external pitch estimators.

items.title: Layer-wise Probing of Whisper's Encoder Representations for Bengali Phone-like Units
items.authors: Munim Thahmid(BUET); Sadia Sharmin(BUET)
items.abstract: We investigate where Bengali phone-like units become linearly separable across the encoder layers of OpenAI's Whisper. Phone-like segments are obtained via MMS forced alignment on uromanized transcripts, and lightweight linear probes are trained per layer under speaker-disjoint evaluation. Whisper-small and Whisper-medium both peak in the mid-to-late layers, whereas Whisper-large-v3 forms a broad late-layer plateau with markedly less final-layer degradation. A self-supervised baseline (wav2vec2-XLSR) shows a far steeper late-layer decline, suggesting that supervised ASR training preserves phonetic detail deeper into the encoder. Per-class F1 analysis reveals that aspirated stops and affricates are separable from early layers, while nasals and sibilants drive mid-layer gains. We further validate these findings with ABX discriminability, alignment-confidence filtering, duration stratification, and an English MFA cross-lingual baseline.

items.title: Aligning MusicLLM with Emotion using Instruction Tuning and Feedback-Driven Alignment
items.authors: Takuya Hasumi(LY Corporation); Welly Naptali(LY Corporation)
items.abstract: This paper investigates whether music large language models (MusicLLMs) can be aligned for emotion regression. While MusicLLMs have shown strong performance in music information retrieval tasks, their ability to predict arousal and valence scores remains limited, since emotion regression has not been an explicit training objective. To examine whether MusicLLMs can be aligned with emotion, we train MusicLLMs on emotion regression and compare two strategies: instruction tuning and feedback-driven alignment. Our experiments show that task-aware instruction tuning enables MusicLLMs to predict emotion levels to some extent, although the accuracy remains limited. Applying feedback-driven alignment with a verifiable numerical reward substantially improves performance on both arousal and valence over instruction tuning alone. We further show that our approach improves emotion regression performance while maintaining MusicQA capability.

items.title: MultiLinguahah : A New Unsupervised Multilingual Acoustic Laughter Segmentation Method
items.authors: Sofia Callejas(Université Paris-Saclay; Universidad de Chile); Nahuel Gomez(Universidad de Chile); Catherine Pelachaud(Sorbonne University); Brian Ravenet(Université Paris-Saclay); Valentin Barriere(Universidad de Chile)
items.abstract: Laughter is a social non-vocalization that is universal across cultures and languages, and is crucial for human communication, including social bonding and communication signaling. However, detecting laughter in audio is a challenging task, and segmenting it is even more difficult. Currently, Machine Learning methods generally rely on costly manual annotation, and their datasets are mostly based on English contexts. Thus, we propose an unsupervised multilingual method that sets up the laughter segmentation task as an anomaly detection of energy-based segmented audio sequences. Our method applies an Isolation Forest on audio representations learned from BYOL-A encoder. We compare our method with several state-of-the-art laughter detection algorithms on four datasets, including stand-up comedy, sitcoms, and general short audio from AudioSet. Our results show that state-of-the-art methods are not optimized for multilingual contexts, while our method outperforms them in non-English settings.

items.title: Boundaryless Speech-to-Syllable Representations with Hierarchical CNN for Linguistically Inspired Automatic Stress Detection
items.authors: Namrata Mokshagundam(IIIT Hyderabad); Sai Harshitha Aluru(IIIT Hyderabad); Chiranjeevi Yarra(IIIT Hyderabad)
items.abstract: In stress-timed languages like English, word stress placement can change meaning, making automatic syllable stress detection vital for Computer Assisted Language Learning (CALL) systems, as L2 learners often misplace stress. Existing approaches rely on manually annotated boundaries or forced alignment, which require extensive labeling and suffer from alignment inaccuracies. We propose a fully boundary-independent framework using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for hierarchical time-compression, converting frame-level embeddings into compact syllable-level representations without explicit segmentation. To enforce the linguistic constraint that each word contains exactly one stressed syllable, we also incorporate a Post-net2.0 loss. Experiments on the ISLE corpus with German (GER) and Italian (ITA) learners show consistent improvements over boundary-dependent and prior boundary-independent SOTA models, achieving 94.86% (GER) and 96.24% (ITA), with gains up to 18.67% and 16.12%.

items.title: Instantaneous Pitch Estimation via Wave-U-Net-Based Fundamental Waveform Enhancement
items.authors: Junya Koguchi(CyberAgent); Tomoki Koriyama(CyberAgent)
items.abstract: Instantaneous pitch estimation plays an important role in analyzing steep pitch variations such as speech prosody and singing techniques. Conventional approaches estimate instantaneous frequency after isolating the fundamental waveform from signals that contain harmonics and noise, which makes the accuracy sensitive to imperfect fundamental filtering. In this study, we formulate fundamental waveform filtering as a speech enhancement problem. Specifically, we train a Wave-U-Net model to extract a fundamental waveform from an input speech signal. The instantaneous pitch is then obtained by computing the instantaneous frequency from the analytic signal of the estimated fundamental waveform. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms conventional deterministic approaches and provides accurate and robust instantaneous pitch estimation across diverse domains, including speech, singing voice, musical instruments, and degraded speech signals.

title: Target Speaker Extraction, Speech Separation and Audio Understanding
