items.authors: Fernando López(Telefónica Innovación Digital; Universidad Autónoma de Madrid); Santosh Kesiraju(Brno University of Technology); Jordi Luque(Telefónica Innovación Digital)
items.abstract: Recent advances in large audio language models (LALMs) are primarily assessed using multiple-choice question answering (MCQA). However, subtle changes such as shifting choice order yield substantially different results. Moreover, textual questions and options contain linguistic hints that let models infer correct answers without relying on the audio. Existing MCQA frameworks ignore these concerns and report a single accuracy number. We dive into MCQA evaluation and conduct a systematic study spanning three benchmarks (MMAU, MMAR, MMSU) and four models: Audio Flamingo 2, Audio Flamingo 3, Qwen2.5-Omni-7B-Instruct, and Kimi-Audio-7B-Instruct. Our findings show that language bias is present across benchmarks, and models are sensitive not only to choice ordering but also to paraphrasing of questions and options. Finally, we propose a simpler evaluation protocol and metric that account for these variations and provide a more detailed assessment of LALMs within the MCQA framework.

items.title: Lost in Phonation: Voice Quality Variation as an Evaluation Dimension for Speech Foundation Models
items.authors: Harm Lameris(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Shree Harsha Bokkahalli Satish(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Joakim Gustafson(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Éva Székely(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Recent advances in Speech Foundation Models (SFMs) enable direct processing of raw audio, allowing models to respond to subtle paralinguistic variation. However, how these models interpret non-lexical cues remains largely unstudied. We introduce VQ-Bench, a controlled evaluation suite featuring a parallel dataset of synthesized modal, breathy, creaky, and end-creak phonation types. We evaluate SFM sensitivity through open-ended generation across four ecologically valid domains, alongside speech emotion recognition. Our results reveal performance gaps: while a leading commercial API failed basic biometric sanity checks, other models exhibited systematic shifts in agency, empathy, and leadership based on phonation. Our findings also highlight gender asymmetries in salary and leadership endorsements, demonstrating that SFMs may mirror or amplify human social biases. This work establishes a reproducible framework for ensuring responsible paralinguistic interpretation in speech-based AI.

items.title: Audio2Tool: Speak, Call, Act - A Dataset for Benchmarking Speech Tool Use
items.authors: Ramit Pahwa(Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies); Apoorva Beedu(Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies); Parivesh Priye(Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies); Rutu Gandhi(Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies); Saloni Takawale(Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies); Aruna Baijal(Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies); Zengli Yang(Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies)
items.abstract: Voice assistants increasingly rely on SpeechLMs to interpret spoken queries and execute complex tasks, yet, existing benchmarks lack domain breadth, acoustic diversity, and compositional reasoning complexity to evaluate tool-calling performance. We introduce Audio2Tool, a large scale dataset comprising 30,000 queries designed to assess tool-calling capabilities of SpeechLMs across three primary domains: Smart Car, Smart Home, and Wearables. Our benchmark features a multi-tier complexity hierarchy, ranging from simple direct commands to complex multi-intent and needle-in-a-haystack extraction to isolate distinct failure modes. To ensure realism, we employ zero-shot voice cloning TTS and diverse noise profiles to simulate in-the-wild conditions. Evaluations of state-of-the-art SpeechLMs and ASR-LLM pipelines show strong performance on simple commands but significant degradation under compositional and acoustic challenges. Code and dataset are publicly available on the project page: https://audio2tool.github.io/.

items.title: ML-KD-DRI-GAN: Teacher-Guided Denoising and Triplet-Adversarial Training for Robust Spoken Language Understanding
items.authors: Ankit Kumar(Galgotias University, India); Munir Georges(Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt, Germany)
items.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors substantially degrade Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) by distorting semantic representations. We propose Multi-level Knowledge-Distillation DRI-GAN (ML-KD-DRI-GAN), a teacher-guided adversarial denoising framework that maps noisy embeddings onto a clean semantic manifold. A teacher model is first trained on clean transcripts, after which the student model is learned through (i) multi-level latent alignment at the generator to denoise noisy embeddings and (ii) Bi-discriminator-cooperated distillation (Bi-DCD) at the discriminator to transfer teacher discriminative knowledge. We further introduce a synthetic generator to produce hard negatives and enforce triplet separation among clean, denoised, and synthetic samples to improve robustness. Experiments on noisy SLU benchmarks show consistent gains over GAN-BERT baselines. On the SLURP dataset, ML-KD-DRI-GAN achieves absolute improvements of 4.49% and 6.46% under moderate and severe ASR noise.

items.title: Discrete vs. Continuous: A Comprehensive Study of Unified Audio Understanding in LALMs
items.authors: Jing Peng(Tsinghua University); Zichao Nie(Tsinghua University); Zhisheng Zhang(Tsinghua University); Jingran Xie(Tsinghua University); Zhiyong Wu(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) utilize either continuous features or discrete tokens, yet the optimal representation paradigm for general audio understanding remains debated. Existing benchmarks often focus on narrow domains or evaluate encoders outside LALM contexts. To address these gaps, we systematically evaluate continuous and discrete representations across speech, sound and music. Utilizing our UniARC framework with dual evaluation strategies across model scales from SmolLM2-135M to Llama-3-8B, we analyze the dynamic relationships of data volume, model capacity, and computational efficiency. Our results reveal the pivotal role of semantic constraints in tokenization for audio understanding and demonstrate that scaling backbones fail to compensate for information loss in audio representation, especially in data-limited tasks. These findings offer practical guidance for balancing semantic density, fidelity, and efficiency in future LALMs.

items.title: Towards Enabling Multilingual Multitask SpeechLLMs in Data-Scarce Settings
items.authors: Seraphina Fong(University of Trento; Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Marco Matassoni(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Alessio Brutti(Fondazione Bruno Kessler)
items.abstract: Speech-based Large Language Models (SpeechLLMs) are moving towards supporting multiple languages and tasks. However, prior work often studies multilinguality and multitask learning separately or use large training corpora. We present a study of multilingual multitask SpeechLLMs under low-resource conditions, extending beyond ASR to speech translation and topic classification. Building on evidence that high-resource ASR pretraining enables cross-lingual transfer, we examine whether this generalizes to multitask SpeechLLMs. Using only 3-5 hours of labeled data per task and language, we show that bootstrapping from ASR-pretrained projectors enables effective multitask adaptation. We find that cross-lingual performance is influenced by language similarity, while zero-shot generalization does not extend to unseen tasks. Overall, our results demonstrate that ASR-pretrained bootstrapping and limited target-language finetuning enable multilingual multitask SpeechLLMs in low-resource settings.

title: Corpus Creation, Summerisation and Understanding
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 12 - Oral 6 - Corpus Creation, Summerisation and Understanding

items.title: Segment-level Tree Search for Long Meeting Document Summarization
items.authors: Sangwon Ryu(POSTECH); Heejin Do(ETH AI Center); Jun Seo(POSTECH); Daehui Kim(KT); Yunsu Kim(LILT); Gary Geunbae Lee(POSTECH); Jungseul Ok(POSTECH)
items.abstract: Meeting documents are challenging to summarize due to their length and complex conversational structure. Existing approaches typically adopt multi-stage pipelines that extract information prior to summarization; however, these approaches often suffer from cumulative error propagation without intermediate validation, a limitation further amplified by short and low-quality reference summaries. We propose segment-level summarization via Monte Carlo Tree Search (S3), a training-free framework that constructs a final summary by composing segment-level summary candidates. S3 partitions a long document into segments and generates multiple summary candidates per segment, forming nodes of a search tree. The best-scoring combination is selected via self-reward-guided tree search and refined into the final output. Despite using a 7B model, S3 achieves performance comparable to larger 72B models while producing length-appropriate summaries.

items.title: A Unified and Reproducible Experimentation Framework for Speech Understanding
items.authors: Jing Peng(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Junhao Du(AISpeech); Chenghao Wang(AISpeech); Hanqi Li(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.); Yi Yang(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.); Xiaoyu Gu(AISpeech); Guanyu Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.); Yixuan Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.); Haoyu Li(ETH Zurich); Zhangjie Zhao(Hangzhou Dianzi Univ.); Li Jiang(Hangzhou Dianzi Univ.); Haoran Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.); Wenming Tu(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.); Yucheng Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.); Jiaqi Guo(AISpeech); Hui Zhang(AISpeech); Shuai Fan(AISpeech); Wenbin Jiang(Hangzhou Dianzi Univ.); Shuai Wang(Nanjing University); Kai Yu(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.)
items.abstract: Speech foundation models and Speech LLMs have advanced speech understanding, yet deployment-oriented model selection is hindered by non-comparable evaluations caused by mismatched post-processing, and by training results that are hard to reproduce across data scales and pipelines. We present SURE, a unified experimentation framework that standardizes prediction formats, normalization, and scoring. SURE evaluates strong systems across paradigms, from conventional pipelines to Speech LLMs, on representative tasks under realistic acoustic and linguistic stressors. Beyond evaluation, SURE introduces an agent-assisted training conversion flow that maps paper and code into versioned, runnable training pipelines under a unified protocol on matched open-data subsets. Overall, SURE improves comparability and reproducibility for deployment-oriented evaluation.

items.title: Bridging Languages and Modalities: Lightweight Cross-Lingual Text and Speech Summarization for Low-Resource Scenarios
items.authors: Chaimae Chellaf(LIA - Avignon Université; Lundi Matin); Salima Mdhaffar(LIA - Avignon Université); Yannick Estève(LIA - Avignon Université); Stéphane Huet(LIA - Avignon Université)
items.abstract: Cross-lingual summarization aims to condense written or spoken content in one language into a coherent and concise summary in another language. This task requires understanding the source language's nuances, filtering for importance, and reconstructing meaning in a different grammar and vocabulary; these operations are particularly difficult to perform when the available data are scarce to train models. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that uses multilingual sentence and utterance embeddings to process both speech and text inputs under strict data constraints. Based on the CrossSum dataset and a new cross-lingual speech evaluation dataset we collected for three low-resource languages, our experimental results highlight the strong potential of our approach for cross-lingual summarization, particularly in low-resource spoken language scenarios.

items.title: Easper: An Accessible ASR Pipeline for Language Documentation
items.authors: Aso Mahmudi(The University of Melbourne); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne); Ekaterina Vylomova(The University of Melbourne); Nick Thieberger(The University of Melbourne)
items.abstract: Audio transcription is a critical bottleneck in language documentation. While multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models like Whisper offer solutions, field linguists often lack the expertise to utilise them. We present Easper, an open-source, no-code workflow enabling linguists to iteratively fine-tune ASR models via cloud resources directly from ELAN annotations. Deploying ASR also raises a cold start problem: deciding which recordings to transcribe first to bootstrap an accurate model. Using Easper, we evaluate transcription prioritisation strategies on three Vanuatu languages (Bislama, Nafsan, Nguna). We fine-tune models by recording session, comparing Character Error Rate trajectories when prioritising acoustic cleanliness versus linguistic richness. We demonstrate that prioritising lexically rich narratives and increasing acoustic-phonetic repetition, even in noisy environments, leads to faster improvements in transcription quality.

items.title: VāṇīSetu: A Human-AI Collaborative Framework for Scalable Conversational Speech Corpus Creation in Low-Resource Settings
items.authors: Rishabh Kumar(IIT Bombay); Dhruv Kudale(IIT Bombay); Chriss Philip Saji(UST); Abhinav Painuli(University of Delhi); John Nirmal(BharatGen); Ganesh Ramakrishnan(IIT Bombay)
items.abstract: We present VāṇīSetu, a human-AI collaborative framework for constructing high-quality speech corpora in low-resource languages. As a case study, we apply VāṇīSetu to create KrishiVāṇī, a Hindi dataset of agricultural speech. VāṇīSetu integrates automatic speech recognition (ASR), lightweight and large language model-based post-correction, and structured, multi-stage human validation implemented through an enhanced annotation tool, Vāgyojaka. Our key technical contribution is a role-separated, incentive-linked validation architecture (Annotator → Validator → Verifier) with threshold-gated quality control, which, to our knowledge, has not been previously deployed for low-resource Indic conversational speech corpus creation. In a controlled annotation study, we show that mT5-based post-correction yields a 61.1% reduction in annotation effort, while preserving transcript fidelity. We further show that smaller fine-tuned LMs, outperform larger LLMs for in-domain correction.

items.title: IPA-Guided Dual Transcription for Data-Centric Speech Corpus Refinement
items.authors: Jeong-Ju Choi(Dencomm); Young-Ik Kim(Dencomm); Jin NamGoong(Dencomm); Jaeyeon Jang(Dencomm; The Catholic University of Korea)
items.abstract: High-quality speech corpora require consistent alignment between spoken and written text, yet the many-to-many mapping between them introduces ambiguity, leading to transcription inconsistencies that ultimately degrade performance on downstream tasks. To mitigate this inherent ambiguity, we propose a data-centric framework that leverages IPA-guided dual transcription to achieve consistent spoken-written alignment. The framework combines (1) a phoneme intermediate conditional speech-to-text model that outputs both IPA and orthographic text, and (2) a fine-tuned large language model that generates consistent spoken-written pairs from orthographic and phonetic inputs. By grounding normalization in phonetic realizations rather than text alone, the framework enables iterative refinement of noisy or domain-specific corpora. Experiments show that IPA-guided dual transcription yields substantial performance improvements in text normalization and domain ASR through corpus refinement.

title: Spoofing, Deepfake Detection and Watermarking
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Long Oral 3 - Spoofing, Deepfake Detection and Watermarking [Cross-area long papers Oral session]

items.title: Learning to Evade: Adaptive Attacks on Audio Watermarking
items.authors: Weikang Ding(UMKC); Hanqing Guo(University of Hawaii at Manoa); Rui Duan(UMKC); Guangjing Wang(University of South Florida); Yuanda Wang(Michigan State University); Mingzhe Chen(University of Miami); Qiben Yan(Michigan State University)
items.abstract: Advances in generative audio have intensified copyright concerns, making audio watermarking increasingly important for asserting ownership. However, existing audio watermarking methods are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. We find that watermark decoder message probabilities follow normal distributions, a property exploited by defenses to detect manipulations. This paper introduces an adaptive audio watermark attack method (AWM) designed to bypass existing defense strategies. AWM uses a two-stage optimization: the first stage ensures attack success, while the second improves audio quality. To evade detection, it estimates normal distribution parameters from limited samples of the target audio, and then adaptively steers decoded probabilities back into the estimated range. Evaluated on two watermarking methods across three voice datasets, AWM achieves high success while bypassing state-of-the-art detectors: detection rates are below 10% for replacement and creation, and 0% for removal.

items.title: Joint Fullband-Subband Modeling for High-Resolution SingFake Detection
items.authors: Chia-Yu Hu(National Taiwan University); Xuanjun Chen(National Taiwan University); Sung-Feng Huang(NVIDIA Taiwan); Haibin Wu(Independent Researcher); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University; NTU AI-CoRE); Jyh-Shing Roger Jang(National Taiwan University)
items.abstract: Rapid advances in singing voice synthesis have increased unauthorized imitation risks, creating an urgent need for better Singing Voice Deepfake (SingFake) Detection, also known as SVDD. Unlike speech, singing contains complex pitch, wide dynamic range, and timbral variations. Conventional 16 kHz-sampled detectors prove inadequate, as they discard vital high-frequency information. This study presents the first systematic analysis of high-resolution (44.1 kHz sampling rate) audio for SVDD. We propose a joint fullband-subband modeling framework: the fullband captures global context, while subband-specific experts isolate fine-grained synthesis artifacts unevenly distributed across the spectrum. Experiments on the WildSVDD dataset demonstrate that high-frequency subbands provide essential complementary cues. Our framework significantly outperforms 16 kHz-sampled models, proving that high-resolution audio and strategic subband integration are critical for robust in-the-wild detection.

items.title: Latent-Mark: An Audio Watermark Robust to Neural Codec Compression
items.authors: Yen-Shan Chen(National Taiwan University; CyCraft AI Lab); Shih-Yu Lai(National Taiwan University; RIKEN-CCS; MoonShine Animation Studio); Ying-Jung Tsou(National Taiwan University); Yi-Cheng Lin(National Taiwan University); Bing-Yu Chen(National Taiwan University); Yun-Nung Chen(National Taiwan University); Hung-yi Lee(NTU AI-CoRE; National Taiwan University); Shang-Tse Chen(National Taiwan University)
items.abstract: While existing audio watermarking techniques have achieved strong robustness against traditional digital signal processing (DSP) attacks, they remain vulnerable to neural compression. This occurs because modern neural audio codecs act as noise filters and discard the imperceptible waveform variations used in prior watermarking methods. To address this limitation, we propose Latent-Mark, the first zero-bit audio watermarking framework designed to survive neural codec compression. Our key insight is that robustness to the encode-decode process requires embedding the watermark within the codec's invariant latent space. We achieve this by optimizing the audio waveform to induce a detectable directional shift in its encoded latent representation, while constraining perturbations to align with the natural audio manifold to ensure imperceptibility. To prevent overfitting to a single codec's quantization rules, we introduce Cross-Codec Optimization, jointly optimizing the waveform across multiple surrogate codecs to target shared latent invariants. Extensive evaluations demonstrate robust zero-shot transferability to unseen neural codecs, achieving competitive resilience against traditional DSP attacks while preserving perceptual imperceptibility. We hope our work will inspire future research into universal watermarking frameworks capable of maintaining integrity across increasingly complex and diverse generative distortions.

items.title: Temporal Transition-Aware Multi-Head Modeling for Partially Spoofed Audio Detection and Localization
items.authors: Yunsu Kim(Sungkyunkwan University; University of Toronto); Juyeob Lee(Sungkyunkwan University); Eunil Park(Sungkyunkwan University; Jaume I University)
items.abstract: Partially spoofed audio localization aims to detect short manipulated spans within an utterance. Most prior work formulates the task as binary frame authenticity or boundary detection, which overlooks how neighboring frames evolve across manipulations. In this paper, we argue that directional inter-frame changes provide a more reliable localization cue, and propose a transition-aware framework that classifies Real to Fake and Fake to Real transitions. Our method combines a multi-scale GRU backbone for local continuity and long-range flow with a multi-head objective: a frame head for authenticity, a transition head for adjacent-frame transitions, and a refinement head that fuses both signals for temporally coherent predictions. Experiments on the PartialSpoof Dataset and the PartialEdit-E1/E2 show state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of temporal-order modeling for partially spoofed audio localization at a challenging 20 ms resolution.

items.title: Lightweight Detection and Model Attribution of Synthetic Speech via Residual Statistical Fingerprints
items.authors: Matías Pizarro(Ruhr University Bochum); Mike Laszkiewicz(LKA NRW); Dorothea Kolossa(Technische Universität Berlin); Asja Fischer(Ruhr University Bochum)
items.abstract: As speech generation technologies advance, so do risks of impersonation, misinformation, and spoofing. We present a lightweight, training-free method for synthetic speech detection and source model attribution. Our method builds on model-specific fingerprints that are computed as the average of the differences between audio signals and their filtered versions, referred to as residuals. Leveraging the Mahalanobis distance of the residual for a given audio signal to these model-specific fingerprints allows to identify the source model as well as to distinguish real from fake audio. A broad set of experiments across multiple synthesis systems and languages demonstrate a supreme performance of the proposed approach on four tasks: open-world single-model attribution, closed-world multi-model attribution, real vs. synthetic speech classification, and out-of-domain detection.

items.title: DeepFense: A Unified, Modular, and Extensible Framework for Robust Audio Deepfake Detection
items.authors: Yassine El Kheir(DFKI); Arnab Das(DFKI); Yixuan Xiao(University of Stuttgart); Xin Wang(National Insitute of Informatics); Feidi Kallel(DFKI); Enes Erdem Erdogan(DFKI); Ngoc Thang Vu(University of Stuttgart); Tim Polzehl(DFKI); Sebastian Möller(Technical University of Berlin)
items.abstract: Speech deepfake detection is a well-established research field with different models, datasets, and training strategies. However, the lack of standardized implementations and evaluation protocols limits reproducibility, benchmarking, and comparison across studies. In this work, we present DeepFense, a comprehensive, open-source PyTorch toolkit integrating the latest architectures, loss functions, and augmentation pipelines, alongside over 100 recipes. Using DeepFense, we conducted a large-scale evaluation of more than 400 models. Our findings reveal that while carefully curated training data improves cross-domain generalization, the choice of pre-trained front-end feature extractor dominates overall performance variance. Crucially, we show severe biases in high-performing models regarding audio quality, speaker gender, and language. DeepFense is expected to facilitate real-world deployment with the necessary tools to address equitable training data selection and front-end fine-tuning.

title: Audio-Visual and Multimodal Perception
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Long Oral 15 - Audio-Visual and Multimodal Perception [Cross-area long papers Oral session]

items.title: Dr. SHAP-AV: Decoding Relative Modality Contributions via Shapley Attribution in Audio-Visual Speech Recognition
items.authors: Umberto Cappellazzo(Imperial College London); Stavros Petridis(Imperial College London; Natwest AI Research); Maja Pantic(Imperial College London; Natwest AI Research)
items.abstract: Audio-Visual Speech Recognition (AVSR) leverages both acoustic and visual information for robust recognition under noise. However, how models balance these modalities remains unclear. We present Dr. SHAP-AV, a framework using Shapley values to analyze modality contributions in AVSR. Through experiments on six models across two benchmarks and varying SNR levels, we introduce three analyses: Global SHAP for overall modality balance, Generative SHAP for contribution dynamics during decoding, and Temporal Alignment SHAP for input-output correspondence. Our findings reveal that models shift toward visual reliance under noise yet maintain high audio contributions even under severe degradation. Modality balance evolves during generation, temporal alignment holds under noise, and SNR is the dominant factor driving modality weighting. These findings expose a persistent audio bias, motivating ad-hoc modality-weighting mechanisms and Shapley-based attribution as a standard AVSR diagnostic. Project website: https://umbertocappellazzo.github.io/Dr-SHAP-AV

items.title: Assessing True Generalisability of Audio-Visual Speech Recognisers
items.authors: Zhaofeng Lin(Trinity College Dublin; Imperial College London); Stavros Petridis(Imperial College London; NatWest AI Research); Maja Pantic(Imperial College London; NatWest AI Research); Naomi Harte(Trinity College Dublin)
items.abstract: Current Audio-Visual Speech Recognition (AVSR) models achieve near-perfect performance on the standard LRS3 benchmark, raising concerns of adaptive overfitting. To systematically assess true generalisability, we construct a highly controlled, unseen evaluation set subsampled from the massive MultiVSR dataset. Unlike standard out-of-distribution benchmarks, our subset strictly matches the acoustic, visual, and demographic distributions of the LRS3 test set. Evaluating five state-of-the-art architectures reveals a universal performance collapse, proving that current systems fail to generalise even under strictly aligned conditions. Through a fine-grained attribute analysis across seven factors, we isolate the specific drivers of this degradation. Furthermore, we uncover a profound lexical bias, expose distinct error patterns, and surprisingly reveal that audio-visual performance even lags behind audio-only settings. We release our matched test set for future benchmarking.

items.title: The Lipreading Gap: Do VSR Models Perceive Visual Speech Like Human Lipreaders?
items.authors: Rishabh Jain(Trinity College Dublin); Naomi Harte(Trinity College Dublin)
items.abstract: Visual speech recognition (VSR) models now surpass human lipreaders on benchmarks, but do such gains establish human-like visual speech perception? To explore this, we compare three VSR systems with human baselines on the MaFI word-level lipreading dataset using word, character, phoneme, and viseme-level metrics. Although models achieve higher overall accuracy, they succeed and fail on different words than humans. A text-only n-gram baseline given only a few initial phonemes rivals human lipreading. VSR word-level errors are consistently better explained by training word frequency than by the visual informativeness of words. Viseme accuracies, confusion matrices and human-model correlations further show that models gain most on visemes humans find hardest, and show much weaker dependence on visual clarity. Our work demonstrates that VSR systems rely primarily on language cues from training data rather than visual perception, failing to bind visual features into meaningful words.

items.title: The Illusion of Balanced Multimodal Sentiment Analysis: Beyond the Limits of Optimization-Based Methods
items.authors: Ioanna Kaffeza(Mines Paris-PSL University); Efthymios Georgiou(University of Bern); Alexandros Potamianos(National Technical University of Athens; Archimedes AI; Synaptic Bloom PBC)
items.abstract: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) remains constrained by modality imbalance, yet the field continues to rely on optimization-based balancing methods that promise more than they deliver. We provide three contributions: 1) a unified evaluation framework testing gradient and loss-based balancing strategies under controlled settings; 2) a theoretical diagnosis explaining why these methods fail, as they conflate fitting speed with discriminative contribution; and 3) a research agenda toward held-out discriminative modality valuation. Experiments on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI reveal three shortcomings: no strategy reliably outperforms Late Concatenation; performance is sensitive to hyperparameters; and even ratio calibration fails to yield consistent gains. The core issue is fundamental: loss is not utility, and gradients are not importance. Modality imbalance remains unresolved, motivating utility estimation from held-out performance.

items.title: MOV-AAD: A Large-Scale Multimodal Dataset for Auditory Attention Decoding During Moving Conversations
items.authors: Xiaomin He(Columbia University); Vishal Choudhari(Columbia University); Tristan J. Spratt(Columbia University); Aarya Raghavan(Columbia University); Richard T. Lee(Columbia University); Nima Mesgarani(Columbia University)
items.abstract: Auditory attention decoding (AAD) is often evaluated on static, simplified speech scenes that poorly match everyday listening. We introduce MOV-AAD, a large-scale dataset for studying auditory attention under moving, naturalistic conversations. MOV-AAD combines 64-channel EEG with synchronized physiological recordings, including eye tracking, respiration, galvanic skin response, heart rate, peripheral oxygen saturation, body temperature, body motion, and photoplethysmography, enabling analysis of cross-modal neural and physiological markers of attention and listening effort. This dataset uses a more ecologically valid listening paradigm with dynamically moving conversational speech sources and behavioral measures of attentional engagement. MOV-AAD supports research on robust AAD in realistic spatial dynamics, multimodal attention modeling, listening effort, and intersubject neural responses, providing a resource for benchmarking selective auditory attention in naturalistic listening.

title: Speech Production and Perception 1
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 1 - Poster 1 - Speech Production and Perception 1

items.title: SELFIX: An Interactive System for Natural Self-Voice Approximation
items.authors: Pavo Orepic(University of Zurich); Steven Moran(University of Zurich; University of Neuchâtel); Volker Dellwo(University of Zurich; )
items.abstract: Most of us feel discomfort when we hear our recorded voice. This is because our voice is filtered by head vibrations during natural speech. Characterizing this filter may therefore recreate natural self-voice. Previous attempts relied on spectral equalization and failed to converge on a universal filter, likely due to unguided search across vast acoustic spaces. We introduce SELFIX, an interactive system that constrains this search with perceptually motivated dimensions, such as pitch and vocal-tract control. In a preliminary study (N = 25), participants repeatedly adjusted four randomized, unlabeled sliders. Consistent adjustments with high match and confidence ratings support SELFIX's validity. While all participants boosted low frequencies, males also lowered pitch and increased vocal-tract length, indicating that self-voice approximation extends beyond mere spectral equalization. These findings establish a structured acoustic basis for scalable, personalized self-voice modeling.

items.title: Noise Scaling Factor for the One-Dimensional Voice Production Model
items.authors: Tsukasa Yoshinaga(University of Osaka); Takeshi Ikuma(Louisiana State University); Brad H. Story(University of Arizona)
items.abstract: Sounds generated by turbulence at the glottis, such as those observed in breathy voice, affect voice quality. Although aerodynamic noise originating in the vocal tract has been incorporated in one-dimensional (1D) acoustic models, the accuracy of these models has rarely been examined. In this study, we evaluated the scaling factor used in a 1D noise model for vowel /a/ and /u/ by comparing with results from three-dimensional (3D) flow simulations that explicitly computes sound generation from turbulent airflow. Results showed that, for normal phonation in the vowel /a/, the conventional scaling factor yielded good agreement with the 3D results. In contrast, in breathy phonation where the glottis did not fully close, and in configurations with supraglottal constrictions of vowel /u/, the optimal scaling factor changed from the conventional value. These findings suggest that turbulence noise modeling in 1D approaches needs to be adjusted to the flow configuration of the vocal tract.

items.title: Improved modeling of vocal fold contacting and de-contacting in a geometric vocal fold model
items.authors: Tianyi Zhang(TU Dresden); Zihao Huang(TU Dresden); Peter Birkholz(Dresden University of Technology, Germany)
items.abstract: This paper presents a geometric model of the vocal folds for more natural-sounding articulatory speech synthesis. In contrast to similar models, we propose a biomechanically-motivated more gradual opening and closing of the glottis during the phases of partial contact of the vocal folds. This was combined with a mechanism to skew the glottal area waveform to the left or right. The model was implemented in the articulatory speech synthesizer and compared against a similar model without the improved contacting and de-contacting mechanisms in a perception experiment with synthetic sentences for a range of pre-phonatory model settings. In an A/B comparison, the synthetic sentences with the new model were preferred over the same sentences with the previous model in 58.1 % of the comparisons. In addition, the mean opinion scores for the quality on a five-point scale were 3.02 and 2.68 for the new and previous models, respectively.

items.title: The Effect of Neck Skin Vibration on the Periauricular Acoustic Receiver
items.authors: Ruoyan Li(Huawei); Yuhao Sun(Huawei); Fan Fan(Huawei)
items.abstract: During self-voicing, vocal cord vibrations propagate through the vocal tract and surrounding tissues, generating air-borne acoustic components radiated from the oral cavity as well as structural vibrations in the neck and its surface. This study investigates the impact of neck skin vibrations on periauricular acoustic receivers during self-voicing. The recordings were acquired under self-speech conditions using an array of microphones positioned at various locations on the head. Comparative analyses were conducted using experiments with a dummy head, real human speech tests and simulations. The results showed that periauricular acoustic receivers located near the neck detected significant air-borne acoustic components associated with neck skin vibrations. This finding holds significant implications for refining self-speech simulation models that treat mouth radiation as the sole acoustic source.

items.title: Investigating Human-Model Discrepancies in Speech Quality Assessment via Acoustic and Prosodic Perturbations
items.authors: Masato Takagi(Nagoya Institute of Technology); Masaya Kawamura(LY Corporation); Reo Shimizu(LY Corporation); Yuma Shirahata(LY Corporation)
items.abstract: Mean opinion score (MOS) prediction models are widely used as proxy metrics in text-to-speech (TTS) research, yet their ability to capture quality differences beyond acoustic fidelity remains unclear. We investigate this via controlled perturbations on speech: acoustic degradation, prosodic errors, and manipulation of speaker-specific characteristics such as pitch and speaking rate. We obtained MOS predictions for these speech samples from both human listeners and the model, and analyzed the differences in their perceptual characteristics. Results show that most models track acoustic degradation well, while all are insensitive to prosodic errors despite large subjective score drops. For speaker characteristics, models exhibit a double dissociation: strong mean fundamental frequency (F0) biases absent in human ratings, yet insensitivity to speaking rate and F0 variability that humans notice. These findings highlight limitations of scalar MOS prediction beyond acoustic fidelity.

items.title: Do speech foundation models perceive speaker similarity as humans do?
items.authors: Minoru Kishi(Keio University); Hayato Yagi(Keio University); Shinnosuke Takamichi(Keio University; The University of Tokyo); Yuki Saito(The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: This study presents a comparative analysis between the speaker embeddings of speech foundation models and human subjective perception of speaker similarity. Human listeners have the ability to judge speaker similarity on a continuous scale discerning how similar two voices are. In contrast, speech foundation models embed speaker characteristics into numerical representation. However, a question remains: does the numerical distance between speaker embeddings in these models truly align with the similarity perceived by humans? To address this, we conduct a comprehensive investigation using more than 40 models to compare model-derived distances with human-perceived similarity scores. Furthermore, we identify which factors in model configuration contribute most to a speaker embedding that mirrors human perception. Our findings provide insights for the development of more perceptually grounded speech foundation models.

items.title: What Makes Us Hate Our Own Voice? Large-scale experiments on Playback–Imagery Gaps and Individual--Speech Feature Effects
items.authors: Koki Fukuda(Keio University); Shinnosuke Takamichi(Keio University; The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: This study examines factors associated with the playback-imagery gap underlying voice confrontation. Listening to one's recorded voice (playback) can be uncomfortable and has been attributed to a mismatch between expected self-voice (imagery) and the recording, yet the factors associated with this gap remain unclear. With Japanese participants (N = 459), we compared impression ratings after playback of one's recorded utterances versus imagery of producing the same utterances using counterbalanced block order. Playback produced more negative affective evaluations than imagery, especially higher discomfort, whereas self-likeness did not show the same pattern. Exploratory trait-acoustic interactions suggested listener-specific weighting of acoustic cues in self-voice evaluation. The gap also varied with order and block structure, suggesting contextual modulation. These results provide evidence relevant to self-voice aversion and motivate listener-adaptive models and more controlled follow-up studies for self-voice applications.

items.title: SGAD: A State-Guided Adaptive Decision Framework for Robust EEG-Based Auditory Attention Switch Decoding
items.authors: Yuting Ding(Southern University of Science and Technology); Xuefei Wang(Southern University of Science and Technology); Ximin Chen(Southern University of Science and Technology); Chunlin Li(Capital Medical University); Fei Chen(Southern University of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: Achieving robust EEG-based auditory attention switch decoding (AASD) is crucial for intelligent hearing aids. However, its application is limited as EEG non-stationarity complicates sequential decision-making, and insufficient control of potential confounding factors may overestimate performance. Therefore, we propose a state-guided adaptive decision (SGAD) framework that infers attention transition states via causal state detection and dynamically modulates temporal smoothing through state-guided adaptive gating. We further introduce six hierarchical evaluation protocols to assess generalization across audio, speaker, and subject dimensions. Experimental results show that SGAD improves decoding accuracy and stability while maintaining low response latency across evaluation scenarios. Performance variations across protocols further suggest data partition-related biases. Together, these findings advance robust AASD for neuro-steered hearing applications.

items.title: LipAdapter: Text-to-Video Alignment is All You Need for Lip-to-Speech
items.authors: Souvik Ghosh(IIIT Hyderabad); C. V. Jawahar(IIIT Hyderabad); Vinay Namboodiri(University of Bath)
items.abstract: Lip-to-Speech synthesis aims to generate intelligible, natural-sounding, and temporally synchronized speech from silent visual recordings of a speaker. Although recent end-to-end models have shown promising results, they require large amounts of training data and often lack out-of-dataset generalization. In this work, we introduce LipAdapter, a generic and efficient modular framework that adapts an existing frozen pre-trained Text-to-Speech model into a lip-synchronized speech generator. LipAdapter bridges the modularity gap between frozen Visual Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech models by aligning phoneme representation and lip embeddings via a novel text-to-video alignment module. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks in English while using 15× less training data than previous methods. We also demonstrate the model's zero-shot capabilities in multilingual lip-to-speech synthesis in French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. Code and demo are available at: https://lipadapter.github.io/.

items.title: How Bilingual Are SSL Speech Models? Cross-Lingual Probing of Articulatory Encoding with Finnish and Russian EMA
items.authors: Ailín Pollio San Pedro(University Grenoble Alpes); Tomi Kinnunen(University of Eastern Finland); Alexandre Nikolaev(University of Eastern Finland); Ruchi Pandey(University of Eastern Finland)
items.abstract: SSL speech models capture rich phonetic, prosodic, and acoustic patterns from raw audio, yet how they encode articulatory information across diverse languages remains unclear. Using EMA data from bilingual Finnish–Russian speakers, we evaluate cross-lingual correlations between SSL latent representations and articulatory movements. Models achieve strong prediction performance (Pearson r up to 0.68) even with ~5 minutes of training data, with multilingual models outperforming monolingual ones. Intermediate layers encode articulatory features most effectively, and tongue movements are more predictable than lip movements. We also assess the impact of task type (read versus spontaneous speech) and language proficiency, finding higher accuracy for structured tasks and strong generalization across proficiency levels. These results enhance the interpretability of SSL models and show their potential for speech-technology applications.

title: Cross-Linguistic and L2 Phonetic Studies
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 2 - Poster 2 - Cross-Linguistic and L2 Phonetic Studies

items.title: Perception of English /iː/–/ɪ/ by Japanese Listeners under Silent-Centre and Devoiced Vowel Conditions
items.authors: Shinichi Tokuma(Chuo University)
items.abstract: This study examined Japanese listeners' perception of the English /iː/-/ɪ/ contrast under 'silent-centre' and devoiced vowel conditions, extending previous 'silent-centre' research by incorporating vowel devoicing and aspiration. The results show that L2 vowel perception is strongly shaped by L1 Japanese phonological knowledge, particularly duration-based effects and clipping-induced effects linked to gemination. Contrary to prediction, stimuli with high-frequency components of the devoiced vowel and the presence of aspiration did not improve identification accuracy. Instead, Japanese listeners with lower English proficiency appeared not to exploit spectral information associated with devoicing or aspiration, which is consistent with earlier findings.

items.title: Applying the Simplified Vocal Profile Analysis to Swiss German Dialects
items.authors: Alessia Wüst(University of Berne); Adrian Leemann(University of Berne)
items.abstract: This work presents the first perceptual investigation of vocal profiles in Swiss German, utilizing data from 127 speakers (aged 18-40) from the Swiss Dialäktatlas. Using Simplified Vocal Profile Analysis, four coders assessed vocal profiles to map geographic and social trends. While inter-rater reliability proved challenging (κ=0.09-0.39), consensus coding revealed clear stratification. Regarding gender, men typically exhibited a relaxed vocal tract ('hypoarticulation'), whereas women showed a tendency toward pharyngeal expansion ('hyperarticulation'). Geographically, Northeast Switzerland is characterized by nasality, while Central Switzerland is marked by pharyngeal expansion - a finding likely confounded by the gender distribution in the sample. Notably, creaky voice remains rare in Swiss German. These results suggest that while vocal profiles function as salient markers of regional and social identity, methodological complexities call for refined protocols in future research.

items.title: The Role of Context and Prosody in the Understanding of English Irony by Chinese L2 Learners
items.authors: Yinan Lin(Nanjing University of Science and Technology); Shanpeng Li(Nanjing University of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: Irony conveys a meaning opposite to its literal expression and is frequently used for humorous, critical, or satirical purposes. Because of its ambiguity, ironic interpretation relies heavily on contextual cues and prosodic features. However, the interplay between context and prosody in second language (L2) irony comprehension remains unclear. This study investigates their relative contributions and examines whether language proficiency affects Chinese English learners’ ability to interpret irony. A perception experiment was conducted using English materials with three contextual and three prosodic conditions. Results showed that context played a dominant role in irony comprehension, while prosody contributed independently when contextual information was limited. Language proficiency had only a minor effect. The findings support the Parallel Constraint Satisfaction Model and offer implications for irony research and English language teaching.

items.title: Cross-linguistic word-medial stop lenition: A Functional PCA approach
items.authors: Seung Suk Lee(McGill University); Morgan Sonderegger(McGill University); Meghan Clayards(McGill University)
items.abstract: Stop lenition between vowels is pervasive, yet fundamental questions remain: to what extent is lenition the same phenomenon across languages, and does it serve a common function? The continuity lenition hypothesis proposes one: weakened stops signal prosodic continuation and aid word segmentation. Previous work supports this idea but has examined few languages with differing methods, limiting cross-linguistic generalizability. We investigate word-medial continuity lenition in large speech corpora across nine languages, using Functional PCA of intensity contours to quantify the degree of lenition. We find a near-universal tendency for word-medial stops to be weaker, with voiced stops most consistent across languages. Exceptions reflect language-specific phonology or corpus artifacts, supporting continuity lenition as a cross-linguistic segmentation cue. Languages vary in whether weakening affects duration and/or intensity, suggesting listeners must learn cue patterns in their language.

items.title: Beyond Speaker Independence: Evaluating Cross-Lingual Acoustic-to-Articulatory Inversion Across Finnish and Russian
items.authors: Ruchi Pandey(University of Eastern Finland); Tomi H. Kinnunen(University of Eastern Finland)
items.abstract: Acoustic-to-articulatory inversion (AAI) remains challenging under domain shifts where changes in speaker attributes and cross-language conditions often degrade performance. We conduct a systematic evaluation under such shifts and establish baseline benchmarks on FROST-EMA, a Finnish-Russian bilingual EMA corpus. FROST-EMA addresses the English bias and limited speaker diversity of existing resources. We benchmark (i) articulatory targets (raw EMA coordinates vs tract variables), (ii) acoustic front-ends (MFCC vs SSL features), and (iii) inversion back-ends (BiLSTM vs a lightweight attention-based sequence model). We further define evaluation protocols for cross-gender transfer (within language) and cross-language transfer (within gender). The results indicate that cross-gender mismatch introduces moderate Pearson correlation declines (approx. 0.05--0.10) relative to the in-domain baseline, whereas cross-language mismatch causes larger drops (approx 0.10- 0.20).

items.title: L2 Speakers Accommodate Differently to AI and Human Voices Across Phonetic Features
items.authors: Nan Gan(University of Zurich); Elisa Pellegrino(University of Zurich)
items.abstract: Phonetic accommodation refers to speakers' adjustment of acoustic-phonetic patterns toward a speech model. Prior work comparing accommodation to human and AI voices has rarely included L2 populations and typically examined a narrow set of phonetic features. This study investigated the accommodation of 28 L1 Mandarin learners of L2 English to a Microsoft Azure TTS-generated voice and a native human voice in a sentence-shadowing task. Acoustic analyses targeted stop-consonant voice onset time (VOT), the tense-lax contrast /i/-/I/ in duration and spectral distance, and speech rhythm. Results showed stronger VOT convergence toward the human voice, but greater adjustment in vowel duration contrast and rhythm toward the AI voice, with no difference in vowel spectral contrast. These findings suggest that model-type effects on L2 phonetic accommodation are feature-dependent and AI and human voices may play complementary roles in supporting L2 phonetic acquisition.

items.title: Disentangling sociophonetic and physiological variation in /s/ acoustics across 12 languages
items.authors: Massimo Lipari(McGill University); Morgan Sonderegger(McGill University); Meghan Clayards(McGill University)
items.abstract: Sibilants, especially /s/, display gendered variation across languages. From acoustic data alone, it can be hard to determine whether this variation is due to performance of social identity or to physiology, e.g. vocal tract length (VTL) variation. In causal terms, there is a direct effect of gender on sibilant acoustics and an indirect effect mediated by VTL, which must be teased apart. To this end, a speaker's VTL can be estimated from their vowel formants, though the consistency of this measure's relationship to sibilant acoustics is largely untested. Using a new multilingual phonetic database of 12 languages (>1,300 speakers) and the tools of causal mediation analysis, we investigate the relationship between VTL and /s/ peak frequency and its causal role in gender effects. We find that estimated VTL predicts peak well across languages. While there are gender differences in peak across nearly all languages, the relative contributions of physiology and performance vary considerably.

items.title: From Rhythm Metrics to Latent Embeddings: Categorising English and Hindi Varieties in Northeast India
items.authors: John Aheibam(Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati); Joyshree Chakraborty(Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati); Priyankoo Sarmah(Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati); Rohit Sinha(Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati)
items.abstract: This study examines speech rhythm across English varieties spoken in Northeast (NE) India using traditional rhythm metrics and computational speech approaches. The dataset includes five NE Indian English varieties from different L1 backgrounds, viz. Angami, Assamese, Khasi, Meiteilon, and Mizo, together with two Hindi varieties spoken by native Hindi speakers and Assamese speakers. Durational rhythm measures were used to investigate language grouping patterns and served as features for the linear mixed-effects models, Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering, and Support Vector Machine analyses. The results revealed considerable overlap among the NE Indian English varieties, whereas the Hindi varieties were more clearly separated. Latent embedding vectors also showed a clear separation between Hindi and English varieties, while the NE Indian Englishes overlapped. A strong correlation between %V and PC1 suggests that temporal rhythmic patterns are partially captured in the embeddings.

title: Spatial Audio 3
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 5 - Poster 1 - Spatial Audio 3

items.title: AURA: Audio-Geometry Conditioned U-Net Refinement with Flow Matching for High-Fidelity Monaural-to-Binaural Synthesis
items.authors: Wenjie Zhang(Harbin Institute of Technology(Shenzhen)); Changjun He(Harbin Institute of Technology(Shenzhen)); Yinghan Cao(Harbin Institute of Technology(Shenzhen)); Shiyun Xu(Harbin Institute of Technology(Shenzhen)); Mingjiang Wang(Harbin Institute of Technology(Shenzhen))
items.abstract: Spatial audio is crucial for immersive listening, and binaural rendering is particularly appealing due to its alignment with human auditory perception. However, synthesizing high-quality binaural audio from monaural input remains challenging, as spatial cues must be inferred while preserving both spatial realism and fine-grained timbral detail, limiting its use in VR/AR and telepresence. To address this issue, we propose AURA, a two-stage binaural synthesis framework that explicitly models the relationship between monaural audio and source direction. The first stage combines global context modeling and local texture extraction to produce a coarse binaural estimate. The second stage refines this estimate with a generative mechanism, enhancing spatial cues and spectral details for high-fidelity output. Extensive experiments show that AURA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both subjective evaluations and objective metrics (Wave-L2: 0.123 vs. 0.128).

items.title: GISNO: Neural Operator-based HRTF Personalization from 3D Meshes via Differentiable Helmholtz Rendering
items.authors: Chen Huang(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Lei Zhou(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Hongqing Liu(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Lu Gan(Brunel University); Liming Shi(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
items.abstract: Individualized head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) are crucial for immersive audio, yet their acquisition remains challenging. Existing deep-learning approaches are often constrained by discrete sampling grids and lose fine morphological details during mesh preprocessing. In this work, we propose a geometrically informed spherical neural operator (GISNO), a framework that reformulates HRTF prediction as a continuous operator-learning problem. By integrating a discretization-invariant neural operator with a differentiable Helmholtz-integral renderer, our model learns to map 3D head geometry to continuous boundary pressure fields. Experiments on the HUTUBS dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms representative baselines in log-spectral distortion. Furthermore, the physics-integrated architecture enables multi-dimensional zero-shot generalization across unseen spatial densities, distances, and frequencies, offering a robust solution for scalable HRTF personalization.

items.title: TTBA: Spatial Prompted Text to Binaural Audio Generation Using Transformer
items.authors: Changjun He(Harbin Institute of Technology); Lianyu Zhou(Harbin Institute of Technology); Yukun Qian(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Shiyun Xu(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Wenjie Zhang(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Mingjiang Wang(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Weiping Chen(Harbin Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Binaural audio can deliver an immersive listening experience, and it is valuable for virtual reality, gaming, and creative content production. While recent text-to-audio models can generate high-fidelity audio, they still struggle to generate binaural signals with directional control and accurate spatial perception. To address this issue, we propose TTBA, a text-to-binaural audio generation model. TTBA combines a cross-arranged discrete representation with a transformer-based autoregressive backbone to jointly model semantic content and spatial cues. We further design a spatial prompt encoder that maps explicit spatial prompts into a conditioning representation, which is fused with text features to guide binaural token generation. We use a monaural generation model as guidance and emphasize both content accuracy and inter-channel discrepancy. Experiments on the BEWO-1M dataset show that TTBA can generate binaural audio with spatial awareness and controllable directionality.

items.title: Spec2Spatial: A Time-Frequency Spatial Attention Network for Binaural Audio Synthesis
items.authors: Changjun He(Harbin Institute of Technology); Wenjie Zhang(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Shiyun Xu(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Lianyu Zhou(Harbin Institute of Technology); Weiping Chen(Harbin Institute of Technology); Mingjiang Wang(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen))
items.abstract: Binaural audio can provide realism and immersion, and it is widely used in scenarios such as virtual reality. The difficulty of binaural recording has motivated research on binaural audio synthesis. Deep learning-based binaural synthesis is promising, but existing methods still perform poorly, especially in reproducing interaural differences. In this paper, we propose Spec2Spatial, a time-frequency spatial attention network for binaural audio synthesis. Specifically, we introduce an interaural spatial attention network to capture left-right relations in the frequency domain. Additionally, we propose a condition fusion residual network that uses sound source position to adjust time-frequency features. Experiments on the Binaural Speech dataset show that Spec2Spatial synthesizes realistic binaural audio, achieving state-of-the-art DILD (1.250), DITD (0.034), and MRSTFT (1.174).

items.title: Geometry-Informed Distributed Acoustic Scene Understanding
items.authors: Yiyuan Yang(University of Oxford); Shitong Xu(University of Oxford); Niki Trigoni(University of Oxford); Andrew Markham(University of Oxford)
items.abstract: Acoustic scene understanding in multi-room environments is a difficult task. Most existing systems use a single centralized microphone array, and they often fail because walls and doors block sound signals. To address this challenge, we propose a geometry-informed distributed acoustic scene understanding framework. Our system leverages distributed microphones and uses an audio spectrogram transformer and a topology-aware graph neural network to fuse spatio-temporal acoustic features. Then, these features are decoded into discrete semantic triplets. Finally, a frozen large language model combines these symbolic observations with the environmental geometry. This allows the system to perform spatial understanding, infer plausible missing transitions, and generate a physically consistent narrative of the scene. Experiments on a custom multi-room simulator demonstrate that our framework outperforms centralized baselines and improves spatial consistency under simulated occlusion.

items.title: Branch-wise Complementary Attention for Acoustic Scene Classification
items.authors: Seung-Gyu Han(Hanyang University); Jinwoo Jung(Hanyang University); Pil Moo Byun(Hanyang University); Won-Gook Choi(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University, Seoul, Republic of Korea)
items.abstract: Acoustic scene classification (ASC) requires lightweight models that effectively capture diverse temporal and spectral cues for mobile devices. Multi-branch convolutional architectures improve receptive field diversity, but their outputs are typically aggregated without explicitly modeling complementary relationships or compensating for branch-specific limitations. We propose a branch-wise complementary attention (BCA) module that allocates channel, time, frequency, and joint time-frequency attention maps across branches according to their receptive field characteristics. By explicitly addressing the inherent limitations of each branch, BCA enhances multi-scale feature integration beyond simple aggregation. Integrated into the Rep-Mobile backbone, BCA consistently outperforms existing attention mechanisms on the TAU Urban Acoustic Scenes 2020 and 2022 Mobile benchmarks.

items.title: CoSTALA: Compositional Spatio-Temporal Audio-Language Alignment via Multi-Grain Hierarchical Contrastive Learning
items.authors: Peiwei Ren(Xi’an Jiaotong Liverpool University); Jinbo Hu(Xiaomi Inc.); Fang Kang(University of Oulu); Shan Liang(Xi’an Jiaotong Liverpool University); Yin Cao(Chinese Academy of Sciences)
items.abstract: Conventional audio language models (ALMs) have made significant progress in achieving alignment between auditory and textual representations, including recent explorations in spatial audio. However, in daily spatial scenarios, they still cannot effectively process multi-event audio sequences. Current approaches primarily rely on coarse-grained contrastive learning with global auditory and textual features, lacking the resolution to distinguish multiple sequential events. To overcome these limitations, we propose CoSTALA—a novel training paradigm that transitions from purely global alignment to fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning. By constructing a multi-granularity hierarchical loss function system, we achieve explicit modeling of temporal dependencies, and successfully anchors individual acoustic events to preserve their semantic purity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoSTALA significantly establish a powerful new framework for spatio-temporal audio understanding.

items.title: Perceptually Weighted Minimum Mean Square Error Precoding for Acoustic Multi-User MIMO in Vehicular Personal Sound Zones
items.authors: Huihui Wei( Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Dengke Deng(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Pengcheng Luo(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Weiyu You(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Xiaojuan Zhang(Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing); Genke Yang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
items.abstract: To address multiuser interference in in-vehicle personal sound zones (PSZ), this paper proposes a perceptually weighted acoustic multi-user MIMO (MU-MIMO) precoding framework. Traditional spatial audio methods often neglect human psychoacoustics, treating cross-talk merely as uniform physical energy. To overcome this, we integrate a psychoacoustic masking model into the Weighted Minimum Mean Square Error (WMMSE) criterion. The algorithm dynamically assigns stronger distortion penalties to perceptually sensitive time-frequency regions while relaxing constraints in zones heavily masked by target speech. By actively coordinating precoding filters, this method minimizes the perceptually weighted MSE, jointly balancing inter-user interference and target-signal distortion. Validated using measured impulse responses from a real car cabin, the approach shows improvements in objective speech quality over baselines, offering a scalable solution for smart cockpit audio.

items.title: SA-HRTF: A Sound-Assisted Approach to Personalized HRTF Modeling
items.authors: Qingyin Zhao(Inner Mongolia University); Siyuan Chen(Inner Mongolia University); De Hu(Inner Mongolia University)
items.abstract: Head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) are essential for immersive binaural audio rendering, whereas generic HRTFs are often inadequate for accurately reproducing individual spatial cues. Although neural-network-based personalized HRTF modeling has progressed rapidly, accurate reconstruction under sparse measurements remains challenging because limited spatial information hinders reliable estimation. To address this issue, we propose a sound-assisted HRTF (SA-HRTF) model that incorporates binaural acoustic information into personalized HRTF estimation. The proposed architecture adopts a dual-branch design: the primary branch exploits structural features from an existing database to generate an initial estimate, while the auxiliary branch extracts perceptual cues from sound signals to provide supplementary predictions. A fusion module combines the outputs of the two branches to produce a more accurate personalized HRTF. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

items.title: Bayesian Model-Based Assessment of Spatial and Source Priors in Sagittal-Plane Sound Localization
items.authors: Yunda Chen(Shenzhen University); Nengheng Zheng(Shenzhen University)
items.abstract: Sagittal-plane localization in the polar dimension is ill-posed, entangling unknown source spectra and head-related transfer functions. Humans may resolve this ambiguity through sensory evidence and learned priors. We evaluated these priors using a Bayesian observer with an ecological source prior and five spatial priors. Models were calibrated against human responses across cochlear implant (CI)-like reductions in spectral resolution. Across conditions, the models captured the decrease in polar and quadrant errors as spectral resolution improved. The ecological source prior provided limited additional benefit within the present model implementation, whereas predictions were more sensitive to spatial-prior configuration. No single spatial prior was consistently preferred, although asymmetric variants showed better overall agreement with human data. These findings support individualized modeling of spatial hearing under reduced spectral resolution.

title: Instruction-following and Controllable Speech Synthesis
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 7 - Poster 9 - Instruction-following and Controllable Speech Synthesis

items.title: ARCHES: An Agent-Based Refinement Cycle for Hierarchical Synthesis of Sound Effects for Variety Shows
items.authors: Wentao Lei(The Hongkong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou); Li Liu(The Hongkong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))
items.abstract: Sound effects for variety shows can greatly improve viewer engagement, which currently relies on a manual process. This approach is heavily dependent on the experience of human editors. While recent advancements in audio generation methods have shown promising performance, they struggle to meet the unique demands of variety shows. The past methods exhibit critical limitations in temporal precision, content diversity, and contextual understanding. To overcome these limitations, we propose ARCHES (Agent-based Refinement Cycle for HiErarchical Synthesis), a novel framework that leverages multi-agent collaboration and retrieval-augmented generation to automatically produce high-quality, contextually appropriate sound effects. The framework contains an iterative workflow of planning, generation, and refinement. The core components of this framework are three modules: the Auditory Unified Retrieval Augmentation (AURA) module for content diversity, the Adaptive eXpert Intelligent Switch (AXIS) module for specific fine-grained refinement, and a Creative Experience Bank (CEB) which allows the system to learn from past generation process. To validate our approach, we constructed the first large-scale, fine-grained dataset for this task, the Variety Show Sound Effect Benchmark (VSSE-Bench). Extensive experiments demonstrate that ARCHES significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) on both objective and subjective metrics. The demos are anonymously available at https://arches-bench.github.io/.

items.title: Scalable Direction-Following TTS via Voice Impression-Guided Pseudo Triplet Construction
items.authors: Kenichi Fujita(NTT); Yusuke Ijima(NTT)
items.abstract: Voice actors often re-read the same script while modifying their delivery in response to performance directions. We study this setting as direction-following TTS, where a system generates a new utterance that reflects a given direction relative to a reference utterance while preserving speaker identity and linguistic content. A key challenge is the lack of training data capturing such relative modifications. To address this, we propose a scalable pseudo-triplet construction pipeline that generates (reference utterance, direction text, modified utterance) triplets. It generates controlled style variations using an impression-controllable TTS model and uses an LLM to produce natural language directions from estimated impression differences. Experimental results demonstrate that pseudo-triplets alone enable stable speaker-preserving modification, and that combining pseudo and recorded data further improves direction alignment while maintaining speaker similarity.

items.title: Poly-InstructTTS: Learning In-the-Wild Expressive Speech Synthesis from Open-Ended Instructions
items.authors: Junhui Zhang(ZuoYeBang Technology); Qianhui Xu(ZuoYeBang Technology); Qingxiang Guo(ZuoYeBang Technology); Dawei Yang(ZuoYeBang Technology); Ling Miao(ZuoYeBang Technology); Qiangqiang Wang(ZuoYeBang Technology); Yang Song(ZuoYeBang Technology)
items.abstract: While recent text-to-speech (TTS) models achieve high naturalness, controlling fine-grained expression via natural-language instructions remains challenging. We introduce Poly-InstructTTS, which learns expressive speech from open-ended instructions using in-the-wild audiovisual data. We build a scalable multi-modal pipeline to construct a 1,000-hour instruction-annotated corpus covering 1,000+ fine-grained emotions and styles. The framework uses a prompt-free GPT with attribute-based thinking tokens, followed by a flow-matching module that injects timbre from a reference audio. We also present a speaker fine-tuning procedure to transfer instruction control to specific speakers while preserving persona. We further extend InstructTTSEval with broader tasks. Experiments show that Poly-InstructTTS delivers strong performance in instruction adherence and expressiveness. Audio demos and the expanded testset are available on our project page.

items.title: Spiking Vocos: An Energy-Efficient Neural Vocoder
items.authors: Yukun Chen(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Zhaoxi Mu(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Andong Li(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Peilin Li(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Xingyu Yang(Xi'an Jiaotong University)
items.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely recognized for their high energy efficiency due to their event-driven nature, offer a promising solution for low-resource scenarios. In this paper, we propose Spiking Vocos, a novel spiking neural vocoder with ultra-low energy consumption. To mitigate the inherent information bottleneck in SNNs, we design a Spiking ConvNeXt module to reduce Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) operations and incorporate an amplitude shortcut path to preserve crucial signal dynamics. Furthermore, to bridge the performance gap with its Artificial Neural Network (ANN) counterpart, we introduce a self-architectural distillation strategy to effectively transfer knowledge. A lightweight Temporal Shift Module is also integrated to enhance the model's ability to fuse information across the temporal dimension. Experiments demonstrate that our model achieves performance comparable to its ANN counterpart with only 14.7% of the energy. The source code and demos are available at https://github.com/pymaste r17/Spiking-Vocos.

items.title: Stabilizing Instruction Supervision for Instruct-TTS via Controllable Diversification and Drift Filtering
items.authors: Yizhong Geng(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Kecan Mao(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Qifei Li(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Cong Wang(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Yingming Gao(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Ruimin Wang(Li Auto); Chunfeng Wang(Li Auto); Hao Li(Li Auto); Ya Li(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
items.abstract: Instruct-TTS systems expand structured style labels into natural-language training instructions through LLM rewriting, yet we find that over 40% of unconstrained rewrites contain semantic drift that corrupts supervision and weakens generalization. We formalize this problem as instruction supervision instability and propose a data-centric stabilization recipe that jointly improves coverage and fidelity through three mechanisms: controllable instruction diversification for systematic expansion, LLM-based drift filtering for quality control, and attribute-aligned supervision that grounds prosody control in acoustic perturbations. On the Chinese split of InstructTTSEval, our recipe raises instruction-following from 34.5% without fine-tuning and 51.0% with naive fine-tuning to 56.4%, while constrained rewriting reduces drift from 40.4% to 15.4%. Ablations confirm the three mechanisms are complementary, and the drift taxonomy may generalize to instruction-driven generation beyond TTS. 1

items.title: Improving Stable Speech Synthesis Post-Training with ChatScorer and Margin-Based Preference Construction
items.authors: Shihao Niu(Tianjin University); Jianguo Wei(Tianjin University); Wenhuan Lu(Tianjin University); Xianghu Yue(Tianjin University); Wei Li(Banma Network Technology Co., Ltd.); Ming Zhou(Banma Network Technology Co., Ltd.); Ming Cai(Banma Network Technology Co., Ltd.); Luo Si(Banma Network Technology Co., Ltd.)
items.abstract: Existing post-training methods for codec-based text-to-speech (TTS) often rely on multiple automatic metrics, such as character or word error rate (CER/WER) for content consistency, speaker similarity (SIM) for speaker preservation, and their weighted combinations as reward signals. However, directly fusing heterogeneous metrics into a single scalar reward can yield weakly separated candidate scores, leading to ambiguous supervision. In this paper, we propose a new post-training framework for stable speech synthesis, which introduces ChatScorer as an auxiliary reward model and combines it with margin-based preference construction. We instantiate the proposed framework using different post-training methods, and experiments on codec-based TTS show that it reduces undesirable outputs and improves generation stability, while maintaining competitive intelligibility and speaker similarity.

items.title: Accent-Emotion Entanglement in LM-Based Text-to-Speech Systems
items.authors: Matthew Hayden(University of Edinburgh); Jinzuomu Zhong(University of Edinburgh); Korin Richmond(University of Edinburgh)
items.abstract: Speaker similarity metrics (SSM) are widely used for quick and easy evaluation of zero-shot text-to-speech (ZS-TTS) systems. However, using a case study of two ZS-TTS systems that have comparable SSM, we show such metrics may fail to capture important speech characteristics such as accent, and that relying on them can hide errors. We identify a phenomenon termed accent-emotion entanglement, whereby emotion conditioning can unintentionally alter accent, which is not reflected in previously reported high speaker similarity scores. We evaluate the systems with accent SMOS listening tests, and visualisation and cosine-distance analysis of embeddings. One has substantial accent variability, with SMOS ranging from 1.17–4.13 and centroid cosine distances up to 0.06, while the other is stable. The results of our proposed approach highlight the limitations of standard speaker similarity metrics, and that targeted subjective and objective measures are needed to reveal hidden synthesis errors.

items.title: How Do Instructions Shape Speech? Cross-Attention Attribution for Style-Captioned Text-to-Speech
items.authors: Nityanand Mathur(Smallest.ai); Hamees Sayed(Smallest.ai); Wasim Madha(Smallest.ai); Apoorv Singh(Smallest.ai); Sameer Khurana(Smallest.ai); Akshat Mandloi(Smallest.ai); Sudarshan Kamath(Smallest.ai)
items.abstract: Style-captioned text-to-speech systems use natural language to control voice characteristics, but how individual words influence acoustic output remains unclear. Understanding this is critical for diagnosing failure modes and improving controllability in expressive TTS. We propose cross-attention attribution for speech diffusion models, adapting the DAAM framework to the speech domain for the first time, and apply it to CapSpeechTTS. Our method extracts per-token heatmaps across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps. We analyze 3,600 (style caption, text transcript) combinations comprising 120 style captions conditioning the generation of 30 text transcripts each, revealing how caption tokens shape waveforms. Results show: (1) style tokens have lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning; (2) style attention correlates with F0 and energy; (3) style conditioning peaks in early steps and deep layers; (4) attention entropy reaches its minimum at layer 17, co-occurring with the style importance peak, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical stage. This is the first study of how natural language influences cross-attention in speech diffusion models.

items.title: Beyond Two-stage Diffusion TTS: Joint Structure and Content Refinement via Jump Diffusion
items.authors: Jiabao Ai(The University of Sheffield); Minghui Zhao(The University of Sheffield); Anton Ragni(The University of Sheffield)
items.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching TTS faces a tension between discrete temporal structure and continuous spectral modeling. Two-stage models diffuse on fixed alignments, often collapsing to mean prosody; single-stage models avoid explicit durations but suffer alignment instability. We propose a jump-diffusion framework where discrete jumps model temporal structure and continuous diffusion refines spectral content within one process. Even in its one-shot degenerate form, our framework achieves 3.37% WER vs. 4.38% for Grad-TTS with improved UTMOSv2 on LJSpeech. The full iterative UDD variant further enables adaptive prosody, autonomously inserting natural pauses in out-of-distribution slow speech rather than stretching uniformly. Audio samples are available at https://anonymousinterpseech.github.io/TTS_Demo/.

items.title: PhonemeCVAE: Contrastive Latent Clustering with Class-Conditioned Priors for Controllable Phoneme Interpolation
