items.authors: Nina Goes(Department for Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Engineering, Erlangen-Nürnberg); Lars Meyer(Max Planck Institute); Katrin Neumann(University Hospital Münster); Paula Andrea Pérez-Toro(Friedrich-Alexander Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg); Andreas M. Kist(Department for Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Engineering, Erlangen-Nürnberg)
items.abstract: In order to achieve precise pronunciation control, high-quality TTS systems rely on structured and disentangled speech representations. We propose PhonemeCVAE, a phoneme-conditioned variational autoencoder that learns a structured continuous latent space for phoneme-level representations. The model introduces class-conditioned Gaussian priors for each phoneme and employs a contrastive objective to promote compact intra-class clustering and clear phoneme class disentanglement. The resulting latent space enables controllable phoneme modifications via interpolation at inference time, allowing smooth transitions between phonological classes and semantically meaningful modifications of synthesized speech. Furthermore, the combination of contrastive regularization and phoneme-conditioned priors forms a structured latent topology in the VAE that generalizes across English speech datasets, supporting consistent phoneme interpolation without compromising synthesis quality.

items.title: TAP-ETS: Time Aligned Phoneme Guiding for EMG-to-Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Dongyub Han(Seoul National University); Injune Hwang(Seoul National University); Jaejun Lee(Seoul National University); Jiwon Lee(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Electromyography (EMG)-to-speech (ETS) synthesis generates speech from articulatory muscle activity without acoustic input. We propose TAP-ETS, a time-aligned phoneme guiding framework that conditions mel-spectrogram generation on frame-wise phoneme sequences through cross-attention. Unlike prior work that treats phonemes as auxiliary supervision, our model injects aligned phoneme embeddings directly into the decoder. We also introduce refinement strategies that redistribute merged semantic guidance over frame-wise EMG signals, enabling the seamless integration of arbitrary phoneme-or text-level correction methods without modifying the synthesis model. On the Gaddy silent EMG benchmark, TAP-ETS reduces WER from 25.12% to 19.77%, achieving state-of-the-art performance and demonstrating the importance of accurate frame-level alignment.

title: Robust ASR: Uncertainty and Confidence
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 8 - Poster 3 - Robust ASR: Uncertainty and Confidence

items.title: Transitional Objective Learning with Connectionist Temporal Classification in Phoneme Recognition
items.authors: Izabela Krysińska(Poznan University of Technology; Pearson Central Europe); Mikołaj Morzy(Poznan University of Technology); Agnieszka Pludra(Pearson Central Europe)
items.abstract: Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) is widely used for phoneme recognition due to its alignment-free training objective, but it often produces highly peaky posterior distributions dominated by the blank token. This is particularly challengingduring early training, when phonemes compete against strong blank token dominance and unstable alignment dynamics. We propose Transitional Objective Learning (TOL), a curriculum-learning framework that mitigates this issue by dynamically transitioning between training objectives of increasing granularity. Instead of optimizing a fine-grained phoneme objective throughout training, TOL begins with coarse-grained phonetic objectives that provide stable learning signals and gradually shifts toward full phoneme-level supervision. Experiments on English, French, and Polish show that TOL consistently reduces Phoneme Error Rate (PER), accelerates convergence, and improves training stability compared to conventional CTC fine-tuning.

items.title: Align-Consistency: Improving Non-autoregressive and Semi-supervised ASR with Consistency Regularization
items.authors: Wanting Huang(University of Iowa); Weiran Wang(University of Iowa)
items.abstract: Consistency regularization (CR) improves the robustness and accuracy of Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) by ensuring predictions remain stable across input perturbations. In this work, we propose Align-Consistency, an extension of CR designed for Align-Refine--a non-autoregressive (non-AR) model that performs iterative refinement of frame-level hypotheses. This method leverages the speed of parallel inference while significantly boosting recognition performance. The effectiveness of Align-Consistency is demonstrated in two settings. First, in the fully supervised setting, our results indicate that applying CR to both the base CTC model and the subsequent refinement steps is critical, and the accuracy improvements from non-AR decoding and CR are mutually additive. Second, for semi-supervised ASR, we employ fast non-AR decoding to generate online pseudo-labels on unlabeled data, which are used to further refine the supervised model and lead to substantial gains.

items.title: COALA: Robust Contextualized Speech-augmented Language Modeling for ASR via Contrastive Regularizer and Biasing Score Estimation
items.authors: Jhih-Rong Guo(National Taiwan Normal University); Bi-Cheng Yan(National Taiwan Normal University); Tien-Hong Lo(National Taiwan Normal University); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)
items.abstract: Contextual biasing seeks to integrate external knowledge into automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems to accurately recognize domain-specific entities. In this paper, we propose COALA1 (COntextualized ASR Leveraging biAsing scoring), a robust framework designed to enhance speech-augmented language models (SLMs) in complex multi-entity scenarios. Considering the inherent context-window limitations of SLMs, identifying relevant target entities from a large-scale biasing list is crucial for effective recognition. To this end, COALA maps SLM latent representations into a specialized discriminative space to quantify the matching intensity between audio segments and candidate entities. Furthermore, we address the training collapse in prior study when handling multi-target utterances—where multiple rare words co-occur. Experimental results on the LibriSpeech benchmark demonstrate that COALA consistently achieves superior contextual biasing performance across various biasing list scales.

items.title: UGPCB: Uncertainty-Gated Phonetic Contextual Biasing for Improving Hotword Recognition in Large Speech Models
items.authors: Yong-Jie Hou(Tsinghua University; Tiangong University); Yun-Fei Shao(Tsinghua University); Wei-Qiang Zhang(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Automatic speech recognition systems exhibit recognition bias when processing hot words. Context bias techniques effectively tackle this issue by integrating user-defined vocabularies, thus enhancing keyword transcription accuracy. Although speech matching technology has advanced context bias techniques by resolving subword fragmentation, existing methods still face challenges with over-bias and homophone misclassification. To address this, this study proposes a training-free decode-time framework named Uncertainty-Gated Phonetic Contextual Bias (UGPCB). This framework employs an entropy-driven gating mechanism and bimodal contrastive penalties, and it is evaluated on the Dolphin base model. The experimental results demonstrate a 16.04% recall improvement (achieving an F1 score of 90.81%) while restricting precision reduction to 0.78%. Even when 1,000 distractors are introduced, the recall still increases by 14.26%, fully demonstrating the method's potential for ASR applications.

items.title: Refining the Latent Bridge: Superior ASR Performance via Adapter-Only Alignment with Diffusion LLMs
items.authors: Puneet Singh Bhooi(IIIT-Delhi); Vinayak Abrol(IIIT-Delhi)
items.abstract: In this work, we validate a parameter-efficient approach to Speech-LLM based ASR that enforces a strict adapter-only alignment protocol. Unlike existing methods that rely on full-parameter or partial backbone updates, we keep both the speech encoder and the LLM frozen, focusing exclusively on the adapter as the sole learnable interface. We demonstrate that this restricted alignment strategy, though often underexplored, is particularly effective for Diffusion-based LLMs. Our results show that Diffusion models are significantly more resilient to the adapter-only bottleneck than Autoregressive (AR) models, yielding higher Real-Time Factors (RTF) and superior ASR performance across various data size splits. While AR models suffer from error propagation and drift when denied full-parameter tuning, the global refinement mechanism of Diffusion proves more scalable and efficient for multimodal LLM integration.

items.title: DASH: Dual-View Self-Distillation with Multi-Layer Hidden Representations for Robust Speech Recognition
items.authors: Jaeeun Baik(Sogang University); Ui-Hyeop Shin(Sogang University); Jiwon Lee(Sogang University); Woocheol Jeong(Sogang University); Hyung-Min Park(Sogang University)
items.abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) often degrades in real-world noisy environments, making noise robustness essential for deployment. Supervised noise-augmented fine-tuning is a common remedy, but it can introduce a robustness-clean trade-off and overfit to specific corruptions, degrading recognition in clean conditions. We propose DASH, a self-distillation framework that improves robustness by learning clean-noisy consistency from paired views. DASH distills hidden representations from multiple encoder layers to capture features from low-level acoustics to high-level semantics, and stabilizes training by minimizing KL divergence between prototype assignment distributions of clean and noisy views. Experiments on LibriSpeech show that DASH consistently improves recognition under diverse noisy conditions while preserving clean accuracy, achieved by a label-free pre-training stage with minimal additional overhead (about 4% of fine-tuning time) beyond standard fine-tuning.

items.title: Whisper-Aware LLM: Self-Supervised Uncertainty Learning for Robust Whispered Speech Recognition
items.authors: Gaopeng Xu(Alibaba); Zhenyu Wang(Alibaba); Zheng Xue(Alibaba); Yinfeng Xia(Alibaba); Haitao Yao(Alibaba)
items.abstract: The signal ambiguity of whispered speech drives ASR systems toward two opposing failure modes: failing to capture whispered speech or hallucinatory transcription of noise. This paper introduces the Whisper-Aware LLM, a framework that teaches an Audio-LLM to perceive and react to this uncertainty. Our model develops an intrinsic self-awareness by learning to quantify the physical deficiencies of acoustic signals through targeted self-supervised tasks. This learned uncertainty is then operationalized via a novel Confidence-Fused Decoding mechanism, which provides both high-level instructions and frame-level attention modulation to the LLM decoder. Our experiments confirm the effectiveness of this approach. The model sets a new state-of-the-art on whispered speech with a 17% relative CER reduction on AISHELL6-Whisper. At the same time, it directly addresses the reliability trade-off, with hallucination rates dropping from over 25% to 4.5%.

items.title: Probing and Mitigating Hallucinations in Speech-augmented Language Models for Automatic Speech Recognition via Small Language Models
items.authors: Bi-Cheng Yan(National Taiwan Normal University); Jhih-Rong Guo(National Taiwan Normal University); Fu-An Chao(National Taiwan Normal University); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)
items.abstract: The widespread success of large language models in natural language processing has spurred the development of speech-augmented language models (SLMs) to extend their reasoning capabilities from textual inputs to spoken ones. Despite impressive performance, SLMs remain susceptible to hallucinations, posing challenges in practical utility. To this end, we first probe hallucinations in SLMs for automatic speech recognition (ASR) via the lens of causal mediation and behavioral analysis. To mitigate fabricated ASR hypotheses, we propose AudioSLM, a compact yet effective ASR framework built upon a small language model, which leverages alignment cues and cross-attention layers to synergistically bolster acoustic modeling and cross-modal interactions. Experiments on LibriSpeech reveal that hallucinations arise from multi-head self-attention modules with an excessive attention bias towards textual tokens. AudioSLM considerably eases ASR hallucinations and outperforms some LLM-based ASR models.

items.title: Rank-Distance Based Confidence Estimation for ASR
items.authors: Nagarathna Ravi(CSIR Fourth Paradigm Institute); Madduri Aiswarya Lakshmi(CSIR Fourth Paradigm Institute); Ragesh M(CSIR Fourth Paradigm Institute); Rajalakshmi Elangovan(CSIR Fourth Paradigm Institute)
items.abstract: Confidence scores in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) are required to assess the correctness of the predicted text. Class probabilities from overconfident ASR decoders do not reflect prediction accuracy. Auxiliary Confidence Estimation Model (CEM) based on binary target scores does not reflect the correctness of partially correct transcripts. CEM based on temporal continuous target scores suffers from inaccurate alignment. We observe the diminishing class probabilities in true-class probability-based CEM. To address the limitations of the State-of-the-Art (SOTA) CEM, we propose a novel continuous target score, named RanD. Then, we present RanD-based CEM for four ASR architectures: Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC), Recurrent Neural Network-Transducer (RNN-T), Token Duration Transducer (TDT), and Attention-based Encoder Decoder (AED). Experiments with Hindi and English ASR show that our approach outperforms SOTA CEM and also generalises to mismatched domains.

items.title: Training-Free Intelligibility-Guided Observation Addition for Noisy ASR
items.authors: Haoyang Li(Nanyang Technological University); Changsong Liu(Nanyang Technological University); Wei Rao(Nanyang Technological University); Hao Shi(Independent Researcher); Sakriani Sakti(Nara Institute of Science and Technology); Eng Siong Chng(Nanyang Technological University)
items.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) degrades severely in noisy environments. Although speech enhancement (SE) front-ends effectively suppress background noise, they often introduce artifacts that harm recognition. Observation addition (OA) addressed this issue by fusing noisy and SE enhanced speech, improving recognition without modifying the parameters of the SE or ASR models. This paper proposes an intelligibility-guided OA method, where fusion weights are derived from intelligibility estimates obtained directly from the backend ASR. Unlike prior OA methods based on trained neural predictors, the proposed method is training-free, reducing complexity and enhances generalization. Extensive experiments across diverse SE-ASR combinations and datasets demonstrate strong robustness and improvements over existing OA baselines. Additional analyses of intelligibility-guided switching-based alternatives and frame versus utterance-level OA further validate the proposed design.

title: Speech Technologies for Language Learning & Assessment
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 10 - Poster 3 - Speech Technologies for Language Learning & Assessment

items.title: Beyond WER: Entity and Disfluency Recall in Accented Conversational ASR
items.authors: Fiza Husain(Stimuler); Ankit Pandey(Stimuler); Yash Singh(Stimuler)
items.abstract: ASR systems optimised for Word Error Rate (WER) often miss named entities and filled pauses in accented conversational English, both critical for language-learning feedback. We present a three-stage pipeline for speakers from India, Indonesia, and Latin America: (1) heuristic SQL filters curating entity-rich training data at ~2.8× the entity density of random sampling, (2) regional LoRA adapters fine-tuned on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B producing both verbatim and corrected transcripts in a single forward pass, and (3) a six-category error taxonomy validated by an LLM-based judge (83.8% agreement, 210 human-labelled samples). The pipeline achieves 80-85% entity recall (up from 53-55%), 76-86% filler recall (up from <5%), and 6-10% WER across 6 k test utterances, outperforming Whisper and a commercial ASR on entity recall while matching a zero-shot 30B model with 10 x fewer parameters. Paired bootstrap tests confirm that curation alone accounts for 2.8-4.2 pp of entity recall gain (p < 0.0001).

items.title: Exploring Hesitation as a Signal for Spoken Grammatical Error Correction
items.authors: Seunghoon Han(Tutorus Labs Inc.); Minyoung Kyoung(Tutorus Labs Inc.); Hyungbae Jeon(Tutorus Labs Inc.)
items.abstract: Traditional spoken GEC pipelines treat disfluencies as noise to be removed before correction. We challenge this assumption for L2 learner speech, hypothesizing that disfluencies signal grammatical uncertainty and provide valuable cues for error correction. We propose a novel hesitation-aware approach that preserves disfluency information via: (1) special marker tokens indicating hesitation positions and types, and (2) hesitation type embeddings that encode disfluency context. Experiments on the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025 show that our method outperforms both rule-based disfluency removal (+2.05%p) and human-annotated fluent transcription (+1.84%p) in F0.5, with gains particularly pronounced near hesitation positions (+2.78%p), demonstrating that disfluencies carry informative signals for spoken GEC and should be leveraged rather than discarded.

items.title: Discriminating Proficiency Levels in L2 Speech: A Comparative Study of Self-Supervised Models in Basque
items.authors: Christoforos Souganidis(University of the Basque Country); Aitor Bellanco(HiTZ Basque Center for Language TeUniversity of the Basque Country); Andoni Sudupe(University of the Basque Country); Inma Hernáez(University of the Basque Country); Ibon Saratxaga(University of the Basque Country); Eva Navas(University of the Basque Country)
items.abstract: Automated speaking assessment is crucial for computer-assisted language learning applications. Research has mainly focused on intermediate proficiency levels in languages with many L2 learners, predominantly English, where learner corpora are available. For low-resource languages lacking large annotated corpora, models based on self-supervised learning can help overcome this problem. In this work, we investigate whether multilingual self-supervised speech models can effectively discriminate C1-level proficiency in Basque, a low-resource language, and show that mHuBERT-147 achieves a statistically significant improvement over wav2vec 2.0 xlsr. To illustrate reproducibility, we replicate our experiments in the ICNALE corpus of L2 English, providing a complementary perspective in different linguistic and proficiency contexts.

items.title: A Multi-Agent Framework to Automate Feedback Generation for IELTS Speaking Test using Multimodal SpeechLMs
items.authors: Hui Xin Koh(The University of Manchester); Yang Wang(The University of Manchester); Chenghua Lin(The University of Manchester)
items.abstract: Automated speaking assessment aims to align evaluations with human judgments. Current regression-based scoring models that rely on handcrafted linguistic features suffer from poor construct coverage and centralised scores, while automatic speech recognition (ASR) methods impose an informational bottleneck by overlooking acoustic and prosodic nuances that are indispensable for analysing fluency and pronunciation. This paper proposes a multi-agent framework using multimodal SpeechLMs for the IELTS Speaking test. By performing direct analysis of the audio without intermediate transcription, it jointly models acoustic-prosodic and linguistic information via four role-based agents that mirror each scoring criterion. Results on a newly built benchmark dataset of IELTS speaking mock tests show that the system achieves higher scoring correlation with human examiners compared to a regression model baseline, while generating reports that exhibit greater semantic similarity to expert feedback.

items.title: A Finetuned SpeechLLM for Joint Multi-Granular L2 Assessment and Natural-Language Rationales
items.authors: Aditya Kamlesh Parikh(Radboud University); Cristian Tejedor Garcia(Radboud University); Catia Cucchiarini(Radboud University); Helmer Strik(Radboud University)
items.abstract: Automated L2 speech assessment can assign proficiency labels, but often lacks interpretability. We propose a rubric-guided SpeechLLM for multi-aspect, multi-granular assessment, trained with a hybrid objective combining supervised fine-tuning and Bounded Direct Preference Optimization. The model jointly predicts ordinal labels at the sentence-level (accuracy, fluency, prosody), word/phoneme-level accuracy, and generates a natural-language rationale in the same response. On SpeechOcean762, our approach matches or outperforms single-granularity models while remaining competitive with prior approaches. We analyze rationale reliability along two axes: self-consistency with model predictions and alignment with ground-truth labels, using sentiment consistency (plausibility) and mention-based agreement (faithfulness). Rationales are plausible at the sentence level, but faithfulness degrades at the word/phoneme level: references are sparse and weakly aligned with token-level labels.

items.title: LOPA: Enhancing Spoken Language Assessment via Latent Ordinal Prototype Alignment
items.authors: Hong-Yun Lin(National Taiwan Normal University); Fu-An Chao(National Taiwan Normal University); Bi-Cheng Yan(National Taiwan Normal University); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)
items.abstract: Fueled by increasing model scale and multimodal inputs, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for Spoken Language Assessment (SLA). While effective, this paradigm often overlooks the intrinsic ordinal structure of language acquisition. This paper works around the necessity of large-scale MLLMs by introducing Latent Ordinal Prototype Alignment (LOPA) for SLA, a prototype-based regularizer that enforces an ordinal geometric prior directly on the latent space. Coupled with Semantic-Anchored Layer Routing (SALR), which adaptively harvests multi-depth representations from a frozen Whisper encoder, our framework achieves an RMSE of 0.361. This performance rivals billion-parameter systems without the need for LLM-based fine-tuning. Further analysis reveals that SALR's synergy with LOPA offers interpretable, criterion-aligned preferences, thereby supporting an efficient and ordinal-aware modeling alternative to current scaling-centric models for SLA.

items.title: Adaptive Multimodal Expert Specialization by Meta-Learning for Spoken English Assessment
items.authors: Cong-Thanh Vu(JAIST); Candy Olivia Mawalim(JAIST); Hung Le(JAIST); Chee Wee Leong(ETS); Guy Sivan(Vericant.com); Shogo Okada(JAIST)
items.abstract: In the conversational artificial intelligence era, a learner's voice is vital, yet automated scoring often fails to capture them due to data scarcity and privacy constraints. We propose a meta-learning-based framework for adaptive multimodal expert specialization, transforming the system into an adaptive listener. Instead of a one-size-fits-all model, our approach uses a mixture of experts architecture in which subnetworks learn to specialize in diverse vocal profiles. This synergy enables the model to rapidly "learn to learn" from limited samples, thus providing a personalized and accurate reflection of a speaker's true capabilities. Our framework achieves an F1-score greater than 84% in classification and a mean squared error of 0.225 in regression. By optimizing deep model performance under extreme data constraints, this framework offers a robust, scalable solution for automated English coaching that balances adaptation with predictive accuracy. Our code is publicly available.

items.title: Using Phonological-Level Wav2Vec2 for Mandarin Automatic Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis
items.authors: Jinghao Chen(UNSW Sydney); Mostafa Shahin(UNSW Sydney); Beena Ahmed(UNSW Sydney)
items.abstract: Automatic mispronunciation detection and diagnosis (MDD) plays a crucial role in L2 Mandarin pronunciation learning. While end-to-end (E2E) based MDD methods have substantially improved phoneme-level detection accuracy, diagnostic feedback remains limited, as segmental and tonal errors are not explicitly separated. In this paper, we propose a phonological feature-based MDD framework that models both segmental and tonal attributes within a unified Wav2Vec2-CTC architecture. Experimental results show that the proposed method reduces False Acceptance Rate (FAR) by 10.1% and Diagnostic Error Rate (DER) by 23.6% compared with the phoneme-only baseline system. By decomposing phonemes into low-level phonological components, the proposed approach enables more detailed and interpretable diagnostic feedback for L2 learners.

items.title: Domain-Aware Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis Using Language-Specific Statistical Graphs
items.authors: Hanh Nguyen(NEU); Tuong Tu Huu(VNPT AI; HUST); Huan Vu(NEU, VNPT AI); Thien Van Luong(NEU, VNPT AI); Tien Cuong Nguyen(VNPT AI); Thi Thu Trang Nguyen(HUST)
items.abstract: Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis (MDD) has gained increasing importance in computer-assisted language learning and speech technology in recent years. In this paper, we propose a method for constructing statistical graphs that enable models to learn phoneme confusion patterns represented as directed graphs. Furthermore, we introduce a language-specific strategy to capture systematic pronunciation differences across various native language (L1) backgrounds. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through extensive experiments on the L2-ARCTIC benchmark, where it achieves an F1-score of 59.52%, outperforming several competitive baselines.

items.title: Light-weight Pronunciation Assessment via Discrete Speech Token Surprisal
items.authors: Syeda Faiza Ahmed Sara(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Shammur Absar Chowdhury(Qatar Computing Research Institute)
items.abstract: Training automated pronunciation assessment often relies on labeled learner errors or non-native corpora that are costly to collect. We propose a lightweight framework trained only on native speech resources, operating unsupervised or lightly calibrated with a small set of scored utterances. At inference, learner speech is discretized with an SSL encoder and a K-means codebook. A token language model trained on native sequences computes surprisal where higher surprisal indicates phonotactic deviation. We add a transcript-guided Text2DUnit–DTW module that predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens to derive error-sensitive features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused via simple regression. On SpeechOcean762, PCC improves from 0.60 to 0.66 with transcript guidance, near supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC shows consistent gains.

items.title: ALFreeD: Teacher-Guided Few-Shot Pronunciation Assessment via Segmentation-Free Deviation Modeling
items.authors: Meenakshi Sirigiraju(IIITH); Nevin K Mathew(Saintgits College of Engineering); Reni K Cherian(Saintgits College of Engineering); Chiranjeevi Yarra(IIITH)
items.abstract: Automatic pronunciation assessment (APA) of L2 learners is critical in computer-assisted language learning. Existing approaches typically rely on canonical phonemes, its aligned boundaries and large labeled data, which is costly and cumbersome. To address these, we propose ALFreeD, a segmentation-free APA framework guided by teacher's speech without the need of canonical phonemes using minimal labeled data. In this, pronunciation quality is assessed by quantifying deviation between learners' and teacher's utterances. First, frame-level embeddings are extracted using HuBERT, and deviation scores are computed between them after obtaining their temporal correspondence with DTW. Next, utterance level pronunciation deviation vector is obtained by suppressing variabilities other than pronunciation quality with i-vector framework and is passed to a MLP for predicting quality. Experiments on SpeechOcean762 demonstrate competitive performance with recent E2E methods using minimal labeled data.

items.title: Automatic Assessment of L2 Speech Intelligibility: Segmental Error Ranking
items.authors: Agnieszka Pludra(Pearson Central Europe); Izabela Krysińska(Pearson Central Europe); Matuesz Jekiel(Adam Mickiewicz University)
items.abstract: Current CAPT systems prioritize identification and correction of all learner deviations from native speech, thereby overlooking the main goal of language acquisition: effective communication. In response, we propose an intelligibility-centered approach, which targets only selected segmental aspects of speech influencing communicative effectiveness. We employ a regression model based on phoneme substitution errors. Using AdaBoost feature importance, we propose an intelligibility-based ranking of segmental errors, shedding light on the relationship between the mispronunciation of individual phonemes and overall speech intelligibility. This approach, validated on human ratings of speech samples from VoxPopuli, speechocean762, and an internal dataset, not only predicts intelligibility levels but also directs ESL learners toward the acquisition of the most critical phonemes. By foregrounding intelligibility over nativeness, it supports more learner-centered and inclusive CAPT solutions.

title: Spoken Dialogue Systems

items.title: A System-Agnostic Approach to Modelling Interaction Quality in Spoken Dialogue Systems
items.authors: Paul Gering(University of Sheffield); Roger K. Moore(University of Sheffield)
items.abstract: Previous studies have used system-dependent (SD) input features, such as system log data, and machine learning to automatically evaluate user interactions with spoken dialogue systems. However, this approach lacks generalisability across different systems. This study implements a system-agnostic (SA) approach, using acoustic, textual and temporal features to model interaction quality (IQ). Across two experimental phases, we compare the performance of IQ classifiers trained on static and fine-tuned SD and SA features. We found that while the SD features were superior in a static pipeline, the SA features achieved comparable performance when end-to-end fine-tuning was employed. Therefore, our results demonstrate that SA features, when fine-tuned, offer a viable, system-independent alternative for IQ modelling, enabling more scalable evaluations across different dialogue systems.

items.title: Considerate Listener Modeling for Korean Streaming Backchannel Prediction
items.authors: Yong-Seok Choi(Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute); Seung Hi Kim(Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute); Sung Yup Lee(Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute)
items.abstract: Mistimed backchannels can interrupt ongoing speech and degrade user experience. A Considerate Listener concentrates backchannel interventions near pause-proximate regions in real time, since backchannels cluster around speaker pauses. However, not all pauses invite a backchannel. Pauses that follow utterances calling for a reply may be pragmatically inappropriate for backchannel intervention. Acoustic cues alone may not capture the linguistic context needed to distinguish these cases, so acoustic-only predictors tend to over-predict. We therefore propose a zero look-ahead streaming backchannel predictor combining pause-aware soft scaling with Q-Former fusion of partial ASR hypotheses. We introduce Semantic False Discovery Rate (Semantic FDR) to quantify backchannel predictions in pragmatically inappropriate pause regions. On a Korean counseling corpus, our approach reduces Semantic FDR by 53.8% and improves Macro-F1 by 2.16 pp compared to an acoustic-only baseline.

items.title: Context Projector: Complementary Keyword and Dialogue Context Embeddings for LLM-based ASR
items.authors: Esaú Villatoro-Tello(Idiap Research Institute); Sergio Burdisso(Idiap Research Institute); Shashi Kumar(Idiap Research Institute; EPFL); Hasindri Watawana(Idiap Research Institute; EPFL); Srikanth Madikeri(University of Zurich); Manjunath K E(Uniphore); Jeena Prakash(Uniphore); Thibault Bañeras-Roux(Idiap Research Institute); Kadri Hacioglu(Uniphore); Petr Motlicek(Idiap Research Institute; Brno University of Technology); Andreas Stolcke(Uniphore)
items.abstract: Contact-center dialogue systems require both accurate transcripts and reliable recognition of business-critical entities. We introduce a hybrid keyword and context projector (CP) approach for LLM-based ASR. Rather than appending raw dialogue history, CP encodes previous turns into compact contextual tokens, complemented by automatically extracted keywords. The module is trained while keeping the backbone frozen, enabling parameter-efficient adaptation. Experiments on realistic, multi-domain contact-center data show that naive raw-context prompting can degrade performance, whereas the proposed approach improves the tradeoff between overall and bias-word error, achieving average relative reductions of up to 2.5% overall and 7.2% on bias words. These results show our approach to be an effective and practical enhancement of context-aware LLM-based ASR.

items.title: DP-BCT: A Dual-Path model for predicting BackChannel Timing
items.authors: Jin Yea Jang(Seoul National University; Korea Electronics Technology Institute); Saim Shin(Korea Electronics Technology Institute); Gahgene Gweon(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Backchannel timing prediction is challenging because responses occur at varying latencies relative to Backchannel Opportunity Points (BOPs). Dual-Process Theory motivates testing whether backchannel fast/slow functional categories exhibit distinct BOP-relative latency distributions; where BOP-relative latency is the signed interval between a BOP and an annotated backchannel onset. Using K-MIND, a 115-hour Korean dyadic corpus, Cox Proportional Hazards analysis confirms significant differences in BOP-relative latency distributions across four functional categories (all p < .001), supporting a DPT-based fast group/slow group distinction. Based on this result, the Dual-Path Backchannel Timing Prediction Model (DP-BCT) decouples the fast/slow groups into the Fast Path and Slow Path for frame-level onset and functional category prediction. DP-BCT improves backchannel timing prediction accuracy over SP-BCT, a single-path baseline, raising Macro-F1 from 0.4862 to 0.6254.

items.title: From Awareness to Adherence: Bridging the Context Gap in Spoken Dialogue Systems via Context-Aware Decoding
items.authors: Che Hyun Lee(Seoul National University); Heeseung Kim(University of Seoul); Sungroh Yoon(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Despite the success of end-to-end (E2E) spoken dialogue systems, maintaining strict context adherence in multi-round conversations remains a challenge. While prior works attribute these failures to models forgetting dialogue history, we highlight an equally critical but overlooked bottleneck: a gap between latent context awareness and active adherence. Although models internally recognize relevant past utterances, strong parametric priors often overshadow these signals during decoding. To bridge this gap, we propose an audio-adapted Context-Aware Decoding (CAD) approach. By leveraging internal attention mechanisms to isolate key historical rounds, our approach contrasts output distributions with and without this key context during inference, directly amplifying multimodal contextual signals. Evaluations on the Audio MultiChallenge benchmark demonstrate significant improvements in Semantic Memory and Self Coherence subtasks, successfully enforcing strict, context-faithful adherence.

items.title: From Reactive to Proactive: Assessing the Proactivity of Voice Agents via ProVoice-Bench
items.authors: Ke Xu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Yuhao Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Yu Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
items.abstract: Recent advancements in LLM agents are gradually shifting from reactive, text-based paradigms toward proactive, multimodal interaction. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on reactive responses, overlooking the complexities of proactive intervention and monitoring. To bridge this gap, we introduce ProVoice-Bench, the first evaluation framework specifically designed for proactive voice agents, featuring four novel tasks. By leveraging a multi-stage data synthesis pipeline, we curate 1,182 high-quality samples for rigorous testing. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art Multimodal LLMs reveals a significant performance gap, particularly regarding over-triggering and reasoning capabilities. These findings highlight the limitations of current models and offer a roadmap for developing more natural, context-aware proactive agents.

items.title: Integrating Facial Generation into Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Systems
items.authors: Jingjing Jiang(Nagoya University); Atsumoto Ohashi(Nagoya University); Ryuichiro Higashinaka(Nagoya University)
items.abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models, such as Moshi, enable natural, low-latency voice conversations. However, they remain limited to the audio modality, lacking the facial expressions that are integral to human communication. We present Moshi-Face, the first full-duplex dialogue model that jointly processes the user's audio and facial input while simultaneously generating speech and facial motion. We first construct a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) as a face codec that encodes 3D head meshes extracted from facial videos into compact discrete tokens, referred to as face tokens, and conversely reconstructs 3D meshes from these tokens. We then extend Moshi with a Face Transformer module that generates face tokens non-autoregressively, enabling Moshi-Face to produce synchronized audio and face tokens in real time. Experiments show that Moshi-Face achieves audiovisual alignment at low latency while preserving the dialogue quality of the original audio-only model.

items.title: Optimal Linguistic Complexity for Dialogue System Speech in Noise: Convergent Evidence from Automatic and Human Transcription
items.authors: Lubos Marcinek(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Jonas Beskow(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Joakim Gustafson(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Spoken dialogue systems must synthesise responses that are reliably understood in noisy conditions, yet the optimal linguistic complexity for both ASR and human listeners remains empirically underexplored. We address this gap with two studies. Study 1 measured ASR accuracy for 168,000 synthesised utterances spanning five complexity levels, two TTS systems, twelve noise types, and seven SNRs. Study 2 (pilot, N = 15) had human listeners transcribe synthesised utterances at three complexity levels across four noise environments and three SNRs. Both studies show a U-shaped pattern: natural grammatical sentences (Level 3, 9–16 words) outperform telegraphic forms (Level 1) by 43% in ASR WER and by 45% in human transcription error. The grammar advantage paradoxically grows as conditions improve. These findings reject adaptive simplification and establish a 9–19 words as optimal for system output.

items.title: Mitigating Scoring Errors and Compensating for Nonverbal Subtests in Speech-Based Dementia Assessment
items.authors: Franziska Braun(Technische Hochschule Nürnberg); Christopher Witzl(Technische Hochschule Nürnberg); Andreas Erzigkeit(Geromed GmbH); Hartmut Lehfeld(PMU Klinikum Nürnberg); Thomas Hillemacher(PMU Klinikum Nürnberg); Tobias Bocklet(Technische Hochschule Nürnberg); Korbinian Riedhammer(Technische Hochschule Nürnberg)
items.abstract: Early detection of cognitive impairment relies on neuropsychological tests to minimize subjectivity by assessing multiple cognitive domains. Speech-based evaluation can support diagnostics and improve accessibility, but transcription errors and the omission of nonverbal subtests (e.g., motor skills) limit accuracy. Beyond conventional test scores, speech-derived features can provide additional insights into cognitive status. This study investigates the speech-based evaluation of the German "Syndrom-Kurz-Test," a standardized dementia screening test comprising verbal and motor subtests. We train models that integrate transcript-derived scores and Whisper embeddings per verbal subtest to reduce scoring errors. To compensate for missing motor subtests, we then leverage these fused representations to approximate expert overall ratings. Despite omitting subtests, our models strongly correlate with expert ratings and efficiently and accurately discriminate between cognitive status groups.

items.title: HASS: Hierarchical Simulation of Logopenic Aphasic Speech for Scalable PPA Detection
items.authors: Harrison Li(UC Berkeley); Kevin Wang(UC Berkeley); Cheol Jun Cho(UC Berkeley); Jiachen Lian(UC Berkeley); Rabab Rangwala(UCSF); Chenxu Guo(Zhejiang University); Emma Yang(Columbia University); Lynn Kurteff(UCSF); Zoe Ezzes(UCSF); Willa Keegan-Rodewald(UCSF); Jet Vonk(UCSF); Siddarth Ramkrishnan(UCSF); Giada Antonicelli(Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language); Zachary Miller(UCSF); Marilu Gorno Tempini(UCSF); Gopala Anumanchipalli(UC Berkeley)
items.abstract: Building a diagnosis model for primary progressive aphasia (PPA) has been challenging due to the data scarcity. Collecting clinical data at scale is limited by the high vulnerability of clinical population and the high cost of expert labeling. To circumvent this, previous studies simulate dysfluent speech to generate training data. However, those approaches are not comprehensive enough to simulate PPA as holistic, multi-level phenotypes, instead relying on isolated dysfluencies. To address this, we propose a novel, clinically grounded simulation framework, Hierarchical Aphasic Speech Simulation (HASS). HASS aims to simulate behaviors of logopenic variant of PPA (lvPPA) with varying degrees of severity. To this end, semantic, phonological, and temporal deficits of lvPPA are systematically identified by clinical experts, and simulated. We demonstrate that our framework enables more accurate and generalizable detection models. Code: anonymous.4open.science/r/HASS-890D

items.title: Listening Between the Lines: Joint Learning of ASR Embeddings and LLM-Augmented Linguistics for Dementia Detection
items.authors: Olivier Jiyoun Jung(Ewha Womans University); Jonghyeon Park(NAVER Cloud); Myungwoo Oh(NAVER Cloud)
items.abstract: Early detection of dementia through speech analysis offers a non-invasive screening alternative, but capturing both acoustic and linguistic biomarkers remains challenging. We propose a multimodal framework leveraging Whisper for dual-purpose extraction: acoustic representations from encoder outputs and transcripts via automatic speech recognition (ASR). For the acoustic pathway, temporal networks with attention pooling aggregate variable-length sequences into fixed-dimensional embeddings. For the linguistic pathway, we prompt a large language model (LLM) to extract interpretable features spanning lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, semantic coherence, and discourse patterns. A gated fusion network integrates both modalities. On ADReSS and ADReSSo, our method achieves F1-scores of 89.47% and 90.14%, demonstrating effective integration of acoustic and LLM-augmented linguistic features. Ablation shows that multimodal fusion consistently outperforms either modality alone.

items.title: LoRA-Tuned Large Language Models for Dementia Detection via Multi-View Speech-Derived Features
items.authors: Jonghyeon Park(NAVER Cloud); Olivier Jiyoun Jung(Ewha Womans University); Myungwoo Oh(NAVER Cloud)
items.abstract: Early detection of dementia enables timely intervention, and reflecting cognitive impairment, spontaneous speech offers a non-invasive screening modality. Conventional approaches often focus on a single representational dimension—such as acoustic descriptors, pause modeling, automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts, or multimodal fusion—limiting integrative reasoning across heterogeneous cognitive symptoms. We propose a low-rank adaptation (LoRA)-tuned large language model (LLM) that performs structured multi-view reasoning over four complementary speech-derived signals: ASR transcripts with pause markers, discourse-level topic cues, temporal fluency statistics, and phonological sequences. These cues are encoded within a unified prompt, enabling a single LLM to learn a coherent decision function without modality-specific encoders or late-stage fusion. On ADReSSo, our best model achieves an F1-score of 90.14%, and ablation confirms the complementary contribution of each view.

items.title: PAN-Mask: Pathology-Aware Neurological Masking with End-to-End Learnable Weights for Neurological Disorder Detection from Speech
items.authors: Qi Sun(Tsinghua University); Junhao Fan(Georgetown University); Boao Jing(Tsinghua University); Ziqi Chen(Tsinghua University); Guodong Lin(Tsinghua University); Wei-Qiang Zhang(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Self-supervised models like WavLM advance pathological speech classification but rely on content-agnostic random masking, which overlooks sparse, localized clinical biomarkers. We propose PAN-Mask (Pathology-Aware Neurological Masking), a task-aware regularization framework. A lightweight detector computes and aggregates six interpretable acoustic descriptors via learnable attention to estimate frame-level pathology salience. By selectively masking high-salience segments, PAN-Mask discourages shortcut learning and compels the encoder to capture robust, distributed representations. Joint optimization enables the model to learn task-discriminative patterns aligned with clinical biomarkers without manual design of feature importance. Evaluated on six datasets across three disorders and five languages using identical hyperparameters, PAN-Mask yields 8.31-22.72% accuracy gains (avg. 13.82%) over random masking and provides interpretable clinical insights.

items.title: Gated Multi-graph Fusion via Graph Attention Networks for Alzheimer’s Disease Detection
items.authors: Jinyu Li(Tianjin University); Xiao Wei(Tianjin University; Chinese Academy of Sciences); Bin Wen(Tianjin University, Chinese Academy of Sciences); Kai Li(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Yuqin Lin(Fuzhou University); Xiaobao Wang(Tianjin University); Longbiao Wang(Tianjin University, Huiyan Technology (Tianjin) Co., Ltd); Jianwu Dang(Chinese Academy of Sciences)
items.abstract: Spontaneous speech is a vital non-invasive biomarker for Alzheimer’s Disease (AD), yet many systems overlook nonlinear structural disruptions and clinical heterogeneity in pathological language. We propose a Multi-View Gated Graph Attention Network that transcribes audio via Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) to construct semantic, dependency, and co-occurrence graphs, characterizing speech through a "content-structure-flow" framework. Notably, the co-occurrence graph leverages Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) from a normative corpus to quantify narrative logic and linguistic deviation. To address symptomatic diversity, an adaptive gated fusion mechanism dynamically integrates these views. Evaluated on the ADReSSo dataset, our model achieves 90.00% accuracy. Ablation results confirm that the PMI-based graph and heterogeneity-aware gating are essential for robust classification across diverse clinical populations. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/opeacc/AD.

items.title: From Echo to Accuracy: Robust Voice Quality Assessment Using Blind Unsupervised Diffusion-based Dereverberation
items.authors: Sven Franz(Jade University of Applied Sciences); Tanja Grewe(Jade University of Applied Sciences); Bernd T. Meyer(Carl von Ossietzky University); Jörg Bitzer(Jade University of Applied Sciences)
items.abstract: Objective voice quality measures are sensitive to reverberation, which limits their robustness in clinical applications. This study investigates whether blind diffusion-based dereverberation enables room-independent assessment of voice quality using Smoothed Cepstral Peak Prominence (CPPS). Anechoic voice samples from two databases were convolved with impulse responses of real therapy rooms and subsequently dereverberated. Effects on CPPS level and the rank order of voice qualities were analyzed. For low-reverberation recordings, no systematic CPPS bias was introduced by dereverberation. In reverberant conditions, CPPS reductions were compensated after processing. For continuous speech, voice quality rankings were reconstructed, and CPPS values approached their anechoic reference levels across databases. These findings indicate that blind dereverberation can effectively mitigate room-acoustic distortions in objective voice quality assessment of continuous speech.

items.title: Queer inclusion in speech datasets: An audit and taxonomy of practical tensions
items.authors: Brooklyn Sheppard(University of Calgary; Meta); Anaelia Ovalle(Meta); Adina Williams(Meta); Levent Sagun(Meta)
items.abstract: In this paper, we examine speech datasets for their inclusion of LGBTQIA+, or queer, voices and provide a taxonomy of tensions to better understand why there is a lack of such voices in current speech technology datasets. Through an audit of six diverse speech datasets, we find that measurable queer representation is low (0–1.4% of speakers) - insufficient for robust disparity measurement. We take this community as a case study to consider what challenges and tensions are associated with collecting speech data from marginalized communities. For comparison, we audit an additional two datasets from the speech sciences that were created by, for, and with the queer community. We note that many customs in speech dataset collection efforts in AI and speech technology research may conflict with values emphasized in participatory approaches with marginalized communities, and provide a taxonomy describing these tensions.

items.title: Sexualised synthetic personas encode and amplify gendered power asymmetries through voice
items.authors: Alice Ross(University of Edinburgh); Ariadna Sanchez(University of Edinburgh); Elin Kanhov(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Catherine Lai(University of Edinburgh); Éva Székely(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: This work examines sexualised AI-generated English-speaking voices offered by a popular commercial platform. New technologies may enable sexual empowerment and greater diversity in gender expression, yet toxic masculinity, heteronormativity, and the abuse of women and LGBTQ+ people remain pervasive online. Drawing on a Feminist HCI perspective, we examine how commercial voice AI systems reproduce and circulate particular performances of gender. We conducted a listening experiment with a diverse group of listeners, combining quantitative adjective selection, qualitative free-text responses, and acoustic analysis. Participants evaluated male- and female-coded voices presented with either sexualised scripts or neutral text. Results reveal a narrow range of gender expression, largely binary and heteronormative. Female-coded voices are more frequently described using sexualised and submissive terms, while male-coded voices are more often associated with dominance and positive traits.

items.title: Lived Experiences of Power and Agency: Achieving Voice Sovereignty in Assistive Speech Technology for Nonbinary Users
items.authors: Maxwell Hope(University of Delaware); Juliana Francis(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Joakim Gustafson(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Éva Székely(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Speech-generating devices (SGDs) are essential tools for many speech-disabled individuals, yet current systems often reinforce normative assumptions about identity and communication. Prior research on gender expansive SGD users has largely focused on gendered voice options, with less attention to broader identity alignment and the technological conditions that shape users' agency. This study examines how gender expansive SGD users experience power over their voices using thematic analysis of qualitative survey data. Three themes emerged: (1) integration of SGDs into daily life, (2) identity expression, and (3) power and agency. Participants expressed the need for more responsive and reliable technology, inclusive and customizable voices, and greater autonomy in defining how their voices sound and are perceived. Ultimately, their perspectives call for a reimagining of SGD systems as tools for reclaiming the power of one's voice and the ability to define and enact one's will through it.

items.title: TMASC: Transmasculine Attitude and Speech Corpus
items.authors: Sidney Wong(University of Otago; Te Pūnaha Matatini Centre of Research Excellence for Complex Systems)
items.abstract: We introduce the Transmasculine Attitudes and Speech Corpus (TMASC), a multimodal corpus of 196 transmasculine individuals, including questionnaire responses and 66 audio recordings. The questionnaire includes items exploring the vocal health of transmasculine individuals. The audio recordings include cough and throat-clearing samples, a reading passage, and additional session-specific questions. This paper outlines the development of this corpus and the data collection procedures. To illustrate the utility of this corpus, we present three case studies demonstrating how this crowd-sourced multimodal corpus can be used to support transmasculine individuals. These include the integration of perceptual and acoustic data, the identification of group-level characteristics, and the calibration of acoustic measurements.

items.title: No-Shot Text-to-Speech: Limitations of Zero-Shot TTS and its Evaluation Methods in Representing Queer and Transgender Voices
items.authors: Juliana Francis(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Robin Netzorg(University of California, Berkeley); Joakim Gustafson(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Éva Székely(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Gender expansive voices remain underrepresented in speech datasets, which could cause challenges with generalizability in zero-shot Text-To-Speech (TTS) systems. We evaluate six zero-shot TTS models on two datasets: one containing non gender expansive voices (N-GE) and one with gender expansive (GE) voices from self-identified speakers. Human ratings found that 2 of the 6 models synthesize less similar GE voices compared to N-GE voices, and 3 have improved performance for GE voices. Automated evaluations yield conflicting results, with speaker similarity and automated mean opinion score predictors rating performance of GE voices inconsistently between models and human ratings. This highlights a potential blind spot in evaluation pipelines, emphasizing a need for more representative data and metrics that better capture human perceptual judgments. Our findings stress the need to include transgender, queer, and minority communities in creation of better datasets and model training.

items.title: The First Dravidian Speech Datasets for Transphobic and Homophobic Hate Speech: Creation, Annotation, and Multimodal Benchmarking
items.authors: K N Lakshmi(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); K HEMAVARDHAN REDDY(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); A VENKATA SATYA(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); Kota Venkata VAMSHIDHAR REDDY(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); JYOTHISH LAL G(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); Premjith B(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); Jesin James(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: Hate speech targeting the LGBTQIA+ community is under-explored in low-resource languages, particularly in speech. We address this gap by creating the first Dravidian speech datasets for homophobic and transphobic hate speech in Telugu and Malayalam, consisting of an Elicited Speech Dataset and a Social Media Audio Extract Dataset. These corpora fill a critical resource gap by capturing paralinguistic cues, which are essential for identifying hate speech from audio. We additionally provide a multimodal baseline that fuses Wav2Vec 2.0 acoustic embeddings and IndicBERT linguistic embeddings using attention-based fusion, and evaluate robustness across matched, cross-domain, and hybrid conditions. Results show strong performance in-domain but degradation under domain shift, highlighting challenges in acoustic transfer. Our primary contribution is the development and analysis of the first Dravidian LGBTQIA+ speech hate-speech datasets, enabling future research on speech-based detection.

items.title: Masculinity and Sexual Orientation as Predictors of f0 Variation in the Speech of Australian English Speaking Men
items.authors: Timothy Shea(Macquarie University); Hannah White(LMU Munich); Joshua Penney(Macquarie University); Anita Szakay(Macquarie University); Felicity Cox(Macquarie University)
items.abstract: The effect of sexual orientation (SO) on the fundamental frequency of men's voices has been widely studied since the late twentieth century. Less widely studied has been the effect on fundamental frequency of men's orientations towards traditional masculinity, and no study has yet investigated the impact of either of these variables in the Australian English (AusE) context. Presented here are the results of an examination of the effect of SO and orientation toward masculinity on three f0-derived variables, using speech data elicited from 77 male speakers of AusE. Referential topic (LGBTQ vs neutral) was also investigated. Results demonstrated that none of these independent variables significantly impacted local f0, but that SO, orientation toward masculinity and topic all affected f0 dynamicity, and SO and topic both affected f0 range. In all cases, however, these effects occurred in complex interactions with each other and with speaker age.

items.title: Towards participatory speech dataset curation: A queer case study and conceptual framework
items.authors: Brooklyn Sheppard(University of Calgary; Meta); Anaelia Ovalle(Meta); Adina Williams(Meta); Levent Sagun(Meta)
items.abstract: In this paper, we motivate the need for a participatory speech dataset creation framework through a case study of the LGBTQIA+, or queer, community - a community with documented concerns about AI and reported harms, including attempts to develop 'gaydar' technologies that purportedly identify individuals as queer. We review common speech data collection practices, why these methods may be unsuitable for engaging with queer speakers, and discuss previous efforts in participatory AI with queer community engagement, as well as participatory endeavours specific to speech data collection for other marginalized communities. From this review, we develop a conceptual framework for participatory speech data curation by, for, and with marginalized communities drawing on insights from co-design and knowledge sharing. We propose a framework comprising overlapping and two-way processes of defining a community, project formulation, modes of participation, and personal autonomy.

title: Multimodal Emotion Recognition
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 3 - Oral 3 - Multimodal Emotion Recognition

items.title: Comparative Reasoning: Making an Audio Language Model Better at Comparing Emotions
items.authors: Abinay Reddy Naini(Carnegie Mellon University; The University of Texas at Dallas); Jaeyeon Kim(Carnegie Mellon University); Chao-Han Huck Yang(NVIDIA); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University); Carlos Busso(Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) can reason about audio, yet it remains unclear whether they can perform comparative judgments between two speech signals along emotional, environmental, linguistic, prosodic, and interpersonal dimensions. We study this question in the context of speech emotion recognition (SER), where the model determines which utterance exhibits higher arousal, valence, or dominance. We introduce a reasoning-guided ordinal SER framework that conditions an LALM on paired speech inputs. The model is trained using reasoning traces generated from both semantic audio descriptions and acoustic evidence derived from GeMAPS features, enabling interpretable comparative decisions. Beyond direct supervision, we also employ direct preference optimization to encourage stronger separation for emotional differences. Experiments show that the proposed framework improves preference prediction while requiring only 5% of the training data used by conventional ordinal SER systems.

items.title: Exploring the effect of the visual channel in vocal expression of affect in an Irish (Gaelic) synthetic voice
items.authors: Anna Maria Giovannini(Trinity College Dublin); Zihan Wang(Trinity College Dublin); Ailbhe Ní Chasaide(Trinity College Dublin); Christer Gobl(Trinity College Dublin)
items.abstract: This paper explores the effects of the visual context on the perception of emotion in synthesised speech. Vocal stimuli targeting the affects angry, happy, sad, bored and relaxed were created through voice source modifications to a synthetic utterance. These were combined with facial expressions targeting the same affects with the addition of interested. A perception test was conducted with the following combinations: (i) voice only (no visuals), (ii) congruent (matching vocal and visual affect) and (iii) incongruent (opposing vocal and visual affect). The initial hypothesis that the addition of congruent visual context would enhance the perception of the targeted affect received little support. While this points to a dominance of the vocal channel, the results for the incongruent stimuli underline the importance of the visual channel. A second hypothesis that the visual information would allow for better discrimination among high- (or low-) activation states was largely borne out.

items.title: ParaSpeechCLAP: A Dual-Encoder Speech-Text Model for Rich Stylistic Language-Audio Pretraining
items.authors: Anuj Diwan(The University of Texas at Austin); Eunsol Choi(New York University); David Harwath(The University of Texas at Austin)
items.abstract: We introduce ParaSpeechCLAP, a family of dual-encoder models that map speech and text style captions into a shared embedding space, supporting rich intrinsic (speaker-level) and situational (utterance-level) descriptors, such as pitch, texture, and emotion, beyond the narrow set handled by existing models. We train separate Intrinsic and Situational models alongside a unified Combined model, finding that specialized models are stronger on individual style dimensions while the unified model excels on compositional evaluation. We further show that ParaSpeechCLAP-Intrinsic benefits from an additional classification loss and class-balanced training. We demonstrate performance on style caption retrieval, speech attribute classification, and usability as inference-time reward models for style-prompted TTS. ParaSpeechCLAP models outperform baselines on most metrics across all three applications. Our models and code are released at https://github.com/ajd12342/paraspeechclap.

items.title: Daily Affect Inference from Longitudinal Speech-based Journals: A Comparison of Acoustic and Linguistic Models
items.authors: Michelle D Schlicher(TUM University Hospital); Andreas Triantafyllopoulos(TUM University Hospital); Nadine N Schmitt(University of Tübingen; FA-University of Erlangen-Nuremberg); Johanna Löchner(FA-University of Erlangen-Nuremberg); Björn W Schuller(TUM University Hospital; Imperial College London)
items.abstract: Speech-based journaling provides both acoustic cues and semantically rich content, offering strong potential for mental health monitoring. But how well do current models infer indicators such as mood and stress from naturalistic data? We introduce a longitudinal corpus of 61 speakers and 769 daily recordings, labeled with the Multidimensional Mood Questionnaire and Perceived Stress Scale, to compare eGeMAPS and wav2vec2 models with GBERT-large and zero-shot Mistral-7B-Instruct. We reveal that linguistic models clearly dominate at the population-level: GBERT reaches .122 concordance for arousal, and Mistral .466 for valence and .360 for stress, whereas acoustic results are near zero. Mistral, however, is geared towards inferring trait-like differences rather than daily speaker variations. The acoustics indicate a relation between pause variations and valence at the speaker-level. We conclude that our models are limited in their ability to monitor individuals and require personalization.

items.title: Enhancing Visual Paralinguistics: Motion-Guided Spatial Denoising for Non-Verbal Interaction Analysis
items.authors: Junjie Wan(Harbin Inst. of Tech.)
items.abstract: In Human-Computer Interaction, non-verbal cues like micro-gestures are essential for understanding human intent alongside speech. However, extracting these subtle movements in unconstrained environments is difficult due to severe visual clutter and spatial ambiguity. We propose a signal processing-inspired framework centered on a Motion-Guided Spatial Refinement Module (MG-SRM). Rather than relying solely on heavy spatial encoders, MG-SRM utilizes multi-order temporal differences to explicitly filter out static background artifacts in pose heatmaps. In addition, we introduce a Class-Learnable Fusion (CLF) strategy that adapts modality weights based on action semantics, prioritizing input streams according to the target micro-gesture. Experiments on the challenging MA-52 dataset show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance by directly improving the signal-to-noise ratio of micro-movements. Our proposed framework is highly accurate and computationally efficient, providing a robust visual frontend for multimodal conversational systems.

items.title: Modality Importance is Not Static: Temporal Dynamics via Gating in Multimodal Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Jiyeon Ryu(GIST); SeongHun Noh(Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST)); Jin-Hyuk Hong(Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST)); Woojin Kang(Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST))
items.abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition is inherently dynamic, as the importance of text, speech, and visual signals changes across time. However, most existing systems rely on static fusion, implicitly assuming time-invariant modality contribution and ignoring temporal variation. We present a temporal fusion framework that models modality importance as a time-varying, class-conditional distribution. A GRU-based module applies emotion-query gating to adapt modality weights over dialogue context. Under 6-class IEMOCAP LOSO evaluation, temporal modeling improves over static fusion (+9.01 in mean(F1, UA)), and gating further improves over temporal modeling without gating (+1.63), while outperforming Transformer-based fusion with fewer parameters. Perturbation-based occlusion and Area Over the Perturbation Curve(AOPC) provide evidence that modality importance is non-stationary across time, suggesting multimodal emotion recognition as a dynamic decision process rather than a static fusion problem.

title: Speaker Verification: Architectures, Losses, and LLMs
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 4 - Oral 8 - Speaker Verification: Architectures, Losses, and LLMs

items.title: ReDimNet2: Scaling Speaker Verification via Time-Pooled Dimension Reshaping
items.authors: Ivan Yakovlev(Palabra AI); Anton Okhotnikov(Palabra AI)
items.abstract: We present ReDimNet2, an improved neural network architecture for extracting utterance-level speaker representations that builds upon the ReDimNet dimension-reshaping framework. The key modification in ReDimNet2 is the introduction of pooling over the time dimension within the 1D processing pathway. This operation preserves the nature of the 1D feature space, since 1D features remain a reshaped version of 2D features regardless of temporal resolution, while enabling significantly more aggressive scaling of the channel dimension without proportional compute increase. We introduce a family of seven model configurations (B0-B6) ranging from 1.1M to 12.3M parameters and 0.33 to 13 GMACs. Experimental results on VoxCeleb1 benchmarks demonstrate that ReDimNet2 improves the Pareto front of computational cost versus accuracy at every scale point compared to ReDimNet, achieving 0.287% EER on Vox1-O with 12.3M parameters and 13 GMACs.

items.title: Text-Independent Speaker Verification Using Discrete Audio Tokens
items.authors: Zheng Liang(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Junjie Li(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
items.abstract: Neural audio codecs (NACs) enable efficient audio compression and have achieved success in downstream tasks such as speech synthesis. However, their discrete representations consistently underperform traditional spectral features in automatic speaker verification (ASV). We empirically demonstrate that speaker cues are implicitly preserved in discrete tokens but remain underutilized by conventional ASV training paradigms. To address this, we propose a Cross-Feature Knowledge Distillation (CFKD) framework. By guiding the codec-based student to mimic the embedding space of a strong Fbank-based teacher, CFKD provides structured supervision for effective utilization of speaker information in tokens. Experiments on the VoxCeleb benchmarks show that CFKD substantially improves the ASV performance of codec-based systems, allowing them to approach the accuracy of Fbank-based teacher models and highlighting the potential of discrete audio tokens for diverse speech tasks.

items.title: Temporal Ensembling Threshold and Neighbor-Aware Label Mixup for Speaker Verification with Open-Set Noisy Labels
items.authors: Zhihua Fang(Xinjiang University; AGIBOT); Shumei Tao(Xinjiang University); Liang He(Xinjiang University; Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: During large-scale speaker dataset collection, noisy labels are unavoidable and seriously affect model training. Existing methods mainly alleviate noisy label effects via sample selection or label correction, but for open-set noisy samples, corrected labels remain inaccurate. This paper proposes a Temporal Ensembling Threshold and Neighbor-Aware Label Mixup (TET-LM) method. This method models the embedding similarity with a two-component GMM in each epoch and calculates the ensemble threshold using exponential moving average to distinguish clean labels from noisy labels. In addition, we generate mixed labels through the neighbor-aware mechanism to effectively mitigate the correction bias of open-set noisy samples. We further design a multi-stage training strategy. Experiments on VoxCeleb show TET-LM improves system robustness under various noisy label conditions, with EER and minDCF reduced by 54% and 42% over standard methods (52% and 40% vs. the best baseline).

items.title: Mixture Consistency Learning for Robust Speaker Verification in Noisy Environments
items.authors: Seung-bin Kim(University of Seoul); Chan-yeong Lim(University of Seoul); Jungwoo Heo(University of Seoul); Hyun-seo Shin(University of Seoul); Kyo-Won Koo(University of Seoul); Jisoo Son(University of Seoul); Kyung-Wha Kim(Supreme Prosecutor's Office); Ha-Jin Yu(University of Seoul)
items.abstract: Speaker verification (SV) systems often experience performance degradation in real-world environments due to diverse noise. A common solution is to add a speech enhancement (SE) frontend; however, most SE modules are trained to reconstruct predefined "clean" reference signals that still contain remaining noise and channel variability. This can lead the SE module to restore non-discriminative factors as well, thereby degrading SV performance. To address this limitation, we propose a Mixture Consistency Learning-based Speaker Verification (MCL-SV) system. Instead of relying on reference signals, MCL-SV enforces that the sum of the separated speaker and background representations matches the original input mixture, so that the enhanced signal is aligned with the input itself in a self-supervised manner. Experiments on multiple datasets show that MCL-SV consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results among recent noise-robust SV systems.

items.title: Adapting Audio Large Language Models for Speaker Verification
items.authors: Yiming Ren(Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory); Xuenan Xu(Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory); Shuai Wang(Nanjing University); Chao Zhang(Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; Tsinghua University); Baoxiang Li(Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory)
items.abstract: This paper investigates adapting Audio Large Language Models (ALLMs) for speaker verification (SV). We reformulate SV as an audio question answering task and conduct zero-shot evaluations on public benchmarks, showing that current ALLMs have limited zero-shot SV capability and struggle in diverse acoustic conditions. To address this challenge, we perform supervised fine-tuning on SV data. A rule-based hard pair sampling strategy is proposed to construct more challenging training pairs. Lightweight fine-tuning substantially improves performance, though a gap remains between ALLMs and conventional models. We then extend the approach to text-dependent SV by jointly querying ALLMs to verify speaker identity and spoken content, yielding results competitive with cascaded ASR—SV systems. Our findings demonstrate that, with proper adaptation, ALLMs have strong potential as a unified framework for robust SV systems while maintaining general audio understanding capabilities.

items.title: Speaker Verification with Speech-Aware LLMs: Evaluation and Augmentation
items.authors: Thomas Thebaud(Johns Hopkins University); Yuzhe Wang(Johns Hopkins University); Laureano Moro-Velazquez(Johns Hopkins University); Jesus Villalba-Lopez(Johns Hopkins University); Najim Dehak(Johns Hopkins University)
items.abstract: Speech-aware large language models (LLMs) can accept speech inputs, yet their training objectives largely emphasize linguistic content or specific fields such as emotions or the speaker's gender, leaving it unclear whether they encode speaker identity. First, we propose a model-agnostic scoring protocol that produces continuous verification scores for both API-only and open-weight models, using confidence scores or log-likelihood ratios from the Yes/No token probabilities. Using this protocol, we benchmark recent speech-aware LLMs and observe weak speaker discrimination (EERs above 20% on VoxCeleb1). Second, we introduce a lightweight augmentation that equips an LLM with ASV capability by injecting frozen ECAPA-TDNN speaker embeddings through a learned projection and training only LoRA adapters. On TinyLLaMA-1.1B, the resulting ECAPA-LLM achieves 1.03% EER on VoxCeleb1-E, approaching a dedicated speaker verification system while preserving a natural-language interface.

title: Evaluation, Benchmarking, and Reliability of Audio Systems
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 5 - Oral 4 - Evaluation, Benchmarking, and Reliability of Audio Systems

items.title: CAQA-Net: Continual Audio Quality Assessment Across Speech and Music Domains
items.authors: Naiyuan Li(Ningbo University); Xiaoxun Wu(Ningbo University); Yuheng Huang(Ningbo University); Diqun Yan(Ningbo University; Ningbo University of Finance and Economics)
items.abstract: With the rapid advances of audio generation models and audio processing techniques, new types of distortions and audio domains are introduced, posing challenges to static audio quality assessment (AQA) models. Traditional AQA models cannot keep pace with the dynamic and diverse nature of real-world audio data. To address this issue, we propose CAQA-Net, a systematic continual learning framework for AQA, in which the model continuously acquires new knowledge from a sequence of tasks while retaining previously learned knowledge. The framework adopts a dual-branch and multi-head architecture that combines a trainable waveform encoder with a spectrogram-based semantic anchor. A knowledge-distillation regularizer preserves old knowledge, while a prototype-based gating mechanism supports task-agnostic inference. Results demonstrate that the proposed method successfully balances plasticity and stability, achieving performance within 0.036 SRCC (4.6%) of the joint-learning upper bound.

items.title: The First Environmental Sound Deepfake Detection Challenge: Benchmarking Robustness, Evaluation, and Insights
items.authors: Han Yin(KAIST); Yang Xiao(University of Melbourne); Rohan Kumar Das(Fortemedia); Jisheng Bai(Xi’an University of Posts & Telecommunications; Xi’an Lianfeng Acoustic Technologies Co., Ltd.); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne)
items.abstract: Recent progress in audio generation has made it increasingly easy to create highly realistic environmental soundscapes, which can be misused to produce deceptive content, such as fake alarms, gunshots, and crowd sounds, raising concerns for public safety and trust. While deepfake detection for speech and singing voice has been extensively studied, environmental sound deepfake detection (ESDD) remains underexplored. To advance ESDD, the first edition of the ESDD challenge was launched, attracting 97 registered teams and receiving 1,748 valid submissions. This paper presents the task formulation, dataset construction, evaluation protocols, baseline systems, and key insights from the challenge results. Furthermore, we analyze common architectural choices and training strategies among top-performing systems. Finally, we discuss potential future research directions for ESDD, outlining key opportunities and open problems to guide subsequent studies in this field.

items.title: Benchmarking Language Modeling for Lossless Compression of Full-Fidelity Audio
items.authors: Phillip Long(University of California); Zachary Novack(vUniversity of California); Chris Donahue(Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: Autoregressive "language" models (LMs) trained on raw waveforms can be repurposed for lossless audio compression, but prior work is limited to 8-bit audio, leaving open whether such approaches work for practical settings (16/24-bit) and can compete with existing codecs. We benchmark LM-based compression on full-fidelity audio across diverse domains (music, speech, bioacoustics), sampling rates (16kHz-48kHz), and bit depths (8, 16, 24-bit). Standard sample-level tokenization becomes intractable at higher bit depths due to vocabulary size (65K for 16-bit; 16.7M for 24-bit). We propose Trilobyte, a byte-level tokenization schema for full resolution audio, improving vocabulary scaling from O(2b) to O(1) and enabling the first tractable 24-bit LM-based lossless compression. While LMs consistently outperform FLAC and yield state-of-the-art compression at 8-bit and 16-bit, we observe that compression gains become more modest as bit depth increases beyond 8-bit.
