To reduce exposure bias, we employ a Frozen-LM Conditioning training strategy that conditions the LMs on predicted tokens from earlier checkpoints to reduce the gap between teacher-forcing training and autoregressive inference. We further apply DPO to better align outputs with perceptual preferences. Experiments on Libri2Mix show that GenTSE surpasses previous LM-based systems in speech quality, intelligibility, and speaker consistency.

items.title: Online Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction with Viseme-Guided Lightweight Visual Pretraining
items.authors: Zixuan Li(Inner Mongolia University); Xueliang Zhang(Inner Mongolia University); Lei Miao(Lenovo); Zhipeng Yan(Lenovo); Ying Sun(Lenovo); Chong Zhu(Lenovo)
items.abstract: Audio-visual target speaker extraction (AV-TSE) leverages visual information to recover a target speech signal from multi-speaker mixtures. However, existing systems are often built with non-causal architectures and incur high computational cost, which limits real-time deployment. While some studies reduce the overall complexity by designing lighter separation backbones, comparatively little attention has been paid to improving deployability by optimizing the visual branch. In this work, we revisit the design of visual cues and employ visemes as the visual guidance signal. Compared with conventional VSR-pretrained visual representations, viseme pretraining yields a more lightweight, robust, and interpretable cue. In addition, we propose an online viseme-guided TSE system that achieves strong performance under the lowest computational budget.

items.title: LLM-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Audio-Visual Speech Enhancement
items.authors: Chih-Ning Chen(National Taiwan University); Jen-Cheng Hou(Academia Sinica); Hsin-Min Wang(Academia Sinica); Shao-Yi Chien(National Taiwan University); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica); Fan-Gang Zeng(University of California Irvine)
items.abstract: In existing Audio-Visual Speech Enhancement (AVSE) methods, objectives such as Scale-Invariant Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SI-SNR) and Mean Squared Error (MSE) are widely used; however, their correlation with perceived speech quality is often suboptimal and provides limited interpretability for optimization. This work proposes a reinforcement learning-based AVSE framework with a Large Language Model (LLM)-based interpretable reward model. An audio LLM generates natural language descriptions of enhanced speech, which are converted by a sentiment analysis model into a 1-5 rating score serving as the PPO reward for fine-tuning a pretrained AVSE model. Compared with scalar metrics, LLM-generated feedback is semantically rich and explicitly describes speech quality improvements. Experiments on the AVSEC-4 dataset show that the proposed method outperforms a supervised baseline and a DNSMOS-based RL baseline in PESQ, STOI, neural quality metrics, and subjective listening tests.

title: Speech Synthesis Evaluation 2
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area7 - Oral 6 - Speech Synthesis Evaluation 2

items.title: MOS-Bias: From Hidden Gender Bias to Gender-Aware Speech Quality Assessment
items.authors: Wenze Ren(National Taiwan University); Yi-Cheng Lin(National Taiwan University); Wen-Chin Huang(Nagoya University); Erica Cooper(National Institute of Information and Communications Technology); Ryandhimas Zezario(Academia Sinica); Hsin-Min Wang(Academia Sinica); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica)
items.abstract: The Mean Opinion Score (MOS) serves as the standard metric for speech quality assessment, yet biases in human annotations remain underexplored. We conduct the first systematic analysis of gender bias in MOS, revealing that male listeners consistently assign higher scores than female listeners, a gap that is most pronounced in low-quality speech and gradually diminishes as quality improves. This quality-dependent structure proves difficult to eliminate through simple calibration. We further demonstrate that automated MOS models trained on aggregated labels exhibit predictions skewed toward male standards of perception. To address this, we propose a gender-aware model that learns gender-specific scoring patterns through abstract binary group embeddings, thereby improving overall and gender-specific prediction accuracy. This study establishes that gender bias in MOS constitutes a systematic, learnable pattern demanding attention in equitable speech evaluation.

items.title: TDScore: Learning Synthetic Speech Quality Predictors from TTS Training Dynamics without Human annotation
items.authors: Natacha Miniconi(Le Mans Université); Meysam Shamsi(Le Mans Université); Anthony Larcher(Le Mans Université)
items.abstract: Subjective listening tests are the standard for evaluating synthetic speech quality, but they are costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. Automatic speech synthetic quality predictors reduce reliance on human ratings, but still depend on large amounts of human-annotated data and generalize poorly across languages, speakers, and synthesis paradigms. This paper proposes a framework without human annotation for learning synthetic speech quality predictors by exploiting training dynamics of text-to-speech systems as pseudo annotation. Synthetic speech is collected from multiple TTS models at different training checkpoints and paired with training-derived metadata such as iteration index and loss. A quality predictor is trained from audio without human perceptual labels. Experiments on benchmark datasets covering multiple languages show that iteration annotation correlates with human annotation across datasets and languages.

items.title: Exploring Active Sampling Strategies for Pairwise Comparisons in Speech Synthesis Evaluation
items.authors: Cassia Valentini-Botinhao(The University of Edinburgh); Andrea Lorena Aldana Blanco(The University of Edinburgh); Dan Wells(The University of Edinburgh); Aidan Pine(National Research Council Canada); Korin Richmond(The University of Edinburgh)
items.abstract: Subjective tests are the gold standard for text-to-speech evaluation. Tests based on preference tasks are favoured by participants and are less prone to listener-dependent biases. Despite their advantages, preference-based tests are less widely adopted than absolute rating tests like MOS due to the misconception that all possible pairs must be tested in order for results to be reliable. In this paper, we compare different approaches for pair selection in AB and BWS tests, contrasting random selection with two active sampling methods: a sorting-based method and an information-gain-based method called ASAP. We found that the ASAP method reveals more significant differences compared to others, and that BWS tests are more effective than AB tests for the same test duration. This is evident in both number of significant differences and system rank correlation, with ASAP further amplifying the improvements.

items.title: Decoding the Ear (DeEAR): A Framework for Objectifying Expressiveness from Human Preference Through Efficient Alignment
items.authors: Zhiyu Lin(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Li Auto Inc.); Jingwen Yang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Li Auto Inc.); Jiale Zhao(Li Auto Inc.); Meng Liu(Li Auto Inc.); Sunzhu Li(Li Auto Inc.); Zhengjun Yue(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shenzhen Loop Area Institution); Benyou Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Shenzhen Loop Area Institution)
items.abstract: Recent speech-to-speech (S2S) models generate intelligible speech but often lack natural expressiveness. A key bottleneck is the absence of an objective, automatic metric of expressiveness. Existing approaches rely on subjective ratings or low-level acoustic features, which are either costly and unscalable or fail to capture perceptual nuance. We introduce DeEAR, a framework that maps human perception of expressiveness to objective scores. Grounded in phonetics and psychology, DeEAR evaluates speech along three dimensions: Emotion, Prosody, and Spontaneity. With fewer than 500 annotated samples, it achieves strong agreement with expert ratings (SRCC=0.85). DeEAR further enables scalable benchmarking and evaluation-driven data curation. Using DeEAR, we curate 14K expressive utterances to build a bilingual ExpressiveSpeech dataset and fine-tune an S2S model, leading to clear improvements in perceived expressiveness in human evaluations.

items.title: CodecMOS-Accent: A MOS Benchmark of Resynthesized and TTS Speech from Neural Codecs Across English Accents
items.authors: Wen-Chin Huang(Nagoya University); Nicholas Sanders(University of Edinburgh); Erica Cooper(National Institute Of Information And Communications Technology)
items.abstract: We present the CodecMOS-Accent dataset, a mean opinion score (MOS) benchmark designed to evaluate neural audio codec (NAC) models and the large language model (LLM)-based text-to-speech (TTS) models trained upon them, especially across non-standard speech like accented speech. The dataset comprises 4,000 codec resynthesis and TTS samples from 24 systems, featuring 32 speakers spanning ten accents. A large-scale subjective test was conducted to collect 19,600 annotations from 25 listeners across three dimensions: naturalness, speaker similarity, and accent similarity. This dataset does not only represent an up-to-date study of recent speech synthesis system performance but reveals insights including a tight relationship between speaker and accent similarity, the predictive power of objective metrics, and a perceptual bias when listeners share the same accent with the speaker. This dataset is expected to foster research on more human-centric evaluation for NAC and accented TTS.

items.title: MMGenre: Benchmarking Singing Voice Synthesis across Multiple Musical Genres
items.authors: Wenhao Feng(Renmin University of China); Yuxun Tang(Renmin University of China); Jiatong Shi(Carnegie Mellon University); Qin Jin(Renmin University of China)
items.abstract: Singing voice synthesis (SVS) has progressed rapidly, yet its ability to generalize across diverse musical genres remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks are heavily biased toward pop music, limiting systematic analysis of genre-dependent behavior. We introduce MMGenre, a benchmark for multi-genre SVS diagnosis, supported by an automatic pipeline for constructing genre-aligned music scores. MMGenre spans 10 major genres and 26 subgenres, enabling comprehensive analysis of genre-aware synthesis. Extensive evaluation of representative SVS models reveals limited genre discrimination: synthesized vocals across genres exhibit highly similar acoustic characteristics and weak separability. While zero-shot genre adaptation yields only marginal improvements, lightweight genre-specific continued training leads to substantial gains. MMGenre provides a standardized framework for multi-genre SVS evaluation and exposes critical challenges in achieving genre-aware singing voice synthesis.

title: Translation
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 12 - Oral 2 - Translation

items.title: Rubric-Aligned Disentangled Evaluation of Human Simultaneous Interpreting
items.authors: Ziyu Zhang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Satoshi Nakamura(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute,)
items.abstract: Human simultaneous interpreting (SI) is commonly assessed with analytic rubrics separating meaning transfer, delivery quality, and temporal synchrony, yet no automatic metric is designed for rubric-aligned segment-level SI evaluation. We construct a professionally annotated corpus of 1,101 SI segments with scores for meaning transfer (LQ), delivery quality (EXP), and perceived latency (LAT). We show that structured LLM prompting and scalar supervision collapse rubric dimensions, yielding near-zero correlation with human ratings and strong cross-dimension coupling. To isolate supervision structure under identical backbone capacity, we introduce dual regression heads on a LoRA-adapted COMET-KIWI encoder. On a held-out talk-level test set, the model achieves Pearson correlations of 0.388 (LQ) and 0.301 (EXP), improving over frozen COMET-KIWI. Given low absolute rater agreement, we interpret results relative to human consistency and target stable ranking signals for formative assessment.

items.title: ARTIST: Universal Articulatory Space Modeling for Multilingual Indic-to-English Speech-to-Speech Translation
items.authors: Khushal Yadav(IIIT-Delhi); Vinayak Abrol(IIIT-Delhi)
items.abstract: We present ARTIST, a novel end-to-end framework for multilingual Indic-to-English Speech-to-Speech Translation (S2ST) operating in a universal articulatory space. It utilizes a Conformer encoder with intermediate CTC supervision over source articulatory features, explicitly aligning diverse acoustic inputs with quantized, language-agnostic representations. To map these features, we introduce a Convolution-Augmented Differential Transformer decoder designed to capture both local phonetic nuances and global context. We demonstrate exceptional cross-lingual transfer across 11 Indic languages, including extreme low-resource settings (10hr/language). For instance, with only 166M parameters, ARTIST outperforms the 1.2B parameter SeamlessM4T baseline on BLEU, COMET, and chrF. ARTIST also achieves superior VRAM efficiency, establishing a high-performance paradigm for scaling direct S2ST to resource-constrained environments.

items.title: Evaluating and Preserving Lexical Stress in English-to-Chinese Speech-to-Speech Translation
items.authors: Yuchen Song(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute); Xi Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Mingze Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Satoshi Nakamura(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen)
items.abstract: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) systems have achieved impressive progress in semantic accuracy and speech naturalness. However, the cross-lingual transfer of lexical stress-a vital cue for emphasis and speaker intent-remains heavily under-explored, compounded by a lack of reliable automatic evaluation metrics for tonal languages like Chinese. We investigate English-to-Chinese S2ST stress transfer by constructing a stress-annotated Chinese dataset and an XLS-R-based Mandarin stress detector. Integrating this with the English EmphAssess system, we propose a novel objective metric for cross-lingual stress evaluation. Furthermore, we fine-tune CosyVoice3 to build a stress-aware S2ST system. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed S2ST architecture significantly outperforms existing systems in stress translation capability while maintaining competitive translation quality. Furthermore, our evaluation metric exhibits a strong correlation with human subjective judgments.

items.title: Listening or Reading? Evaluating Speech Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Speech-to-Text Translation
items.authors: Jacobo Romero-Díaz(BSC); Gerard I. Gállego(BSC; UPC); Oriol Pareras(BSC); Federico Costa(BSC; UPC); Javier Hernando(BSC; UPC); Cristina España-Bonet(BSC; DFKI GmbH)
items.abstract: Speech-to-Text Translation (S2TT) systems that cascade Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Text Translation (T2TT) are fundamentally limited by error propagation and the loss of prosodic cues. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting was introduced to address these limitations by providing joint access to both speech and transcription during generation. In this study, we systematically evaluate CoT's actual speech awareness through input attribution analysis, assessment of robustness against corrupted transcripts, and prosody-awareness evaluation. Our results indicate that CoT largely replicates cascaded behavior, relying heavily on textual transcripts. By applying simple training interventions (e.g., injecting noisy transcripts in the CoT), we demonstrate enhanced model robustness and increased acoustic reliance. Our findings challenge the presumed benefits of CoT S2TT and emphasize the necessity for techniques that help integrate acoustic information into the translation process.

items.title: A Multimodal Semi-Supervised Framework for Automatic Construction of a Cross-Lingual Taigi Speech-Chinese Subtitle Corpus
items.authors: Cheng-Hsiu Cho(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Chih-Chung Kuo(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Yu-Siang Lan(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Chao-Shih Huang(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Yan-Ming Lin(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Yuan-Fu Liao(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University)
items.abstract: The lack of labeled data for low-resource languages such as Taigi (Taiwanese) limits AI development. This work addresses the issue by exploiting online videos containing Taigi speech with hard-coded Chinese subtitles. We propose a multimodal semi-supervised framework that combines a trimodal Audio-Visual-Language Model (AVLM) with an iterative pseudo-labeling process inspired by knowledge distillation. A Vision-Language Model fuses OCR outputs and AVLM predictions to generate refined subtitles, enabling automatic construction of a large-scale Taigi speech-Chinese subtitle corpus from unlabeled videos. Experiments show that the AVLM reduces subtitle recognition CER from 36.8% to 9.3%. The resulting 860-hour corpus improves downstream tasks: Whisper's cross-lingual transcription CER decreases from 57.8% to 37.8%, and Taigi-Chinese translation BLEU doubles from 0.2016 to 0.4033. These results demonstrate an effective and transferable paradigm for low-resource corpus construction.

items.title: AfriVox-v2: A Domain-Verticalized Benchmark for In-the-Wild African Speech Recognition
items.authors: Busayo Awobade(Intron ); Gabrial Ashungafac(Intron ); Oluwatoni Otokiti(Intron ); Tobi Olatunji(Intron )
items.abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) show strong speech recognition and translation capabilities for high-resource languages. However, African languages remain dramatically underrepresented in benchmarks, limiting their practical use in low-resource settings. While early benchmarks tested African languages and accents, they lacked exhaustive real-world noise and granular domain evaluations. We present AfriVox-v2, a comprehensive benchmark designed to test speech models under realistic African deployment conditions. AfriVox-v2 introduces "in the wild" unscripted audio for all supported languages. We also introduce strict domain verticalization, evaluating model accuracy across ten sectors including government, finance, health, and agriculture and conducting targeted tests on numbers and named entities. Finally, we benchmark a new generation of speech models, including Sahara-v2, Gemini 3 Flash, and the Omnilingual CTC models. Our results expose the true generalization gap of modern speech models in specialized, noisy African contexts and provide a reliable blueprint for developers building localized voice AI.

title: Child Speech and Health
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 13 - Oral 5 - Child Speech and Health

items.title: Correct Then Detect: Zero-Shot FVMC Annotation for Child Language Sample Analysis
items.authors: Shuwei Hou(University at Buffalo); Wei Bo(University at Buffalo); Varun Shijo(University at Buffalo); Chuhui Liu(University at Buffalo); Manav Kanaganapalli(University at Buffalo); Ling-Yu Guo(University at Buffalo); Wenyao Xu(University at Buffalo)
items.abstract: The Finite Verb Morphology Composite (FVMC) is a clinically validated metric for identifying Developmental Language Disorder (DLD), yet its computation requires labor-intensive manual annotation of obligatory tense contexts. Since no annotated corpora exist for training, large language models (LLMs) have been the only approach to automated FVMC annotation. Rather than prompting LLMs end-to-end, we present the first zero-shot framework that decomposes the task into grammar correction and obligatory context detection, followed by alignment to label each context as correct, incorrect, or omitted. Evaluated on the ENNI child narrative dataset, our best configurations achieve F1 scores of 97.05%, 60.15%, and 70.23% for correct, incorrect, and omitted contexts, improving by 1.99, 4.72, and 6.21 points over the strongest LLMs as of February 2026 (GPT 5.2 and Sonnet 4.6 Reasoning Models). The proposed paradigm enables scalable, cost-efficient automated language assessment.

items.title: Detection of Incorrect Place of Articulation in Polish Sibilants Using Convolutional Autoencoders
items.authors: Wojciech Pieniążek(Silesian University of Technology); Oliwia Skórzewska(Silesian University of Technology); Maria Filipek(Silesian University of Technology); Zuzanna Miodońska(Silesian University of Technology)
items.abstract: Incorrect production of sibilant consonants is among the most common speech disorders in children, and its effective treatment depends on early diagnosis. This study proposes and investigates a method for detecting the incorrect place of articulation in productions of Polish voiceless retroflex fricatives and affricates in child speech. The approach combines convolutional autoencoders (classical, sparse, and multi-task variants) for feature extraction with support vector machines. The speech corpus included children aged 4-8 years: 149 speakers for fricative and 151 for affricate sounds. The best-performing models employ multi-task learning achieving sensitivities of up to 84.32%. The results demonstrate that autoencoder-based embeddings are effective for feature extraction and classification in challenging pediatric speech datasets.

items.title: SpiroPhonia: Non-Invasive Respiratory Health Assessment from Spontaneous Speech
items.authors: Roksana Khanom(University of Maryland); Shafia Supty(DR. M R Khan Shishu Hospital & Institute of Child Health); Nirupam Roy(University of Maryland); Ashok Agrawala(University of Maryland)
items.abstract: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) remains a major global health challenge, emphasizing the need for accessible and non-invasive detection. Since speech production is fundamentally linked to respiratory physiology, its disruptions can serve as indirect indicators of pulmonary impairment. This study introduces SpiroPhonia, a machine learning framework that leverages spontaneous speech for respiratory health assessment. We evaluated SpiroPhonia on a new dataset of 201 speakers (102 with COPD, 99 healthy controls). By integrating statistical analysis with recursive feature selection, we identified a compact set of discriminative speech markers. Our best model achieved 78% accuracy, 80% F1-score, and 87% AUC. This performance on spontaneous speech is competitive with methods using controlled laboratory recordings. Findings demonstrate that everyday speech encodes robust respiratory biomarkers, paving the way for continuous health monitoring via voice-enabled technologies.

items.title: Effects of Co-speech Gesture on the Acoustic Realization of Focus in Cantonese-speaking Children With and Without Autism Spectrum Disorder
items.authors: Zhuoran Li(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Si Chen(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yitian Hong(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Bingxin Liu(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Ho-Yi Ku(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Jiayue Gao(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Chun-Sing Wong(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Angel Chan(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Zhuoming Chen(The First Affiliated Hospital of Jinan University); Haoyan Ge(Hong Kong Metropolitan University); Bin Li(City University of Hong Kong); Li Sheng(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Po-yi Tempo Tang(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Ratree Wayland(University of Florida)
items.abstract: The effect of co-speech gesture on the acoustic realization of focus remains comparatively understudied. Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) show diﬀiculties in both prosodic focus marking and gesture-speech integration. This study investigated how co-speech gesture shapes focus prosody in 22 autistic and 25 typically developing (TD) Cantonese-speaking children. The results indicated that iconic gestures increased the duration of on-target syllables in both groups. However, TD children shortened the duration of post-focus syllables across gesture types, reinforcing the prosodic prominence of the on-focus syllable. In contrast, the ASD group exhibited distinct patterns: a duration-shortening effect was observed for both on-target and post-target syllables with deictic gestures. The results are in line with the Weak Central Coherence theory and the Enhanced Perceptual Functioning Model of ASD, which posit diﬀiculties with multimodal integration.

items.title: Paediatric-HGNN: A Hybrid Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Detecting Disfluency in Children’s Speech via Multiscale Acoustic Fusion
items.authors: Rashini Liyanarachchi(University of New South Wales); Rachael Mackay(Resourced Music Therapy); Alison Short(Western Sydney University); Aditya Joshi(University of New South Wales); Erik Meijering(University of New South Wales)
items.abstract: Automated stuttering detection (ASD) systems struggle with paediatric speech due to high acoustic variability in developing voices and the subtle distinction between pathological stuttering and typical developmental disfluencies. We introduce Paediatric-HGNN, a framework using a Сontext-aware Part-whole Interaction Network (CaPIN) tailored for paediatric data. Instead of conventional 1D signal modelling, our approach builds a heterogeneous graph capturing hierarchical relationships between lexical units (word nodes) and fine-grained acoustic segments (frame nodes). Trained on curated paediatric corpora (UCLASS and FluencyBank), Paediatric-HGNN achieves 82.4% weighted accuracy and a Typical Disfluency F1-score of 0.386. Modelling hierarchical lexical-acoustic interactions captures developmental "searching" behaviour, offering a more robust and interpretable tool for early clinical intervention.

items.title: Reasoning Beyond Transcription: Audio Language Models on Child Stuttering Speech
items.authors: Chibuzor Okocha(University of Florida); Christan Grant(University of Florida); Zoey Liu(University of Florida)
items.abstract: Child speech differs from adult speech in acoustics, prosody, and linguistic structures. Speech disfluencies (such as repetitions) further challenge automatic understanding. While Audio–Language Models (ALMs) show strong semantic reasoning from speech audio, their ability to reason about disfluent child speech in mixed-speaker settings remains unexplored. We investigate this through two tasks: child-focused semantic summarization and speech entailment. Experiments use recordings of children who stutter in mixed-speaker interviews without explicit speaker separation. Models are instruction-guided to focus on the child, preserve clinically relevant disfluencies, and avoid adult-speech leakage. Evaluation combines LLM-based judges and reference-based metrics, anchored by transcript-oracle baselines to isolate errors. Results show that while ALMs extract high-level meaning from stuttered speech, reasoning degrades significantly with increased disfluency and speaker interference.

title: Medical Dialogue and Conversational Understanding
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 13 - Oral 10 - Medical Dialogue and Conversational Understanding

items.title: Unlocking In-Context Learning in Audio-Language Models from Decentralized Medical Audio
items.authors: Ran Piao(Eindhoven University of Technology); Tsai-Ning Wang(Eindhoven University of Technology); Martijn den Dekker(Erasmus MC); Linda Moonen(Rijnstate Hospital); Hareld Kemps(Máxima MC Hospital); Yuan Lu(Eindhoven University of Technology); Aaqib Saeed(Eindhoven University of Technology)
items.abstract: Clinical audio diagnosis in low-resource settings requires models that identify conditions from minimal examples without large annotated corpora. We propose Federated Self-Contextualization (FSC), a multimodal language model framework for in-context clinical audio diagnosis across federated hospital clients. FSC constructs pseudo-label episodes via unsupervised clustering of audio representations, bypassing scarce real diagnostic labels, and enables contextual reasoning from support-query pairs. Our progressive three-stage pipeline first aligns audio embeddings with the language model via caption-based pretraining, then adapts it for episodic in-context inference through federated optimization. At test time, given a small labeled support set, the model diagnoses an unseen query through multimodal reasoning. On held-out respiratory and cardiac conditions, FSC achieves 71.6% accuracy in 2-way 2-shot evaluation, outperforming audio-language baselines by over 9%.

items.title: Speech-based Psychological Crisis Assessment using LLMs
items.authors: Terumi Chiba(Tsinghua University); Yang Luo(Peking University Huilongguan Clinical Medical School, Beijing; WHO Collaborating Centre for Research and Training in Suicide Prevention); Ziyun Cui(Tsinghua University); Yongsheng Tong(Peking University Huilongguan Clinical Medical School; WHO Collaborating Centre for Research and Training in Suicide Prevention); Chao Zhang(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Psychological support hotlines provide critical support for individuals experiencing mental health emergencies, yet crisis-level assessment largely relies on human operators whose judgments may vary with training and staffing constraints. This paper studies automated three-way crisis-level classification from authentic hotline speech under privacy-sensitive and data-scarce conditions. We propose an LLM-based pipeline that converts non-verbal acoustic cues into explicit textual evidence through paralinguistic injection, enabling a text LLM to use vocal affect that is otherwise lost in ASR transcripts. We also explore reasoning-enhanced training, where LLM-generated diagnostic rationales are used as auxiliary supervision to regularise the classification objective. With chunk-based data augmentation and 5-fold cross-validation, our system achieves a macro F1-score of 0.802 and an accuracy of 0.805, outperforming acoustic, zero-shot LLM, and speech-aware LLM baselines.

items.title: Investigating LLMs Behavior in Depression Severity Prediction
items.authors: Jiawei Yu(Utrecht University); Yun Hao(University of Groningen); Heysem Kaya(Utrecht University)
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly applied to depression assessment, yet it remains unclear whether few-shot learning provides effective supervision for depression severity prediction. We conduct a study on PHQ-8 prediction, evaluating five LLMs across 0-10-shot settings and introducing a contradictory-label intervention to test label dependence. Across models, increasing shot count yields limited and non-monotonic gains, and performance is largely insensitive to corrupted demonstration labels, suggesting that few-shot examples may serve more as structural cues than effective supervision. In contrast, replacing full transcripts with symptom-focused excerpts consistently improves performance while reducing token usage by approximately 80% per session. Prediction averaging further provides stable gains without modifying prompt design. Our findings indicate that context relevance matters more than demonstration quantity, offering guidance for cost-effective clinical deployment.

items.title: Beyond WER: A Paired Acoustic Stress Test for Ambient Clinical Scribes
items.authors: Xiao-Hang Jiang(USTC); Han-Jie Guo(USTC); Ying-Si Liang(USTC); Yang Ai(USTC); Zhen-Hua Ling(USTC); Lei Jiang(iFLYTEK); Zhi-Yang He(iFLYTEK)
items.abstract: Ambient clinical scribes increasingly combine Automatic Speech Recognition with Large Language Models to automate documentation. However, traditional metrics like Word Error Rate mask systemic safety degradation. We present a paired acoustic stress test to isolate the causal impact of noise on clinical reasoning. For the same dialogues, we inject diverse noise types while keeping the downstream model configuration frozen. Crucially, we uncover a dangerous disconnect between signal fidelity and clinical safety. Stationary ambient noise increased the Word Error Rate by a negligible 0.71 percentage points yet nearly doubled the rate of unsafe outputs. Our analysis reveals that minor acoustic perturbations can invert clinical meaning without substantially inflating error rates. Furthermore, we demonstrate a lightweight mitigation strategy that mitigates safety degradation under noisy conditions without requiring model fine tuning.

items.title: Benchmarking Speech Systems for Frontline Health Conversations: The DISPLACE-M Challenge
items.authors: Dhanya E(IISc); Ankita Meena(IISc); Manas Nanivadekar(IISc); Noumida A(Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore); Victor Azad(Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore); Ashwini Nagaraj Shenoy(NITK); Pratik Roy Chowdhuri(NITK); Shobhit Banga(Josh Talks); Vanshika Chhabra(Josh Talks); Chitralekha Bhati(IISc); Shareef babu Kalluri(MAHE); Srikanth Raj Chetupalli(IIT Bombay); Deepu Vijayasenan(NITK); Sriram Ganapathy(IISc)
items.abstract: The DIarization and Speech Processing for LAnguage understanding in Conversational Environments - Medical (DISPLACE-M) challenge introduces a conversational AI benchmark for understanding goal-oriented, real-world medical dialogues. The challenge addresses multi-speaker interactions between frontline health workers and care seekers, characterized by spontaneous, noisy and overlapping speech. As part of the challenge, medical conversational dataset comprising 40 hours of development and 15 hours of blind evaluation recordings was released. We provided baseline systems across 4 tasks - speaker diarization, automatic speech recognition, topic identification and dialogue summarization - to enable consistent benchmarking. System performance is evaluated using diarization error rate (DER), time-constrained minimum-permutation word error rate (tcpWER) and ROUGE-L. This paper describes the Phase-I evaluation - data, tasks and baseline systems - along with the summary of the evaluation results.

items.title: AuscuTSLM: Patient-Level Multimodal Question Answering from Multi-Site Auscultation Recordings
items.authors: Fan Wu(ETH Zurich); Tsai-Ning Wang(Eindhoven University of Technology); Nicolas Zumarraga(ETH Zurich); Ning Wang(ETH Zurich); Markus Kreft(ETH Zurich); Kevin O'Sullivan(ETH Zurich); Paula Manso Zorrilla(); Elgar Fleisch(ETH Zurich; University of St. Gallen); Oliver Aalami(Stanford University); Paul Schmiedmayer(Stanford University); Robert Jakob(ETH Zurich); Patrick Langer(ETH Zurich; Stanford University)
items.abstract: Auscultation is a vital diagnostic tool, yet its utility is often limited by subjective interpretation. While general-purpose Audio-Language Models (ALMs) excel in general domains, they struggle with the nuances of physiological signals. We propose a framework that aligns multi-site auscultation recordings directly with a frozen Large Language Model (LLM) embedding space via gated cross-attention. By leveraging the LLM's latent world knowledge, our approach moves beyond isolated classification toward holistic, patient-level assessment. On the CaReSound benchmark, our model achieves a state-of-the-art 0.865 F1-macro and 0.952 BERTScore. We demonstrate that lightweight, domain-specific encoders rival large-scale ALMs and that multi-site aggregation provides spatial redundancy that mitigates temporal truncation. This alignment of medical acoustics with text foundations offers a scalable path for bridging signal processing and clinical assessment.

title: LLMs and Conversational Interaction
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Long Oral 1 - LLMs and Conversational Interaction [Cross-area long papers Oral session]

items.title: WASIL: In-the-Wild Arabic Spoken Interactions with LLMs
items.authors: Zien Sheikh Ali(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Hamdy Mubarak(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Soon-Gyo Jung(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Hunzalah Hassan Bhatti(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Firoj Alam(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Shammur Absar Chowdhury(Qatar Computing Research Institute)
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) voice assistants are commonly built as cascaded Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) → LLM systems, where recognition errors can distort user intent. Dislikes may also arise from ambiguous, out-of-domain, or non-request turns, making it hard to isolate ASR effects. We release WASIL, in-the-wild Arabic spoken interaction prompts with audio, ASR hypotheses, assistant responses, and explicit like/dislike feedback, covering Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and four major dialects with their labels. We provide low-cost gold transcripts via multi-ASR agreement-guided post-editing and annotate answerability (answerable, ambiguous/needs-clarification, unsupported, not-a-request/noise) to separate intrinsic unanswerability from ASR-induced degradation. Finally, we describe scalable reference-free evaluation of responses from ASR vs. gold transcripts using multi-judge LLM scoring.

items.title: When Machines Speak Like Local Peers: Improving Conversational Experiences with Accent-Adaptive Voice Agents
items.authors: Shubhangi S. R. Garnaik(The State University of New York; Stony Brook University); JiHyun Jeong(The State University of New York; Stony Brook University); Jihoon Ryoo(The State University of New York; Stony Brook University)
items.abstract: Public voice agents often underperform for accented English, reducing usability and trust. LocalMATE is an end-to-end accent-adaptive airport conversational agent that (i) estimates a user's accent with calibrated confidence, (ii) retrieves grounded answers, and (iii) returns accent-conditioned speech with a synchronized talking-face video, using a confidence-gated fallback when uncertain. Our accent estimator (WavLM-Base-Plus with layer-weighted statistics pooling) reaches 85% speaker-disjoint accuracy on L2-ARCTIC (Indian/Korean/Spanish) and 92.3% on out-of-domain Korean-accented Speech Accent Archive. In a within-participant user study (N=20), correct accent adaptation significantly improved confidence and trust (p

items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models Abilities for Addressee, Turn-change, and Next Speaker Prediction in Meetings
items.authors: Ryo Fukuda(NTT); Takatomo Kano(NTT); Siddhant Arora(Carnegie Mellon University); Marc Delcroix(NTT); Naohiro Tawara(NTT); Atsunori Ogawa(NTT); Yuya Chiba(NTT); Atsushi Ando(NTT); William Chen(Carnegie Mellon University); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: We investigate turn-taking in multimodal multi-party conversations using large language models (LLMs). We construct an evaluation framework for three tasks: addressee detection, turn-change prediction, and next speaker prediction. We compare supervised models trained for these tasks, text-based LLMs, multimodal LLMs (MM-LLMs), and human subjects. Experiments on the AMI corpus showed that LLMs outperformed supervised models and humans in next speaker prediction, despite not being trained on the target domain and without access to audio or visual information. An MM-LLM performed better than text-based LLMs on addressee detection and turn-change prediction but remained below human performance, indicating difficulty leveraging raw audio-visual signals. Ablation analyses revealed that conversational context was critical, particularly for next speaker prediction. We observed that human and LLM prediction patterns were similar, and intervals with frequent turn changes were difficult for both.

items.title: MuVAP: Multimodal Multiparty Voice Activity Projection for Turn-taking Prediction in the wild
items.authors: Haotian Qi(KTH); Gabriel Skantze(KTH)
items.abstract: Current multiparty turn-taking models often rely on complex microphone arrays or multi-camera setups, limiting their applicability in human-robot interaction scenarios. We introduce MuVAP, a causal multimodal framework that extends Voice Activity Projection by grounding acoustic predictions in face tracks, enabling speaker-aware turn-taking predictions from a monaural audio stream and a single camera view. To address the combinatorial complexity of modeling multiple speakers, we propose Role-Relative Projection, which maps any N-speaker interaction onto a fixed current versus next floor-holder state. Because existing audiovisual datasets contain disruptive editing cuts that break causal tracking, we introduce the Audio-Visual Conversation Corpus, a 31-hour dataset of unedited, single-camera multiparty conversations. Evaluations demonstrate that MuVAP outperforms strong baselines on Shift-Hold and next-speaker prediction tasks across two-and three-speaker settings.

items.title: TurnGuide: Enhancing Meaningful Full Duplex Spoken Interactions via Dynamic Turn-Level Text-Speech Interleaving
items.authors: Wenqian Cui(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Lei Zhu(Huawei Technologies); Xiao-Hui Li(Huawei Technologies); Zhihan Guo(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Haoli Bai(Huawei Technologies); Lu Hou(Huawei Technologies); Irwin King(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
items.abstract: Full-Duplex Speech Language Models (FD-SLMs) enable real-time spoken interaction by modeling turn-taking behaviors such as interruptions and overlapping speech. End-to-end (e2e) FD-SLMs learn from double-channel conversational audio to capture natural dialogue dynamics, but their conversational quality often degrades compared to text-only models due to long speech sequences and limited high-quality spoken data. Although interleaved text-speech generation may alleviate this issue, inserting discrete text tokens into continuous dual-channel audio can disrupt temporal alignment and interaction fluency. We propose TurnGuide, a turn-level text-speech interleaved framework that dynamically segments assistant speech and jointly generates text and speech. This enables semantic intelligence from LLMs while preserving natural acoustic flow. Experiments show that TurnGuide significantly improves semantic coherence and achieves state-of-the-art performance on diverse turn-taking events.

items.title: Revisiting Active Speaker Detection: An In-the-Wild Benchmark for Generalization and Robustness
items.authors: Le Thien Phuc Nguyen(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Zhuoran Yu(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Khoa Quang Nhat Cao(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Yuwei Guo(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Tu Ho Manh Pham(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Tuan Tai Nguyen(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Toan Ngo Duc Vo(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Lucas Poon(Oregon State University); Tuan Khai Nguyen(University of Sydney); Soochahn Lee(Kookmin University); Yong Jae Lee(University of Wisconsin - Madison)
items.abstract: We present UniTalk, a novel dataset emphasizing challenging scenarios to enhance model generalization for the task of active speaker detection (ASD). Previously established benchmarks such as AVA predominantly comprise old movies and thus exhibit significant domain gaps with real-world video. In contrast, UniTalk covers diverse video types reflecting challenging real-world conditions, including underrepresented languages, noisy backgrounds, and crowded scenes, while being on par with AVA in scale. Extensive evaluations reveal that ASD remains unsolved under realistic conditions: state-of-the-art models near-perfect on AVA fail to reach saturation on UniTalk. Conversely, models trained on UniTalk generalize better to modern in-the-wild datasets including Talkies and ASW. UniTalk thus establishes a new benchmark for ASD, providing researchers with a valuable resource for developing and evaluating versatile and resilient models.

title: Speech and Language Representation
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 4 - Poster 3 - Speech and Language Representation

items.title: ECAPA-TDNN-based Speaker Embedding Framework for Voice Mimicry Assessment
items.authors: Bhasi K.C.(Government Engineering College Barton Hill; APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University); Rajeev Rajan(Government Engineering College Idukki; APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University)
items.abstract: This paper investigates the quality of impersonated (mimicked) speech by extracting speaker embeddings from both spectral and prosodic features. Prosodic features analyzed include loudness, pitch, speaking rate, shimmer, and tempogram ratio, while spectral features cover MFCCs (Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficeints), chroma, tonnetz, spectral roll-off, spectral bandwidth, spectral flux, and spectral centroid. The evaluation begins with a perception test to identify the best mimicked artist. The study then explores whether a Deep Neural Network (DNN) can predict this artist based on the Mean Opinion Score (MOS) test. A correct prediction, called a "hit", occurs when the model's output matches the top-rated artist. Model performance is measured using a top-1 ranking on the MIMICz dataset. Results show that augmented speaker embeddings derived from Emphasized Channel Attention, Propagation and Aggregation (ECAPA) embeddings outperform those derived from other embedding methods.

items.title: Do speech representational spaces encode language family structures?
items.authors: Emily Gaughan(The University of Edinburgh); Peter Bell(The University of Edinburgh)
items.abstract: Learned speech representations are known to contain information about the language spoken, but to what extent do they encode meaningful language family structure? We believe that answering this question is important if we are to incorporate knowledge of language relationships and change into future speech models, to better represent low resource languages and non-standard variants. In this paper, we compare approaches to measuring language family structure in representational spaces, when encapsulated in the form of phylogenetic trees. We analyse six existing tree comparison methods, demonstrating their complementary nature, and show that tree-based methods account for more language family structure than probing classifiers. We evaluate the representation spaces of six common speech encoders or LID models, comparing to a linguistic lexicostatistical top line, and find interesting differences between seen representations, particularly with respect to languages not seen during training.

items.title: Quantifying Dimensional Independence in Speech: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Disentangled Representation Learning
items.authors: Bipasha Kashyap(Deakin University); Björn W. Schuller(TUM University Hospital; Imperial College London); Pubudu N. Pathirana(Deakin University)
items.abstract: Speech signals encode emotional, linguistic, and pathological information within a shared acoustic channel; however, disentanglement is typically assessed indirectly through downstream task performance. We introduce an information-theoretic framework to quantify cross-dimension statistical dependence in handcrafted acoustic features by integrating bounded neural mutual information (MI) estimation with non-parametric validation. Across six corpora, cross-dimension MI remains low, with tight estimation bounds (< 0.15 nats), indicating weak statistical coupling in the data considered, whereas Source-Filter MI is substantially higher (0.47 nats). Attribution analysis, defined as the proportion of total MI attributable to source versus filter components, reveals source dominance for Emotional dimensions (80%) and filter dominance for Linguistic and Pathological dimensions (60% and 58%). These findings provide a principled framework for quantifying dimensional independence in speech.

items.title: Speaker Identity in Non-Verbal Vocalizations: Conditional Distillation and Mixture of Experts Approach
items.authors: Tzu-Chieh Wei(University of Michigan); Yi-Cheng Lin(National Taiwan University); Huang-Cheng Chou(University of Southern California); Kuan-Yu Chen(National Taiwan University); Hsin-Yen Sung(University of Southern California); Shrikanth Narayanan(University of Southern California); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University)
items.abstract: As expressive text-to-speech (TTS) and voice conversion (VC) systems increasingly generate non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) to enhance naturalness, reliable speaker verification (SV) becomes essential to objectively assess identity consistency across both verbal and non-verbal segments. Yet current SV systems generalize poorly to NVVs, and fine-tuning on NVV data causes catastrophic forgetting of speech performance. We present the first systematic study across 10 NVV types and propose a framework combining frozen Data2Vec self-supervised features with ECAPA-TDNN, enhanced by a Mixture of Experts (MoE) module with learned domain-aware routing. A conditional distillation loss on speech inputs via a pretrained teacher retains speech-to-speech accuracy, while a contrastive loss bridges the speech-NVV domain gap. Our method reduces speech-NVV EER from 38.93% to 22.66% over a pretrained baseline, and improves speech EER from 13.17% to 9.24% via distillation.

items.title: GMOD: Voice-Face Association Learning via Graph Mining and Orthogonal Disentanglement
items.authors: Jianrong Wang(Tianjin University; Tianjin Renai College); Kaibin Bi(Tianjin University); Jinghui Li(Tianjin Renai College); Ju Zhang(Tianjin University of Technology); Qi Li(Tianjin University); Ying Guo(Tianjin University); Jing Zhao(Tianjin Beiyang Rongke Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.)
items.abstract: Existing unsupervised voice-face association methods typically rely on clustering to mitigate false-negative conflicts but often struggle with unreliable pseudo-labels due to rigid prototype assumptions. To overcome this, we propose GMOD, a novel graph-based framework. First, we introduce a global similarity graph with a curriculum-guided mining strategy to capture fine-grained identity distributions. This enables the discovery of latent positive samples for multi-positive contrastive learning, robustly mitigating early-stage noise. Second, we design an orthogonal disentanglement mechanism to effectively extract cross-modal shared identity features, thereby enhancing identity consistency. Extensive experiments on the VoxCeleb dataset demonstrate that GMOD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Our code and pre-trained models are available online https://github.com/BKB00001/GMOD.

items.title: Tracing the Origins: Legacy Codec Identification in Neural Audio Transcoding
items.authors: Wonje Heo(DGIST); Shinee Youn(DGIST); Yooshin Kim(DGIST); Chuck Chae(DGIST); Donghoon Shin(DGIST)
items.abstract: Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ)-based neural audio codecs (NACs) enable high-fidelity audio distribution at unprecedentedly low bitrates through discrete token-based representations. However, this shift disrupts traditional forensics, as non-linear neural transcoding obscures the underlying traces of legacy compression. This study defines the forensic gap and proposes a Transformer-based framework designed to leverage the hierarchical and temporal dependencies inherent in RVQ sequences. By modeling inter-layer causal relationships and dynamic forensic significance, our model effectively disentangles superimposed artifacts from legacy-to-neural transcoding. Experimental results achieve 97%+ accuracy for codec identification and robust joint identification performance across 32-128 kbps. These results demonstrate that traditional codec traces persist even after neural transcoding, supporting the feasibility and necessity of neural-codec-aware audio forensics.

items.title: Hamsa: A Manually Annotated Emirati Arabic Corpus for Speech and Language Technologies
items.authors: Mohammed Alyafeai(Technology and Innovation Institute); Hamza Alobeidli(Technology and Innovation Institute); Omar Alkaabi(Technology and Innovation Institute); Shaikha Alsuwaidi(Technology and Innovation Institute); Leen AlQadi(Technology and Innovation Institute); Ahmed Alzubaidi(Technology and Innovation Institute); Maitha Alhammadi(Technology and Innovation Institute); Basma El Amel Boussaha(Technology and Innovation Institute); Hakim Hacid(Technology and Innovation Institute)
items.abstract: Emirati Arabic, a widely spoken Gulf dialect, is severely underrepresented in speech resources, limiting dialectal ASR and NLP applications. We introduce Hamsa, a manually annotated Emirati Arabic speech-to-text corpus containing 11 hours of conversational recordings across multiple emirates. All speech was transcribed and validated by native speakers, capturing natural pronunciation and regional variation. Challenges included informal speech, dialectal diversity, and background noise. We fine-tuned state-of-the-art multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models on Hamsa and achieved significant performance improvements, with Word Error Rates reducing from over 40% to below 25% for Whisper-v2. Hamsa enables dialect-aware ASR, machine translation, automatic subtitling, LLM training, and commercial applications, such as call center automation, filling a critical gap in Emirati Arabic annotated speech resources.

items.title: Sub-band Cepstral Analysis of Speaker-Specific Information: A Case Study of Japanese Word /saN/
items.authors: Shunichi Ishihara(Australian National University); Frantz Clermont(Australian National University); Can Zhang(Australian National University)
items.abstract: This study applies band limited cepstral coefficients (BLCCs) to forensic voice comparison (FVC) to identify speaker-sensitive spectral regions for the Japanese fricative /s/, vowel /a/, and nasal /N/ produced by 306 male speakers. Derived from full band cepstral coefficients via linear transformation, BLCCs allow flexible extraction of sub-band information without re-analysing the signal. Using 0.6-kHz sub-bands shifted in 0.2-kHz increments across 0–8 kHz, FVC experiments were run for each segment. The vowel /a/ and nasal /N/ outperformed the fricative /s/, and all segments showed weak speaker information in the 7–8 kHz region. Speaker-sensitive sub-bands varied across segments and were not always predictable from their articulatory or acoustic characteristics. The findings also demonstrate the effectiveness of the BLCC method in accessing and analysing any local spectral region of interest.

items.title: Hybrid Continual Learning for Low-Resource Australian Aboriginal Language Identification
items.authors: Pravina Mylvaganam(University of New South Wales); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne); Eliathamby Ambikairajah(University of New South Wales); Vidhyasaharan Sethu(University of New South Wales); Jingyao Wu(Massachusetts Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Language identification is an important step toward integrating endangered Australian Aboriginal languages (AALs) into speech technologies supporting language revitalisation and digital inclusion. However, extreme data scarcity limits model performance. Transfer learning from high-resource languages shows promise but often suffers from catastrophic forgetting when adapting to new languages. Continual learning (CL) can mitigate this issue, though it remains challenging with very limited data. To address this, we propose two hybrid continual learning methods: Replay Augmented Elastic Weight Consolidation and Constraint-Guided Knowledge Distillation to adapt pretrained speech models for AAL identification while preserving previously learned knowledge. Experiments on Warlpiri, Dalabon and Dharawal show that the proposed methods outperform fine-tuning and existing CL baselines, improving adaptation to multiple AALs while maintaining performance on previously learnt high-resource languages.

title: Acoustic Signal Analysis and Generation

items.title: Evolution Strategy-Based Calibration for Low-Bit Quantization of Speech Models
items.authors: Lucas RAKOTOARIVONY(Thales)
items.abstract: Quantization has become essential for the efficient deployment of speech processing systems. Although widely studied, most existing quantization methods were developed for vision and NLP architectures, while the specific challenges of audio signals remain largely overlooked. In particular, we show that audio activations can exhibit large calibration ranges, leading to significant information loss when standard calibration techniques are applied. To address this, we propose ESC, an Evolution Strategy-based Calibration method that formulates activation scaling as an optimization problem and solves it using a two-step local-global scheme driven by an evolution strategy. ESC enables unaltered performance under full INT8 quantization and is the first calibration method to achieve near-lossless performance for full INT4 quantization across multiple speech tasks. Integrating ESC with PTQ methods further reduces performance loss, achieving a 1% relative accuracy degradation on the AST model.

items.title: ProLAP: Probabilistic Language-Audio Pre-Training
items.authors: Toranosuke Manabe(Keio University); Yuchi Ishikawa(Keio University; LY Corporation); Hokuto Munakata(LY Corporation); Yoshimitsu Aoki(Keio University); Tatsuya Komatsu(LY Corporation)
items.abstract: Language-audio representation learning typically assumes one-to-one correspondence between audio and text. However, the relationship is inherently many-to-many: an audio segment can be described by multiple levels of specificity and vice versa. This oversimplification prevents models from learning the underlying data hierarchy. Unlike in vision-language domains, extending hierarchical modeling to audio is non-trivial due to complex sound source superposition. To address this, we propose Probabilistic Language-Audio Pre-training (ProLAP), representing inputs as probability distributions in a joint embedding space. For evaluation, we introduce two diagnostic datasets (AudioCaps-HC, AudioCaps-EC) for hierarchical analysis. Through a novel audio traversal task and inclusion tests, we demonstrate that ProLAP significantly outperforms deterministic baselines in capturing semantic hierarchy and yields intuitive uncertainty estimations, without sacrificing audio-text retrieval performance.

items.title: AdaTT: Text-Guided Instrument Timbre Transfer with Target-Adaptive Structural Control
items.authors: Dabin Kim(KAIST); Junwon Lee(KAIST); Juhan Nam(KAIST)
items.abstract: This paper addresses timbral ambiguity in instrument timbre transfer under fine-grained structural conditions. We argue this issue stems from instrument-specific expressive details in these conditions, which conflict with the target timbral properties. For example, imposing a violin's pitch-dominant vibrato contours onto a flute, which naturally exhibits loudness-dominant vibrato, impairs timbral fidelity. We propose AdaTT, a target-adaptive system that ensures high timbral fidelity across diverse timbre transfer scenarios within the ControlNet scheme. It selectively scales the frame-wise influence of pitch and loudness controls via text prompts to match the target instrument's identity. We also present a semi-automatic data construction pipeline to teach the model which expressive details to transform or preserve. Results show AdaTT achieves superior timbral fidelity and naturalness while retaining score-level content. Audio samples are available at https://dabinkim0. github.io/adatt/.

items.title: SARA: A Dual-Stream VAE for High-Fidelity Speech Generation via Integrating Semantic and Acoustic Representations
items.authors: Peijie Chen(Xiamen University); Wenhao Guan(Xiamen University); Weijie Wu(Xiamen University); Kaidi Wang(Xiamen University); Daiyu Huang(DiDi Global Inc.); Zhuanling Zha(DiDi Global Inc.); Junbo Li(DiDi Global Inc.); Jun Fang(DiDi Global Inc.); Qingyang Hong(Xiamen University); Lin Li(Xiamen University)
items.abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) relies on robust speech representations. However, current speech tokenizers face a fundamental trade-off: acoustic codecs preserve high-fidelity audio but lack linguistic constraints, causing content errors during generation, whereas semantic tokens from self-supervised learning (SSL) models ensure precise text alignment but discard some acoustic information. To bridge this gap, we propose SARA, a dual-stream VAE that directly fuses a frozen SSL semantic anchor with a dedicated residual acoustic encoder. This effectively mitigates the dilemma, creating an efficient and compact latent space without relying on complex regularizers. SARA achieves superior reconstruction quality over strong baselines. Furthermore, in downstream zero-shot TTS tasks, it yields highly natural and expressive synthesis quality, and maintains robust generation performance even under accelerated inference, offering a favorable trade-off between synthesis speed and computational cost.

items.title: BeatGain - A Rhythmic Pattern Enhancement Algorithm for Music Listening with Cochlear Implants
items.authors: Benjamin Lentz(Ruhr-Universität Bochum); Theresa Hartmann(Ruhr-Universität Bochum); Anil Nagathil(Ruhr-Universität Bochum); Ian Bruce(McMaster University); Rainer Martin(Ruhr-Universität Bochum)
items.abstract: Cochlear implants (CIs) enable speech understanding in individuals with profound hearing loss, yet music perception often remains limited. As CI users typically prefer music with a clear beat and reduced instrumental complexity, music enhancement strategies commonly emphasize vocals or percussive instruments. We propose a complementary approach that explicitly adapts to the rhythmic structure of a music signal. Percussive events aligned with the main beat are amplified, while weaker off-beat events are attenuated within a music mixing framework. Objective measures indicate reduced complexity compared to both the unprocessed signal and a baseline remixing approach. In a listening experiment, the proposed BeatGain method was significantly preferred over all reference conditions in terms of rhythmic clarity, and in all but one comparisons in terms of overall quality. These results support rhythm-focused processing as a promising extension of music enhancement methods for CI listeners.

items.title: Edit the Moment, Keep the Rest: Time-Localized Audio Editing via Instruction
items.authors: Jinwoo Jung(Hanyang University); Gihun Son(Hanyang University); Won-Gook Choi(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University)
items.abstract: Audio editing aims to modify sound content while maintaining its acoustic context. However, few studies have addressed temporal audio editing with precise control of event timing. We propose edit the moment, keep the rest (EMKR), an instruction-driven framework built on Stable Audio Open that supports adding, removing, replacing, moving, and extending. EMKR is trained with a temporal editing pipeline that constructs triplets (instruction, input audio, target audio), where the instruction carries information about when to edit. It further incorporates an explicit edit interval for precise timing and a source-event mask that preserves the original event instance in moving and extending. Experiments on mixtures from real-world datasets show that EMKR enables time-localized editing of polyphonic audio with 100 ms precision while preserving non-edited regions. This temporal control enables timing-critical editing tasks in polyphonic mixtures. Audio samples are available online.1

items.title: Repurposing a Speech Classifier for Guided Diffusion-Based Speech Generation
items.authors: Rostislav Makarov(University of Hamburg); Timo Gerkmann(University of Hamburg)
items.abstract: Classifier guidance is a way to control diffusion generation by using a noise-conditioned classifier to steer the sampling process toward a target class. One drawback of classifier guidance is that it requires two separately trained models: a classifier and a diffusion model. We therefore study a more compact alternative in which a conventionally trained speech classifier is repurposed as the backbone for diffusion generation. Starting from a frozen noise-conditioned classifier in log-Mel space, we attach a lightweight subnetwork that reuses intermediate classifier representations and train only this subnetwork under a Denoising Score Matching objective. Our work shows that a pretrained classifier can be repurposed for conditional generation, providing an appealing bridge between discriminative modeling and conditional speech synthesis resulting in high speech quality within a single-backbone model, with reduced memory footprint and computational cost.

title: Articulatory, EMG, and Visual Speech Generation
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 7 - Poster 8 - Articulatory, EMG, and Visual Speech Generation

items.title: Exploring Pre-training Benefits on Phoneme Addition through Fine-tuning in Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Masato Murata(CyberAgent; Nagoya University); Koichi Miyazaki(CyberAgent); Tomoki Koriyama(CyberAgent); Tomoki Toda(Nagoya University)
items.abstract: Transfer learning is widely used for low-resource text-to-speech. When the target corpus contains phonemes unseen in pre-training, the model must expand its phoneme inventory during fine-tuning; we call the process "phoneme addition." However, it remains unclear whether the pre-trained ability to generate seen phonemes contributes to this process. This study investigates phoneme addition in two settings: (1) a simulation setup using LLM-generated phoneme-controlled corpora that enables investigation without considering confounding factors, and (2) a real-speech cross-lingual transfer setup (English to Japanese) to validate whether the findings hold in practice. Experiments in both settings showed that while fine-tuning achieved higher naturalness than training from scratch, it required as much or more data to achieve comparable PER for new phonemes. These results indicate that pre-training mainly contributes to naturalness improvement, but offers limited benefit for phoneme addition.

items.title: ES-3DF: Editable Speech-Driven 3D Face Reconstruction via Geometry Texture Disentanglement
items.authors: Jianrong Wang(Tianjin University; Tianjin Renai College); Kaibin Bi(Tianjin University); Jinghui Li(Tianjin Renai College); Ju Zhang(Tianjin University of Technology); Qi Li(Tianjin University); Ying Guo(Tianjin University); Jing Zhao(Tianjin Beiyang Rongke Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.)
items.abstract: Speech-driven facial generation typically relies on 2D synthesis, limiting realism and applicability. We propose ES-3DF, the first framework to reconstruct editable, textured 3D faces directly from speech. ES-3DF employs a Disentangle module that decouples facial features into 3DMM geometry and UV texture maps to enable fine-grained editing. To bridge the modality gap, we introduce a Dual-Branch Alignment module enhanced by a Class-Aware Multi-Slot Memory Bank. By leveraging a novel Multi-Slot InfoNCE loss, this mechanism dynamically aligns speech embeddings with diverse, evolving speaker prototypes, significantly improving identity preservation in the latent space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ES-3DF outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy, identity preservation, and visual quality, underscoring its potential for realistic 3D avatar generation.

items.title: K-DIALECT : Korean Dialect-Aware Face-Based Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Seongyeon Yang(Sungkyunkwan University); Juyeob Lee(Sungkyunkwan University); Eunil Park(Sungkyunkwan University; Jaume I University)
items.abstract: Korean exhibits substantial regional variation, comprising five major dialects in addition to the standard Seoul dialect. These dialects convey distinctive prosodic patterns and reflect important aspects of cultural and speaker identities. However, most Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems are primarily designed for standard language, limiting their ability to represent dialectal characteristics, particularly in low-resource dialect settings. Although face-based speech synthesis provides a viable alternative when reference audio is scarce or noisy, modeling dialectal prosody within this paradigm remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we propose K-DIALECT, a multimodal face-based TTS framework for synthesizing low-resource Korean dialects. The model integrates a face encoder, a dialect-conditioned pitch predictor, and a FiLM-based fusion module. Experiments on six Korean dialects demonstrate improvements in dialectal fluency, naturalness, and modality alignment.

items.title: Feature Design and Generative Modelling in Deep Articulatory Synthesis
items.authors: Charles McGhee(University of Cambridge); Mark J.F. Gales(University of Cambridge); Kate M. Knill(University of Cambridge)
items.abstract: A deep articulatory synthesiser learns a mapping from a set of articulatory features to a set of acoustic features. A growing use case of articulatory synthesis is as an evaluation method for articulatory inversion, the process of estimating articulation from speech. To complete the loop from speech to articulation to speech, information lost during inversion must be added back in to faithfully recreate the input speech. This information can be added explicitly via additional input features or implicitly through generative modelling. However, by adding this information back into the synthesis process, the resulting speech may not be representative of the articulation estimated from inversion. In this work, we explore the impact of different feature inputs and modelling types on the output of a synthesiser, demonstrating that careful design choices are required to make claims about articulation through synthesis results.

items.title: From Tokens to Faces: Investigating Discrete Speech Representations for 3D Facial Animation
items.authors: Pedro R. Corrêa(UNICAMP; Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, GIPSA-lab); Olivier Perrotin(Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, GIPSA-lab); Samir Sadok(Inria at Univ. Grenoble Alpes); Paula D. P. Costa(UNICAMP); Thomas Hueber(Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, GIPSA-lab)
items.abstract: The choice of speech representation is critical in speech-driven 3D facial animation. Representations differ in what they encode: SSL features emphasize segmental and semantic cues, neural codecs yield latents optimized for acoustic reconstruction, and ASR-style objectives produce label-based spaces. We evaluate four speech representation families for 3D facial synthesis, comparing their facial reconstruction quality across two facial decoders using objective metrics and a perceptual evaluation. We additionally conduct probing analyses that relate tokenized representations to phonetic units and to articulatory deformations. We found that encoding phonetic classes is beneficial for accurate facial animation prediction on both semantic and label-based representations with comparable facial animation quality. From the latter, we introduce an Audio Visual Text-to-Speech (AVTTS) pipeline that leverages, as a shared space, discrete representations to decode speech and 3D facial motion.

items.title: Not Quite My Tempo: Voice Activity-aware Speech Synthesis for Lip-Synchronous Dubbing
items.authors: Alejandro Pérez-González-de-Martos(AppTek GmbH); Florian Lux(AppTek GmbH); Angelina Elizarova(AppTek GmbH); Milana Shkhanukova(AppTek GmbH); Andreas Kellner(AppTek GmbH); Mattia Antonino Di Gangi(AppTek GmbH)
items.abstract: Automatic lip-synchronous dubbing requires a speech synthesis model to generate alternating voice and silence patterns in the target language that match the timing of the source clip precisely to ensure an optimal viewing experience. Prior works address this problem by conditioning the speech synthesis process on lip movements extracted from the video signal. In this work, we condition the speech generation on a binary voice-activity signal, which has a lightweight representation and can be produced in multiple ways. We show that the model follows the voice-activity signal with high accuracy while maintaining natural prosody and semantically appropriate pause placement within sentences, as demonstrated through extensive objective and subjective evaluations. By randomly masking this condition during training, we make the feature entirely optional during inference, allowing editors to enforce or relax lip-sync constraints when desired.

items.title: GETS: Guiding EMG-to-Speech Synthesis via Silent Speech Recognition
items.authors: Jiwon Lee(Seoul National University); Jaejun Lee(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Electromyography-to-speech (ETS) offers a promising solution for voicing silent speech, yet conventional methods often struggle to achieve high semantic intelligibility. We introduce GETS, a novel framework that establishes a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) with a Word Error Rate (WER) of 11.89% on the silent EMG test set. GETS comprises a diffusion-based generative network conditioned on EMG signals, integrated with a semantic guidance mechanism derived from silent speech recognition (SSR). Our framework not only demonstrates superior semantic intelligibility by effectively disambiguating underspecified EMG inputs but also faithfully preserves the prosodic characteristics--such as temporal alignment and energy contours--inherent in the original EMG signals. This synergistic fusion of acoustic EMG cues and SSR-based semantic guidance establishes a new benchmark for high-fidelity, naturalistic silent speech communication.

items.title: Enhancing EMG-to-Speech via Silent-Voiced Representation Alignment
items.authors: Jiwon Lee(Seoul National University); Injune Hwang(Seoul National University); Jaejun Lee(Seoul National University); Eungbeom Kim(Seoul National University); Dongyub Han(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Silent Speech Interfaces (SSIs) offer an alternative communication pathway by reconstructing intelligible speech from non-acoustic biosignals such as facial electromyography (EMG). In particular, EMG can capture muscle activity associated with articulatory movements even in the absence of vocalization, serving as a suitable modality for silent speech synthesis. A major challenge in EMG-to-speech (ETS) research is the natural absence of ground-truth speech for silent EMG, along with the scarcity of available data. To address this, we propose a novel Silent-Voiced Alignment (SVA) loss, which introduces a multi-level representation-based alignment objective between utterance-parallel silent and voiced EMG pairs. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly enhances content reconstruction and can be seamlessly integrated into existing ETS frameworks. Furthermore, we demonstrate enhanced intelligibility and robustness under a standardized evaluation protocol.

items.title: Automatic pitch prediction from speech articulation: Where does the f0 information come from?
items.authors: Beliz Ozkan(Université Grenoble Alpes); Jonas Michael(Université Grenoble Alpes); Thomas Hueber(Université Grenoble Alpes); Olivier Perrotin(Université Grenoble Alpes)
items.abstract: While source-filter theory posits independence between the glottal source and vocal tract, empirical studies on silent speech interfaces predict fo from articulatory data. Using a multi-speaker dataset, we found that ultrasound tongue images alone do enable partial fo prediction. To resolve this paradox, we tested four hypotheses. We found no evidence that fo prediction (1) relies on a specific structure other than the tongue (or lips); (2) benefits from increased temporal context. However, (3) models trained on isolated utterances failed to generalise to spontaneous speech. Most importantly, (4) prominent words were predicted more accurately by capturing local correlations between fo and articulatory dynamics. These findings, corroborated by a perceptive experiment, highlight the need for realistic conversational training data and a focus on predicting local prosodic functions—rather than replicating global fo trajectories—to better capture the pragmatic role of fo in communication.

items.title: Speaker-Independent Speech Synthesis from Real-time MRI Articulatory Data
items.authors: Yuto Otani(Tokyo University of Science); Shun Sawada(Nippon Institute of Technology); Hidefumi Ohmura(Tokyo University of Science); Kouichi Katsurada(Tokyo University of Science)
items.abstract: This paper proposes a speaker-independent speech synthesis method that generates speech waveforms from real-time MRI (rtMRI) videos. The proposed model uses EfficientNetV2 for per-frame feature extraction, E-Branchformer for temporal modeling, and BigVGAN-v2 for speech synthesis. Speaker characteristics are acquired from rtMRI videos through cross-modal training with speaker embeddings, enabling speaker-independent synthesis from rtMRI videos alone. Experiments using the USC 75-Speaker Speech MRI Database demonstrate that the proposed method achieves favorable linguistic accuracy for read speech in a speaker-independent setting. F0 correlation analysis indicates that relative prosodic patterns are captured to a reasonable extent, as expected from visual articulatory information, though absolute F0 estimation remains challenging. Speaker similarity results show that although within-gender speaker discrimination proved difficult, speaker identity is reproduced to a reasonable degree.

title: Robust ASR: Hallucinations and Biases
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 8 - Poster 5 - Robust ASR: Hallucinations and Biases

items.title: From Dispersion to Attraction: Spectral Dynamics of Hallucination Across Whisper Model Scales
items.authors: Ivan Viakhirev(Mechanics and Optics University); Kirill Borodin(Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics; BitmanagerAI); Grach Mkrtchian(Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics)
items.abstract: Hallucinations in large ASR models present a critical safety risk. In this work, we propose the Spectral Sensitivity Theorem, which predicts a phase transition in deep networks from a dispersive regime (signal decay) to an attractor regime (rank-1 collapse) governed by layer-wise gain and alignment. We validate this theory by analyzing the eigenspectra of activation graphs in Whisper models (Tiny to Large-v3-Turbo) under adversarial stress. Our results are consistent with the theoretical prediction: intermediate models exhibit Structural Disintegration (Regime I), characterized by a 13.4% collapse in Cross-Attention rank. Conversely, large models enter a Compression-Seeking Attractor state (Regime II), where Self-Attention actively compresses rank (-2.34%) and hardens the spectral slope, decoupling the model from acoustic evidence.

items.title: Error Diversity and Performance Variability in Zero-Shot Children's Speech Recognition
items.authors: Abhijit Sinha(NIT Sikkim); Hemant Kumar Kathania(NIT Sikkim); Paban Sapkota(NIT Sikkim); Mikko Kurimo(Aalto University)
items.abstract: Children's speech recognition remains challenging due to acoustic variability and limited labeled data. This study analyzes the behavior of self-supervised learning (SSL) representations for children's speech recognition under a strict zero-shot adult-to-child transfer setting.
